records.title: Epidemiology
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: Breast cancer is the commonest cancer in women by both incidence and mortality, worldwide and in Singapore. The WHO recorded 2.3 million women diagnosed and 670,000 deaths globally in 2022. Incidence is rising while mortality has remained stable or improved. Male breast cancer accounts for approximately 1% of all breast cancers, usually presents above the age of 60, and may be associated with BRCA2 .

records.title: Risk factors
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: Non-modifiable Risk rises with age. US SEER estimates of the probability of developing breast cancer are 2.1% from birth to age 49 (1 in 49), 2.5% from 50 to 59 (1 in 42), 3.5% from 60 to 69 (1 in 28), 7% from 70 onwards (1 in 14), and 12.9% over a lifetime (1 in 8). Breast cancer is approximately 100 times more frequent in women than in men. Mammographic breast density reflects the proportion of glandular and connective tissue to adipose tissue. Dense tissue occupying 75% or more of the breast carries a higher cancer risk than lower densities. Density is largely an inherited trait, but is also associated with lower physical activity and a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet. Reproductive factors that increase risk are earlier menarche, later menopause, nulliparity, increasing age at first full-term pregnancy, and absence of breastfeeding. A personal history of breast cancer raises the risk of a contralateral cancer. In SEER data, invasive contralateral breast cancer occurred in 4% of patients over an average 7.5 years of follow-up (Nichols et al, J Clin Oncol 2011). A personal history of proliferative breast lesions with atypia (atypical ductal hyperplasia, atypical lobular hyperplasia, LCIS) carries risk independently. Family history carries a graded risk (Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer, Lancet 2001): one affected first-degree relative, twofold; that relative diagnosed before age 30, threefold; that relative diagnosed after age 60, 1.5-fold; two affected first-degree relatives, threefold. High-penetrance germline genes are BRCA1 and BRCA2 , TP53 (Li-Fraumeni), STK11 (Peutz-Jeghers), PTEN (PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome), CDH1 (hereditary diffuse gastric and lobular breast cancer), PALB2 , and the Lynch syndrome genes. BRCA1 carriers are more likely to develop triple-negative disease (70%) and BRCA2 carriers hormone receptor-positive disease (70%). Moderate-penetrance genes include CHEK2 , ATM , BARD1 and RAD51 . A history of therapeutic ionising radiation also raises risk, typically mantle or chest radiotherapy for childhood Hodgkin lymphoma. Modifiable Higher body mass index and perimenopausal weight gain are consistently associated with higher risk in postmenopausal women. In a meta-analysis, each 5 kg of adult weight gain carried a relative risk of 1.11 for postmenopausal breast cancer (95% CI 1.08–1.13; JNCI 2015). The mechanism is presumed to be higher oestrogen levels from peripheral conversion of oestrogen precursors in adipose tissue. The relationship inverts before the menopause, and the explanation is unclear. In pooled individual-level data from the Premenopausal Breast Cancer Collaborative Group, the highest body mass index category at ages 18 to 24 (≥35.0) carried lower risk than the lowest (<17.0), a 4.2-fold gradient (HR 0.24, 95% CI 0.14–0.40; JAMA Oncol 2018). Higher endogenous oestrogen levels raise risk, as does exogenous hormone exposure. The Women's Health Initiative randomised 16,608 postmenopausal women to oestrogen plus progestin or placebo and was stopped after 5.2 years because of an increased risk of invasive breast cancer (HR 1.26; JAMA 2022). Current or recent oral contraceptive use raises risk, and the association disappears within 2 to 5 years of stopping. Smoking and alcohol use also raise risk. Risk prediction models All three models in common use were created and validated in largely White populations, which limits their calibration elsewhere. The Gail model (BCRAT) calculates absolute risk from three ages, two breast variables and one family variable: current age, age at menarche and age at first live birth; number of previous breast biopsies and whether atypical hyperplasia was found; and the number of affected maternal first-degree relatives, together with race and ethnicity. It returns 5-year and lifetime risk of invasive breast cancer, and a 5-year risk above 1.7% defines the increased-risk group. Gail is not suitable for women with a history of breast cancer, DCIS or LCIS, for women with prior chest radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma, or where the history suggests a germline mutation. Two limitations follow from its inputs: it counts only maternal first-degree relatives, so it underestimates risk in the half of families whose cancers lie in the paternal line, and it ignores the age at which the relative was diagnosed. Sensitivity is 28–44% and specificity 66–88%. The Claus model estimates familial risk only and includes no non-hereditary risk factors; concordance between Gail and Claus is low. Tyrer-Cuzick (IBIS) incorporates family history of breast and ovarian cancer beyond first-degree relatives, is intended for women with no history of breast cancer, and returns 10-year and lifetime risk together with the probability of carrying a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation. It generally predicts higher risks than the other models.

records.title: Proliferative and in-situ lesions
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: Proliferative lesions are divided by whether atypia is present. Atypical hyperplasia, ductal or lobular, is usually diagnosed incidentally on biopsy of microcalcifications and raises the risk of both ipsilateral and contralateral cancer. Flat epithelial atypia is also usually incidental, and raises the risk of DCIS and invasive cancer. DCIS and LCIS are distinguished by growth pattern and cytological features rather than by their anatomic location within the ductal-lobular system. DCIS is a proliferation of malignant epithelial cells within the mammary ductal system with no invasion of the surrounding stroma. It differs from lobular carcinoma in radiological appearance, morphology, biological behaviour and anatomic distribution. Five architectural types are described: comedo, which is the type most often associated with invasion, papillary, micropapillary, cribriform and solid. LCIS arises from the lobule at the terminal end of the duct and is distributed diffusely through the breast, so it usually presents without a palpable mass. It is indolent, has low malignant potential, and is not managed as a precursor lesion; it confers risk of subsequent invasive cancer in either breast. Two consequences follow for a core biopsy result: excise any non-classical LCIS (pleomorphic LCIS, or LCIS with necrosis), and any LCIS with imaging-pathological discordance; observe incidental classical LCIS with concordant imaging and no other high-risk lesion requiring excision, with clinical and imaging follow-up decided on risk assessment and multidisciplinary input.

records.title: Invasive carcinoma
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: Grading Invasive carcinoma is graded by the Nottingham criteria, which score gland formation, nuclear atypia and mitotic count from 1 to 3 each. A total of 3–5 is grade 1, 6–7 grade 2 and 8–9 grade 3. Score 1 2 3 Gland (acinus) formation >75% of the carcinoma forming glandular or tubular structures 10–75% forming glandular or tubular structures <10% forming glandular or tubular structures Nuclear atypia / pleomorphism Small nuclei, little increase in size over normal breast epithelium, regular outlines, uniform chromatin, little variation in size Cells larger than normal, open vesicular nuclei, visible nucleoli, moderate variation in size and shape Vesicular nuclei, often prominent nucleoli, marked variation in size and shape, occasionally very large and bizarre forms Mitotic count Cells with definite mitoses in 10 consecutive fields, scored 1 to 3 Histological subtypes Invasive carcinoma of no special type, the category formerly reported as invasive ductal carcinoma, accounts for 76% of invasive breast cancer and tends to metastasise via the lymphatics. Invasive lobular carcinoma accounts for 8%. Compared with ductal carcinoma it is more often bilateral and multicentric, arises in older women, is larger and better differentiated, and metastasises later and to unusual sites including the peritoneum, meninges and gastrointestinal tract. It is associated with CDH1 mutation, and loss of E-cadherin staining distinguishes it from ductal carcinoma. Four special types carry a more favourable prognosis than ductal or lobular carcinoma. Mucinous (colloid) carcinoma, 2.4%, presents later in life as a palpable mass or as a poorly defined mammographic tumour with rare calcifications; it tends to be well circumscribed, and mucin production is the histological hallmark. Tubular carcinoma, 7%, shows a single layer of epithelial cells with low-grade nuclei and apical cytoplasmic snouting arranged in well-formed tubules and glands, with a low incidence of nodal involvement and high overall survival. Cribriform carcinoma. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is morphologically similar to salivary gland tumours, spreads to nodes in fewer than 5% of cases, and is usually triple-negative. The remaining histologies are heterogeneous. Tubulolobular carcinoma has hybrid features of tubular carcinoma and invasive lobular carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry implies a ductal phenotype, but it behaves like lobular carcinoma and tends to be multifocal or multicentric. Papillary carcinoma, 1%, comes in a cystic non-invasive form and an invasive micropapillary ductal form. It is centrally located, may present with bloody nipple discharge, is strongly ER/PR-positive, and involves nodes frequently. Metaplastic carcinoma covers a wide range of patterns including spindle-cell carcinoma, carcinosarcoma, squamous carcinoma of ductal origin, adenosquamous carcinoma, carcinoma with pseudosarcomatous metaplasia and matrix-producing carcinoma. It is larger and faster-growing, commonly node-negative, and typically triple-negative. Phyllodes tumour, under 1%, is classified benign, borderline or malignant on stromal cellularity, infiltration at the tumour edge and mitotic activity. Malignant phyllodes behaves like a sarcoma and metastasises haematogenously, which is why wide local excision is the priority; chemotherapy and radiotherapy are not effective in recurrent or metastatic disease. Mammary Paget disease is intraepithelial adenocarcinoma within the epidermis of the nipple-areola complex. It is predominantly unilateral and develops insidiously as a scaly, fissured, oozing or erythematous nipple-areola complex, often with retraction or ulceration and with itch, tingling, burning or pain. Underlying in-situ or invasive breast cancer is present in more than 85% of cases, frequently without a palpable mass or mammographic abnormality. Treatment follows the underlying breast pathology, and where none is found it follows the DCIS pathway. Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive locally advanced presentation, with nodal involvement and distant metastases common at diagnosis. It is defined clinically rather than histologically, and dermal lymphatic invasion by tumour cells is seen on skin punch biopsy.

records.title: Molecular subtypes
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: Luminal A, 40%, is the commonest subtype and carries the best prognosis. It shows high expression of ER genes, low expression of HER2 genes, and low expression of proliferation-related genes and TP53 , and typically expresses cytokeratins 8 and 18. Luminal B, 20%, shows lower ER expression than luminal A, variable HER2 expression and high expression of proliferation genes, and also expresses cytokeratins 8 and 18. Prognosis is worse than luminal A and most have high recurrence scores. HER2-enriched, 10–15%, shows high expression of HER2 and proliferation gene clusters with low expression of luminal and basal clusters, and is often ER/PR-negative. HER2 signalling drives proliferation, resistance to apoptosis, cell motility and neoangiogenesis. Basal, 10–15%, is triple-negative in most cases, shows high expression of proliferation genes, and is strongly associated with BRCA1 and with sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents such as platinums.

records.title: Receptor assessment
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: A prognostic factor gives information about outcome independent of therapy, such as nodal status, Ki-67 or triple-negative histology. A predictive factor gives information about the likelihood of response to a particular treatment: hormone receptor status predicts response to endocrine therapy, and HER2 status predicts response to HER2-directed therapy. Both hormone receptor and HER2 assessment are therefore run on every invasive cancer, and repeated on a biopsy of recurrent or metastatic disease. Hormone receptors ER and PR are assessed by immunohistochemistry and reported as positive when staining is present in 1% or more of tumour cells. Staining in 1 to 10% of cells is reported as ER-low positive. The Allred score, which sums a proportion score and an intensity score, is the alternative semiquantitative report. HER2 HER2 is both prognostic and predictive. It is a member of the EGFR tyrosine kinase family of four transmembrane receptor proteins (EGFR1, HER2, HER3, HER4). Receptor activation, by ligand binding or by ligand-independent homo- or heterodimerisation, stimulates cellular growth, survival, migration and angiogenesis. A cancer is HER2-positive on immunohistochemistry of 3+, or on demonstrated gene amplification by in-situ hybridisation. Immunohistochemistry is scored on the completeness and intensity of membrane staining and the proportion of invasive tumour cells stained. Score Staining 0 No staining, or incomplete membrane staining in ≤10% of tumour cells 1+ Incomplete membrane staining in >10% of tumour cells 2+ (equivocal) Weak or moderate complete membrane staining in >10% of invasive tumour cells 3+ (positive) Uniform intense membrane staining in >10% of invasive tumour cells The 3+ threshold was 30% before it was revised to 10%. Dual-probe in-situ hybridisation counts HER2 gene copies against the chromosome 17 centromeric probe. Amplification is present, and the cancer is HER2-positive, when the HER2:CEP17 ratio is 2.0 or above and the average HER2 copy number is 4.0 or more signals per cell; a ratio below 2 with fewer than 4 signals per nucleus is negative. The remaining three combinations are equivocal and are retested. The recount resolves them as follows: Copy number below 4 with a ratio of 2 or above: HER2-negative with a comment. Copy number 6 or above with a ratio below 2: HER2-positive. Copy number 4 to 6 with a ratio below 2: HER2-negative with a comment. The final report on an equivocal specimen follows the concurrent HER2 immunohistochemistry together with the recount, not the counts alone. HER2-low and HER2-ultralow A HER2 immunohistochemistry score below 3+ is no longer a single negative category. HER2-low means immunohistochemistry of 1+, or 2+ with negative in-situ hybridisation; HER2-ultralow means a score of 0 with faint incomplete membrane staining in 10% or fewer cells, which the conventional scale does not separate from a complete absence of staining. DESTINY-Breast04 established HER2-low as a targetable category in previously treated advanced disease (N Engl J Med 2022;387:9-20), and DESTINY-Breast06 moved it into chemotherapy-naive hormone receptor-positive disease after at least one endocrine line, with an exploratory HER2-ultralow cohort (N Engl J Med 2024;391:2110-2122). The consequence for reporting is that a score of 0 must be distinguished from 1+, and faint incomplete staining recorded rather than reported as absent.

records.title: Genomic assays
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: Genomic assays are used in hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer to estimate recurrence risk and, for one assay, the benefit expected from adding chemotherapy. Oncotype DX is the only one validated as predictive of chemotherapy benefit; the others are prognostic. Oncotype DX is an RT-PCR platform reading 16 cancer-related and 5 reference genes, modelled into a recurrence score from 0 to 100. Paik et al. (NSABP B-20 validation) tested archived tissue from both randomised arms of NSABP B-20, in node-negative, ER-positive disease, and showed that the score predicts the magnitude of chemotherapy benefit, not only prognosis: a high score (≥31) carried a large benefit (relative risk 0.26, 95% CI 0.13–0.53; absolute 10-year distant recurrence reduction 27.6%) and a low score (<18) carried minimal benefit (relative risk 1.31, 95% CI 0.46–3.78; absolute difference −1.1%), with a significant interaction between score and chemotherapy (P=0.038; J Clin Oncol 2006;24:3726-3734). Two prospective trials define where the score can be acted on. TAILORx randomised the 6,711 women (69%) with a midrange score of 11–25 and node-negative disease, and endocrine therapy alone was non-inferior to chemoendocrine therapy for invasive disease-free survival (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.94–1.24, P=0.26; 9-year invasive disease-free survival 83.3% vs 84.3%; N Engl J Med 2018;379:111-121). A prespecified age interaction (P=0.004) left residual chemotherapy benefit in women aged 50 or younger with a score of 16–25. RxPONDER (SWOG S1007) extended the assay to 1–3 positive nodes with a score of 25 or below. The score-by-treatment interaction was not significant (P=0.35), so the score stayed prognostic but stopped predicting relative chemotherapy benefit, and a prespecified menopausal-status interaction became the governing variable (P=0.008): postmenopausal women derived no benefit (invasive disease-free survival HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.82–1.26, P=0.89) and premenopausal women a clear one (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.43–0.83, P=0.002; N Engl J Med 2021;385:2336-2347). MammaPrint is a 70-gene signature returning a binary low or high genomic risk. It is prognostic only, validated on FFPE tissue for tumours of 5 cm or less with 0 to 3 involved nodes, regardless of receptor status and menopausal status. MINDACT tested it against clinicopathological risk. Among the 1,550 women (23.2%) at high clinical but low genomic risk who forwent chemotherapy, 5-year survival without distant metastasis was 94.7% (95% CI 92.5–96.2), clearing the prespecified 92% boundary; the secondary randomised comparison within that discordant group was underpowered (95.9% vs 94.4%; adjusted HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.50–1.21, P=0.27; N Engl J Med 2016;375:717-729). PAM50 assigns intrinsic subtype and generates a risk-of-recurrence score. Luminal A tumours by PAM50 have a very good prognosis without chemotherapy, whereas luminal B tumours are more likely to recur on endocrine therapy alone. OPTIMA tested risk-of-recurrence-directed treatment in high clinical-risk disease, most of it node-positive, and found it non-inferior to standard chemotherapy (5-year invasive breast cancer-free survival 90.4% vs 91.5%, HR 0.99, 90% CI 0.81–1.20, non-inferiority P=0.013), with 68% of patients falling in the low-score group; this is an ASCO 2026 abstract rather than a full publication (J Clin Oncol 2026;44(suppl):500). ASTER 70s tested the genomic grade index in women aged 70 or older with genomically high-risk ER-positive, HER2-negative disease, and adding chemotherapy did not significantly improve 8-year overall survival (72.7% vs 68.3%, HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.63–1.11, P=0.21) while grade 3 or higher adverse events rose from 9% to 34% (Lancet 2025;406:489-500). Risk calculators such as NHS Predict estimate recurrence and mortality risk and the benefit expected from chemotherapy, but they do not account for all biomarkers or for the interaction between tumour biology and treatment effect, and they do not substitute for a molecular assay.

records.title: Pathological response after neoadjuvant therapy
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: Where systemic therapy is given before surgery, the resection specimen is reported for residual disease. CTNeoBC pooled analysis settled which specimen state to report: clearing tumour from both breast and nodes (ypT0 ypN0 or ypT0/is ypN0) predicted overall survival better (HR 0.36 for both) than clearing the breast alone (ypT0/is, HR 0.51; Lancet 2014;384:164-172). At patient level, pCR defined as ypT0/is ypN0 predicted event-free survival (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.43–0.54) and overall survival (HR 0.36, 0.31–0.42), most strongly in triple-negative disease (event-free survival HR 0.24) and in HER2-positive, hormone-receptor-negative disease treated with trastuzumab (HR 0.15). Residual Cancer Burden (Symmans) grades what remains rather than treating all non-pCR specimens as one bin, using a continuous index with predefined cut points at 1.36 and 3.28 to give classes RCB-0 (pCR) through RCB-III (J Clin Oncol 2017;35:1049-1060). It is a pooled five-cohort single-institution validation rather than a randomised trial, and the index is prognostic only. Better pathological response at trial level does not guarantee better survival, and the strength of pCR as a surrogate differs by subtype.

records.title: Clinical presentation
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: Presentation is by screen-detected mammographic abnormality, a breast mass, skin changes, or symptoms of metastatic disease. The commonest metastatic sites are bone (back or leg pain), liver (abdominal pain, nausea, jaundice) and lung (breathlessness, cough). Brain metastases are more common in the HER2-enriched and basal intrinsic subtypes. Imaging features that raise suspicion differ by modality: mammography: spiculated mass, high density; ultrasound: hypoechogenicity, internal calcification, shadowing, a lesion taller than wide, and spiculated, indistinct or angular margins; contrast-enhanced MRI: irregular or spiculated margins, heterogeneous internal enhancement, enhancing internal septa. Tissue is obtained by core biopsy of the tumour; fine-needle aspiration is sufficient for axillary nodes.

records.title: Staging
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: Staging follows the AJCC 8th edition. T is defined by size, and the criteria are identical for clinical and pathological staging. Inflammatory breast cancer is staged as T4d. All four of the following are required: rapid onset of breast erythema, oedema or peau d'orange, or a warm breast, with or without a palpable mass; a history of less than 6 months; erythema involving at least one third of the breast; pathological confirmation of invasive carcinoma. AJCC 8 carries two parallel stage assignments. The anatomic stage is TNM alone. The prognostic stage combines TNM with histological grade (G1–3) and ER, PR and HER2 status, so a small high-grade triple-negative tumour and a small low-grade hormone receptor-positive tumour of the same size no longer share a stage. The recurrence score enters the prognostic stage in one defined situation: in T1 or T2, N0, M0 disease that is HER2-negative and ER-positive, an Oncotype DX result below 11 assigns prognostic stage IA.

records.title: Work-up
records.subtitle: Breast cancer: histopathology, receptor assessment and staging · Breast
records.body: Staging investigations in non-metastatic disease are directed by symptoms and biochemistry: bone scan for bone pain or a raised alkaline phosphatase; CT abdomen and pelvis for abnormal liver function tests, a raised alkaline phosphatase, abdominal pain or an abnormal abdominopelvic examination; CT thorax for pulmonary symptoms; whole-body PET-CT, or bone scan with CT thorax/abdomen/pelvis, from stage IIIA upwards. In non-metastatic disease (cT1-3, cN0 or above, M0) the work-up also determines whether the patient is a candidate for neoadjuvant systemic therapy. Where pre-operative therapy is being considered, add axillary ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration of suspicious nodes, and CT thorax/abdomen/pelvis and bone scan as clinically indicated. Stage IV or recurrent disease requires CT thorax, CT or MRI abdomen and pelvis, MRI brain if CNS symptoms are present, MRI spine for back pain or symptoms of cord compression, and bone scan with plain radiographs of symptomatic bones. Biopsy recurrent disease and re-evaluate ER, PR and HER2 status on that specimen.
