records.title: Biology and natural history
records.subtitle: Ductal carcinoma in situ · Breast
records.body: Ductal carcinoma in situ is a proliferation of presumably malignant epithelial cells confined within the mammary ductal system, with no invasion of the surrounding stroma. Treatment is directed at preventing progression to invasive carcinoma, and the risk of that progression exceeds 50%. Grade is assigned on nuclear features as low (G1), intermediate (G2) or high (G3). Low-grade and high-grade lesions differ in ploidy, receptor status, proliferation and the HER2 and p53 abnormalities they carry. Low-grade lesions are diploid and ER/PR positive, have a low proliferative rate, and rarely carry HER2 or p53 abnormalities. High-grade lesions are aneuploid and ER/PR negative, have a high proliferative rate, overexpress HER2 and carry p53 mutations. The prognostic features are tumour size, necrosis, nuclear grade and the width of the surgical margin. A core biopsy diagnosis of DCIS understates the disease in a substantial minority: invasive carcinoma is found in 10–20% of excision specimens. That upstaging rate is the reason sentinel node biopsy is considered at the time of surgery.

records.title: Diagnosis and work-up
records.subtitle: Ductal carcinoma in situ · Breast
records.body: Work-up establishes nuclear grade and ER status. ER status does not alter local treatment; it determines whether endocrine therapy for risk reduction is worth offering. The role of breast MRI is unclear. Prospective data give a sensitivity of up to 98% for high-grade DCIS, but MRI overestimates disease extent, and it has not been shown to increase the rate of negative margins or to reduce conversion to mastectomy. Do not decide on mastectomy from MRI findings alone. Where MRI suggests more extensive disease than mammography, such that a markedly larger resection would be needed for complete excision, confirm the extra disease histologically by MRI-guided biopsy first.

records.title: Surgery
records.subtitle: Ductal carcinoma in situ · Breast
records.body: The choice is between breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy or wide excision) with adjuvant radiotherapy, and mastectomy. In a 2015 SEER observational study of more than 100,000 patients, breast conservation with or without radiotherapy gave 10-year breast-cancer-specific mortality similar to mastectomy. Mastectomy is overly aggressive for many women and carries more frequent postoperative complications; conservation is less morbid but carries the higher risk of local recurrence. Criteria for breast conservation: disease that is not multicentric, multicentricity meaning two or more foci separated by significant disease, usually across more than one quadrant; a cosmetically acceptable resection, which in practice means a low ratio of disease size to breast size; histologically negative margins of at least 2 mm. The 2 mm threshold comes from a meta-analysis of 4,660 patients with DCIS treated by conservation and radiotherapy, in which margins under 2 mm were associated with higher rates of ipsilateral breast tumour recurrence than margins of 2 mm or more (J Clin Oncol 2009). The SSO/ASTRO/ASCO consensus guideline adopts the same threshold for conservation plus radiotherapy. Sentinel node biopsy is not staging for the DCIS itself. It is done when the operation would make a later sentinel node biopsy impossible, or when the likelihood of occult invasive cancer is high enough to warrant staging the axilla at the same sitting. Total mastectomy permanently alters lymphatic drainage, so an accurate sentinel node biopsy cannot be performed afterwards if invasive cancer is found unexpectedly in the specimen. Patients requiring mastectomy also have a higher likelihood of harbouring invasive cancer than those with a smaller focus of disease, and should have sentinel node biopsy at the same operation. Patients who are candidates for conservation but opt for mastectomy should have the same discussion. After conservation, sentinel node biopsy remains possible as a second procedure if invasive cancer is found in the specimen, so it is not done up front.

records.title: Radiotherapy after breast conservation
records.subtitle: Ductal carcinoma in situ · Breast
records.body: Radiotherapy after conservation reduces the risk of in-breast tumour recurrence by 50%, with no effect on distant recurrence or mortality. A 2009 meta-analysis (Goodwin et al) pooled EORTC 10853, NSABP B-17, SweDCIS and UKCCCR, 3,925 patients in total. Radiotherapy after conservation reduced all ipsilateral breast events (HR 0.49, P<0.00001), with 9 patients needing treatment to prevent one ipsilateral recurrence, and deaths from vascular disease, pulmonary toxicity and second cancers were not significantly higher in the irradiated women. NSABP B-17 randomised DCIS after wide local excision to 50 Gy or no radiotherapy. At 15 years the ipsilateral invasive recurrence rate was 8.9% with radiotherapy against 19.4% without, and overall survival was similar (83% vs 84%; Fisher, N Engl J Med 1999). UKCCCR randomised 1,701 women after conservation in a two-by-two design, to radiotherapy or none and to tamoxifen or none (Houghton, Lancet 2010). At a median follow-up of 12.7 years, radiotherapy reduced all new breast events (HR 0.41), ipsilateral invasive disease (HR 0.32) and ipsilateral DCIS (HR 0.38), but not contralateral breast cancer. Tamoxifen reduced all new breast events (HR 0.71), recurrent ipsilateral DCIS (HR 0.70) and contralateral tumours (HR 0.44), but not ipsilateral invasive disease. Delivery is whole-breast radiotherapy started within 8 weeks of surgery, 45–50 Gy in daily fractions of 1.8–2 Gy over 4.5–5 weeks, followed by a boost to the surgical bed. The boost gives a small but statistically significant reduction in ipsilateral breast tumour recurrence across all age groups (4% at 20 years), but that evidence is in invasive breast cancer rather than DCIS. Omitting radiotherapy in low-risk disease For fully resected low-risk disease, and particularly for ER-positive disease that will receive endocrine therapy, the absolute reduction in in-breast recurrence may be too small to justify the risks of radiotherapy. There are no strict criteria for low risk; the working definition is low or intermediate grade, size under 2.5 cm, and widely negative margins of at least 3 mm. RTOG 9804 tested this in 636 patients with good-risk DCIS, defined as low to intermediate grade, under 2.5 cm and margins of at least 3 mm, randomised after conservation to radiotherapy or observation. It closed early because accrual fell below projection. At a median follow-up of 7.17 years, the primary endpoint of ipsilateral local failure was 0.9% with radiotherapy against 6.7% with observation at 7 years, with more grade 1–2 toxicity (76% vs 30%) and no difference in disease-free or overall survival (J Clin Oncol 2015). At 15 years radiotherapy had reduced local failure by 50%. Radiotherapy still improves local control in good-risk disease, so omission trades an absolute increase in local failure of 5.8 percentage points at 7 years against the toxicity of treatment. Accelerated partial breast irradiation is the intermediate option. DCIS made up between 6% and 25% of the populations of NSABP B-39/RTOG 0413, OCOG-RAPID, the University of Florence trial and GEC-ESTRO, all of which recruited breast cancer of 3 cm or less. Partial breast irradiation was non-inferior to whole-breast radiotherapy for local control, so DCIS meeting the RTOG 9804 criteria can be treated with partial breast irradiation instead.

records.title: Systemic therapy
records.subtitle: Ductal carcinoma in situ · Breast
records.body: Chemotherapy has no role, because the risk of distant metastatic disease is low and the prognosis good. Systemic therapy after surgery reduces the risk of a subsequent invasive cancer in the ipsilateral or contralateral breast; it is not treatment of the DCIS. Conservation, ER or PR positive: 5 years of endocrine therapy. Mastectomy, ER or PR positive: consider endocrine therapy to prevent contralateral breast cancer. ER and PR negative: consider tamoxifen to prevent a subsequent ER/PR-positive ipsilateral or contralateral cancer, which is a low absolute risk. The options are tamoxifen 20 mg daily and anastrozole. Anastrozole carries loss of bone density, fractures and cardiovascular risk. Tamoxifen carries endometrial cancer and cataract, and is contraindicated after deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, so an aromatase inhibitor may be preferable in that setting, and tamoxifen where osteoporosis dominates. NSABP B-24 randomised patients treated by conservation and radiotherapy to tamoxifen or placebo. At a median follow-up of 13.6 years tamoxifen gave an absolute risk reduction of 3.4% in ipsilateral breast tumour recurrence and 3.2% in contralateral breast cancer, with 10-year cumulative ipsilateral rates of 4.6% invasive and 5.6% non-invasive against 7.3% and 7.2% on placebo, and no difference in overall survival. Higher ER expression predicted benefit. NCCN accordingly suggests 5 years of tamoxifen for ER-positive DCIS treated by conservation. UKCCCR reported the tamoxifen effect separately by radiotherapy status. The reduction in ipsilateral and contralateral events was seen in the women who did not receive whole-breast radiotherapy (ipsilateral HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.98; contralateral HR 0.27, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.59) and not in those who did (ipsilateral HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.75, P=.80; contralateral HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.39 to 2.49, P=1.0). Without a test of interaction, and with the wider intervals in the irradiated subgroup, this does not establish that tamoxifen adds less after radiotherapy. NSABP B-35 compared 5 years of anastrozole with 5 years of tamoxifen in 3,100 postmenopausal women with HR-positive DCIS treated by conservation. At 9 years anastrozole gave a lower incidence of recurrent DCIS or invasive breast cancer (HR 0.73) and better estimated 10-year breast-cancer-free survival (93% vs 89%), with no significant difference in disease-free or overall survival; benefit was seen mostly in women under 60. Anastrozole is comparable to tamoxifen for postmenopausal patients with ER-positive DCIS. NSABP B-43 added trastuzumab to radiotherapy in 2,014 participants. It did not meet its objective of a 36% reduction in ipsilateral breast tumour recurrence, achieving a modest and statistically non-significant reduction of 19%. There is no role for HER2-directed therapy in DCIS.

records.title: Follow-up and prognosis
records.subtitle: Ductal carcinoma in situ · Breast
records.body: History and examination every 6–12 months for 5 years and annually thereafter, with annual mammography. SEER data put 20-year breast cancer mortality after DCIS at 3.3%, the 20-year risk of ipsilateral invasive recurrence at 5.9%, and the risk of contralateral invasive recurrence at 6.2%. Age under 35, high-grade lesions and ER negativity predict death from breast cancer. The aim of treatment is to reduce the risk of a subsequent invasive breast cancer rather than to prolong life; no treatment for DCIS has shown a survival benefit.

records.title: Scope and the shape of the decision
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: Non-metastatic breast cancer divides into early-stage disease (stage I, IIA, and the T2N1 subset of IIB) and locally advanced disease (the T3N0 subset of IIB, and stages IIIA to IIIC). Early-stage disease is normally treated by primary surgery to the breast and regional nodes, with or without radiotherapy, and adjuvant systemic therapy is then chosen on tumour size, nodal count, ER and PR expression, and HER2 status. Neoadjuvant therapy is preferred where it would permit breast conservation, convert a clinically node-positive axilla to ypN0, or generate the in-vivo response readout that directs post-operative escalation; that pathway is covered in the neoadjuvant chapter. Two categories of tumour feature drive everything below, and they are not interchangeable. Prognostic factors describe outcome independent of treatment: nodal status, grade, Ki67, tumour size, triple-negative phenotype. Predictive factors describe the likelihood of response to a specific therapy: HR status predicts response to endocrine therapy, HER2 status to anti-HER2 therapy, and the 21-gene recurrence score to chemotherapy benefit. Clinical risk estimates how much recurrence is available to prevent; a predictive assay estimates whether a given treatment will prevent it. Age under 35 is associated with more aggressive biology, more advanced presentation, ER-negative disease and a higher chance of a germline BRCA1/2 variant.

records.title: Breast surgery
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: Breast conservation versus mastectomy Breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy is equivalent to mastectomy for survival. NSABP B-04 compared radical with total mastectomy, with or without radiotherapy and no adjuvant systemic therapy in any arm; disease-free, relapse-free and overall survival did not differ in either the node-negative or the node-positive stratum, so simple mastectomy is as good as radical mastectomy. NSABP B-06 compared mastectomy, lumpectomy alone, and lumpectomy with radiotherapy, and found no difference in disease-free or overall survival, but substantially higher ipsilateral breast tumour recurrence without radiotherapy (39% vs 14%, P<0.001). The EBCTCG overview of breast conservation with and without radiotherapy quantified the same effect: radiotherapy reduced the 10-year risk of any first recurrence from 35% to 19.3% and the 15-year risk of breast cancer death from 25.2% to 21.4%, with a larger benefit in node-positive disease (Lancet 2011). If breast conservation is chosen, radiotherapy is part of it. Margins and contraindications An adequate margin after lumpectomy for invasive cancer is no tumour on ink. Absolute contraindications: multicentric disease or a high risk of multicentricity such as diffuse mammographic calcification; a contraindication to radiotherapy such as prior thoracic radiotherapy or pregnancy; disease too widespread to excise with negative margins and acceptable cosmesis. Relative contraindications: connective tissue disease such as systemic sclerosis, where healing after radiotherapy is poor; an anticipated poor cosmetic result, for instance a tumour near the nipple or a high tumour-to-breast ratio; and a known or suspected cancer predisposition syndrome, particularly Li-Fraumeni, where radiotherapy carries a second-malignancy risk. Two things are commonly mistaken for contraindications. A germline BRCA1/2 variant does not preclude breast conservation: local recurrence is higher, but most ipsilateral events are new primaries rather than true recurrences, and survival is no different from mastectomy. Extensive DCIS alongside the invasive tumour is also not a contraindication, provided margins are achieved.

records.title: Axillary management
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: Sentinel node biopsy Sentinel node biopsy is the staging operation for a clinically and radiologically negative axilla. A suspicious node is worked up first with ultrasound and needle biopsy: a positive biopsy sends the patient to axillary dissection, a negative one to sentinel node biopsy. NSABP B-32 randomised patients to sentinel node biopsy with immediate completion dissection versus dissection only if the sentinel node was positive, and found no difference in overall survival, disease-free survival or regional recurrence; a negative sentinel node had a 95% negative predictive value for the remaining axilla, with a false-negative rate of 9.8%. Sentinel node biopsy is inappropriate or uninformative in four situations. Pregnancy: isosulfan blue is teratogenic and the radioisotope option is unavailable. Clinically node-positive disease, treated with axillary dissection; patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy are restaged before surgery to reassess suitability. Inflammatory breast cancer, treated with axillary dissection. Patients in whom axillary status will not change adjuvant treatment, the worked example being the CALGB 9343 population (age 70 or older, ER-positive, T1N0, receiving endocrine therapy) who do not need radiotherapy and therefore do not need the nodal information that guides it. A positive sentinel node Completion axillary dissection is now the exception. It remains indicated for three or more positive nodes, and for one to two positive nodes in a patient who declines whole-breast radiotherapy. It is not required for isolated tumour cells (staged N0), for micrometastases, or for one to two macrometastatic nodes in the trial-defined settings below: IBCSG 23-01 randomised patients with sentinel-node micrometastases to dissection or no further axillary surgery and found no difference in disease-free survival, overall survival or breast cancer events. ACOSOG Z0011 (Alliance) changed practice, and its boundaries matter as much as its result. It randomised 891 women with clinical T1–T2 disease, no palpable adenopathy, and one or two sentinel nodes positive on haematoxylin and eosin, all treated with lumpectomy and tangential whole-breast irradiation with nodal fields prohibited, to sentinel node dissection alone or completion dissection. At a median 9.3 years, sentinel node dissection alone was non-inferior for 10-year overall survival (86.3% vs 83.6%; HR 0.85, one-sided 95% CI 0 to 1.16; non-inferiority P=.02 against a margin of 1.3), despite additional non-sentinel macrometastases in 27.3% of the dissection arm (JAMA 2011;305:569-575; JAMA 2017;318:918-926). Three qualifications apply. Ten-year disease-free survival (80.2% vs 78.2%; HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.17, P=.32) and locoregional relapse-free survival (P=.41) were tested for difference rather than non-inferiority, so they are absence of evidence of a difference rather than demonstrated equivalence. The trial closed early at 891 of 1,900 planned patients with 110 of the roughly 500 deaths needed for power, and the timing of this analysis was not prespecified. And 18.9% of patients in an independent analysis of radiation fields received protocol-prohibited nodal irradiation, though the investigators found it evenly distributed between arms and unlikely to have affected the result. The authors set out what the finding does not cover: palpable positive nodes, more than two involved sentinel nodes, omission of whole-breast irradiation, mastectomy without radiotherapy, and neoadjuvant therapy. AMAROS asked whether radiotherapy can replace surgery when the axilla still needs treatment. It randomised 4,806 patients with cN0 T1–2 disease before sentinel node biopsy, delivering the allocated treatment only to the 1,425 who proved sentinel-node-positive, to axillary dissection or axillary radiotherapy covering all three levels and the medial supraclavicular fossa. Five-year axillary recurrence was 0.43% after dissection and 1.19% after radiotherapy, with no significant difference in disease-free survival (86.9% vs 82.7%; HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.51; p=0.18) or overall survival (93.3% vs 92.5%; HR 1.17; p=0.34), and clinical lymphoedema at 5 years of 11% after radiotherapy versus 23% after dissection (Lancet Oncol 2014;15:1303-1310). The event rate was so low that the non-inferiority test was underpowered (one-sided 95% CI 0.00 to 5.27 against a margin of 2.0), so non-inferiority was not formally demonstrated; what the trial shows is excellent axillary control by either route at very different morbidity. SENOMAC is the only trial on this axis to reach its prespecified event target. It randomised 2,766 patients with cN0 T1–3 disease and one or two sentinel-node macrometastases to completion dissection or sentinel node biopsy alone, after mastectomy or breast conservation, with about 89% of both arms receiving nodal-target irradiation. Five-year recurrence-free survival was 89.7% with omission versus 88.7% with dissection (country-adjusted HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.19; P<0.001 against a non-inferiority margin of 1.44) (N Engl J Med 2024;390:1163-1175). The primary overall-survival endpoint matured in 2026 at 94.4% versus 93.4% (HR 0.84, 0.64 to 1.12) with breast-cancer-specific survival of 97.8% versus 97.3% (HR 0.86, 0.55 to 1.34), both interval upper bounds below the 1.44 margin, and significantly better patient-reported arm function at 3 and 5 years (J Clin Oncol 2026;44(suppl):LBA503). That analysis was reported at ASCO 2026 and is not yet a full publication. Because nodal irradiation was given to most of both arms, SENOMAC states its results are comparable with AMAROS rather than with Z0011. A mastectomy patient with one or two positive sentinel nodes, whom Z0011 does not cover, can therefore omit dissection provided the undissected axilla is irradiated. The composite rule after a positive sentinel node: Isolated tumour cells or micrometastases: no further axillary surgery. One to two macrometastases after breast conservation with whole-breast tangential radiotherapy: no further axillary surgery (Z0011). One to two macrometastases after mastectomy, or otherwise outside Z0011 criteria: omit dissection but include the undissected axilla in the radiotherapy field (AMAROS, SENOMAC). Three or more positive nodes: axillary dissection.

records.title: Radiotherapy
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: After breast-conserving surgery Whole-breast irradiation halves the 10-year risk of a first recurrence after breast-conserving surgery (RR 0.52, 19% vs 35%), an effect concentrated in local recurrence, and reduces the 15-year risk of breast cancer death (21% vs 25%, RR 0.82), at a long-term cost of cardiotoxicity, pneumonitis and second malignancy. Omitting radiotherapy in older, low-risk disease CALGB 9343 randomised women aged 70 or older with stage I ER-positive disease after breast conservation to tamoxifen alone or tamoxifen with radiotherapy. At 10 years, locoregional recurrence was higher without radiotherapy (9% vs 2%), while distant disease-free survival, breast-cancer-specific survival and overall survival were comparable. PRIME II tested the same question from age 65, in ER- or PR-positive tumours of 3 cm or less, excluding grade 3 and lymphovascular invasion: ipsilateral recurrence at 10 years was 9.8% without radiotherapy versus 0.9% with it, again with no difference in distant recurrence or overall survival. Within the no-radiotherapy arm, low ER expression carried higher recurrence risk than high (10-year local recurrence 18% vs 9%), which is the argument for confining omission to strongly ER-positive disease. LUMINA asked whether the age threshold can come down when biology is favourable. It enrolled 500 women aged 55 or older with T1N0, grade 1 or 2, luminal A disease (ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative, Ki67 13.25% or below) treated with breast conservation and endocrine therapy without radiotherapy, and reported 2.3% local recurrence and 2.7% recurrence of any type at 5 years. This is a single-arm result and not standard practice. Post-mastectomy radiotherapy Post-mastectomy radiotherapy covers the chest wall and the regional nodes, including the supraclavicular, infraclavicular and axillary fields. Indications: Four or more positive nodes. The 2005 EBCTCG overview reported reduced 15-year local recurrence (7.8% vs 29%) and improved breast-cancer-specific survival (60.1% vs 54.7%). One to three positive nodes, which remains contested. The 2014 EBCTCG overview found reductions in locoregional and overall recurrence and in breast cancer mortality, but its constituent trials predate contemporary systemic therapy or gave none. The British Columbia trial showed a breast-cancer-free survival benefit in premenopausal node-positive women irrespective of node count. T4 disease. Selected T2 and T3 tumours with adverse features: age 50 or under, triple-negative phenotype, high grade, or lymphovascular invasion. Positive margins where further resection is not possible. Fractionation and treatment volume Conventional whole-breast irradiation delivers 45 to 50 Gy in 25 fractions with a 10 Gy boost to the tumour bed; the boost reduces local recurrence, most clearly in women under 50 and in high-grade invasive ductal carcinoma. Whelan's hypofractionation trial gave 42.5 Gy in 16 fractions over 22 days without a boost to 1,234 node-negative women, and found no difference in 10-year local recurrence against a standard course (6.2% vs 6.7%), with inferior local control in high-grade disease (N Engl J Med 2010). Accelerated partial breast irradiation treats only the lumpectomy bed with a margin over five days, and is confined to selected low-risk patients: age 50 or older with invasive ductal carcinoma of 2 cm or less, negative margins of at least 2 mm, no lymphovascular invasion, ER-positive and BRCA -negative; or low-to-intermediate-grade screen-detected DCIS of 2.5 cm or less with adequate margins. Regional nodal irradiation adds the supraclavicular and infraclavicular fields, and the axilla where dissection was not performed. MA.20 randomised more than 1,800 patients after breast conservation and whole-breast irradiation, 90% node-positive and 85% with one to three positive nodes, and improved 10-year disease-free but not overall survival. The EORTC trial randomised about 4,000 patients, half node-positive and a quarter treated by mastectomy, and improved disease-free survival and breast cancer mortality with a non-significant trend in overall survival. Regional nodal irradiation is therefore standard for four or more positive nodes and a considered option for one to three, where both trials showed only non-significant trends. It is also worth considering in node-negative disease with adverse features: T3 or T4 tumours, T2 disease with fewer than 10 nodes dissected, high grade, ER-negative disease, or lymphovascular invasion. Micrometastatic nodal disease does not require it; the added toxicity is pneumonitis and lymphoedema. Sequencing with systemic therapy Radiotherapy follows adjuvant chemotherapy rather than running concurrently, because of radiation recall with doxorubicin and additive pneumonitis risk with taxanes. Early data suggested chemotherapy before radiotherapy reduced distant recurrence without a survival difference (Recht, NEJM 1996), but updated results showed no difference either way (Bellon, JCO 2005). Trastuzumab may be given concurrently with radiotherapy. Endocrine therapy can be too, but because it runs for years and there are theoretical concerns about oncostasis reducing radiosensitivity, it is usually started after radiotherapy finishes.

records.title: Adjuvant chemotherapy: the backbone
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: What chemotherapy adds The EBCTCG 15-year overview established that the proportional risk reductions from adjuvant systemic therapy persist to 15 years: about six months of anthracycline-based polychemotherapy reduced the annual breast cancer death rate by roughly 38% in women under 50 and 20% at ages 50 to 69, largely independent of ER and nodal status, and significantly more than CMF (Lancet 2005;365:1687-1717). Benefit was greatest in younger patients, ER-low and node-positive disease. Anthracycline and taxane The EBCTCG meta-analysis of 123 randomised trials sorted the regimens (Lancet 2012;379:432-444). Adding four cycles of a taxane to a fixed anthracycline backbone reduced breast cancer mortality (RR 0.86, 2p=0.0005), but not where the control arm received counterbalancing extra non-taxane cycles (RR 0.94, 2p=0.33). Standard four cycles of AC and standard six cycles of CMF were equivalent (RR 0.98), while higher-cumulative-dose CAF or CEF regimens beat CMF (RR 0.78, 2p=0.0004) on a significant dose-response trend. Cardiac mortality rose with any anthracycline (RR 1.56, 2p=0.02). The two taxane trials underneath that conclusion agree on recurrence and diverge on survival. CALGB 9344 (INT 0148) added four cycles of paclitaxel after four cycles of AC in 3,121 node-positive patients and reduced recurrence by 17% (HR 0.83, P=.0023) and death by 18% (HR 0.82, P=.0064), with 5-year disease-free survival of 70% versus 65% and overall survival 80% versus 77%; the same factorial found no gain from escalating doxorubicin from 60 to 90 mg/m² and more long-term cardiotoxicity at the higher doses (J Clin Oncol 2003;21:976-983). NSABP B-28 repeated the question in 3,060 node-positive patients with a better prognosis and found the same disease-free survival gain (RR 0.83, P=.006; 5-year 76% vs 72%) with no significant overall survival difference (5-year 85% in both arms) (J Clin Oncol 2005;23:3686-3696). A companion analysis of CALGB 9344 found the paclitaxel benefit concentrated in HER2-positive disease irrespective of ER status (interaction HR 0.59 for recurrence), with little gain in the HER2-negative, ER-positive tumours that made up more than half the trial (N Engl J Med 2007;357:1496-1506). The average benefit of chemotherapy is carried disproportionately by the subtypes least dependent on endocrine therapy. Can the anthracycline be dropped? US Oncology 9735 compared four cycles of docetaxel and cyclophosphamide with four cycles of AC in 1,016 patients with stage I–III disease. At the 7-year update, TC improved both disease-free survival (81% vs 75%; HR 0.74, P=.033) and overall survival (87% vs 82%; HR 0.69, P=.032), with no interaction by hormone receptor or HER2 status and no cardiotoxicity signal (J Clin Oncol 2006;24:5381-5387; J Clin Oncol 2009;27:1177-1183). TC×4 is therefore reasonable for lower-risk disease or where an anthracycline is contraindicated. Six cycles of TC is a different question with a different answer. The ABC trials (USOR 06-090/B-46-I/B-49) pooled three adjuvant trials (n=4,242, high-risk HER2-negative) testing TC×6 for non-inferiority against a taxane-plus-anthracycline regimen at a margin of 1.18. The futility boundary was crossed and the intention-to-treat analysis showed statistical inferiority of TC (invasive disease-free survival HR 1.23, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.50, P=.04; 4-year 88.2% vs 90.7%). At 6.9 years non-inferiority still could not be declared (HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.32) while overall survival did not differ (HR 1.05, P=.64), the anthracycline arm's recurrence advantage offset by more leukaemia (7 vs 1) and non-breast-cancer deaths, and concentrated in hormone-receptor-negative disease (recurrence-free interval HR 1.90) (J Clin Oncol 2017;35:2647-2655; J Clin Oncol 2024;42:1344-1349). The 2023 EBCTCG overview of 15 trials comparing taxane plus anthracycline against TC×6 resolves the contradiction by separating the schedules. Anthracycline-containing regimens had lower recurrence overall (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.93; p=0.0004), at a cost of roughly one AML per 700 women treated, but the advantage sat in concurrent schedules: concurrent TAC×6 beat TC×6 (10-year recurrence 12.3% vs 21%; breast cancer mortality 8.9% vs 13.2%, p=0.0034), whereas sequential AC then a taxane was equivalent to TC×6 (10-year recurrence 14.4% vs 14.9%, RR 0.94, p=0.30). Sequential administration delivers a higher dose per cycle but a lower cumulative anthracycline and taxane dose. Schedule and taxane choice CALGB 9741 tested dose density in a 2×2 factorial of 2,005 node-positive patients, varying interval (every 2 weeks with filgrastim versus every 3 weeks) and sequence (sequential doxorubicin, paclitaxel then cyclophosphamide versus concurrent AC then paclitaxel) at fixed doses. Dose-dense scheduling improved disease-free survival (RR 0.74, P=.010; 4-year 82% vs 75%) and overall survival (RR 0.69, P=.013), with no effect of sequence, and less grade 4 granulocytopenia (6% vs 33%) (J Clin Oncol 2003;21:1431-1439). That first report came at 36 months with 315 of 515 expected events, and the authors state that confidence in the survival benefit at longer follow-up remains to be firmly established. The EBCTCG dose-density overview confirmed it at scale, with lower 10-year recurrence (24% vs 28.3%, RR 0.83, p<0.0001) and breast cancer mortality (RR 0.86, p=0.005) regardless of hormone receptor or nodal status. Primary G-CSF prophylaxis is mandatory on a dose-dense schedule. ECOG E1199 tested taxane and schedule together in 4,950 patients after four cycles of AC. Both prespecified primary comparisons were null: taxane type HR 1.03 (P=.61) and schedule HR 1.06 (P=.33), with a significant taxane-by-schedule interaction (P=.003) that the authors say complicates interpretation. Against the shared every-3-week paclitaxel reference, weekly paclitaxel improved disease-free (HR 1.27, 98.3% CI 1.03 to 1.57, P=.006) and overall survival (1.32, P=.01), three-weekly docetaxel improved disease-free survival only (1.23, P=.02), and weekly docetaxel improved neither. Grade 2–4 neuropathy was 27% with weekly paclitaxel versus 20% (N Engl J Med 2008;358:1663-1671). No experimental arm was tested against another, so the two winners are not ranked. Both are acceptable and the choice is made on toxicity: three-weekly docetaxel causes more neutropenia, febrile neutropenia and infection, weekly paclitaxel more neuropathy, and weekly paclitaxel improved both disease-free and overall survival in the triple-negative subgroup. Adjuvant chemotherapy should start 3 to 6 weeks after surgery; initiation beyond 90 days is associated with worse overall survival. Intensified chemotherapy with stem-cell rescue SUBITO closes the high-dose chemotherapy axis in the population where it had most rationale. In 174 patients with stage III, HER2-negative, homologous-recombination-deficient disease, intensified alkylating chemotherapy with autologous stem-cell rescue gave the same 4-year overall survival as standard chemotherapy followed by a year of adjuvant olaparib (77.0% vs 76.4%; HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.17, p=0.37), with no difference in recurrence-free survival or pCR, at grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia of 99% versus 19% (Lancet Oncol 2026;27:795-807). This is a null superiority result in a trial powered for a hazard ratio of 0.353, not demonstrated equivalence, but the toxicity comparison is not close.

records.title: HR-positive, HER2-negative disease
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: The endocrine foundation Every patient with ER-positive disease should receive at least five years of endocrine therapy. The EBCTCG tamoxifen meta-analysis of 20 trials (21,457 women) showed that five years of tamoxifen roughly halved the recurrence rate during years 0 to 4 (RR 0.53) and reduced breast cancer mortality by about a third throughout 15 years (RR 0.70), largely irrespective of age, nodal status or receipt of chemotherapy, with benefit confined to ER-positive disease (Lancet 2011;378:771-784). PR status does not significantly predict response. In postmenopausal women an aromatase inhibitor is preferred. ATAC compared anastrozole with tamoxifen for five years and at 10 years reported better disease-free survival (HR 0.86) and time to recurrence (HR 0.79), the absolute recurrence difference widening from 2.7% at 5 years to 4.3% at 10 years and recurrence still lower after treatment ended (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.98, p=0.03), but no overall survival difference (HR 0.95, p=0.4) (Lancet 2002;359:2131-2139; Lancet Oncol 2010;11:1135-1141). BIG 1-98 confirmed it independently: at a median 25.8 months, upfront letrozole improved disease-free survival over tamoxifen (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.93, P=0.003) and reduced distant recurrence (HR 0.73, P=0.001) (N Engl J Med 2005;353:2747-2757). The EBCTCG aromatase inhibitor vs tamoxifen meta-analysis of 31,920 postmenopausal women turned that into a mortality claim: five years of an aromatase inhibitor reduced recurrence by about 30% while treatments differed, and cut 10-year breast cancer mortality from 14.2% to 12.1% (RR 0.85), with fewer endometrial cancers and more fractures (Lancet 2015;386:1341-1352). Because the benefit is concentrated in the years the treatments differ, a sequential tamoxifen-then-letrozole schedule performs like letrozole alone rather than like tamoxifen alone. BIG 1-98's sequential arms support starting a perimenopausal patient on tamoxifen and switching to letrozole once menopause is established. The steroidal and non-steroidal agents are interchangeable on efficacy: MA.27 found exemestane equivalent to anastrozole, FACE letrozole equivalent to anastrozole. Menopause is defined by prior bilateral oophorectomy, age 60 or over, or, under 60, by 12 months or more of amenorrhoea with postmenopausal FSH and oestradiol in the absence of chemotherapy, tamoxifen or ovarian suppression. Chemotherapy-induced amenorrhoea of 12 months or more, and treatment with tamoxifen, both require postmenopausal FSH and oestradiol on serial assessment. Premenopausal disease and ovarian suppression SOFT randomised 3,066 premenopausal women to tamoxifen, tamoxifen with ovarian function suppression, or exemestane with ovarian function suppression for five years. Adding ovarian suppression to tamoxifen showed a significance trajectory rather than a settled answer: no significant disease-free survival benefit at the 5.6-year primary analysis (86.6% vs 84.7%; HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.04, p=0.10), a significant disease-free and overall survival benefit at 8 years (83.2% vs 78.9%, p=0.009; overall survival 93.3% vs 91.5%), and a persisting but attenuated benefit at 12 years (disease-free survival HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.98; overall survival HR 0.78, 0.60 to 1.01) (N Engl J Med 2015;372:436-46; N Engl J Med 2018;379:122-137; J Clin Oncol 2023;41:1370-1375). Exemestane with ovarian suppression did better still against tamoxifen alone (HR 0.65, 0.49 to 0.87). Where the benefit sits is the useful part. It concentrated in women who remained premenopausal after chemotherapy; in the lower-risk chemotherapy-naive cohort more than 95% of every arm remained free from breast cancer at 5 years, and tamoxifen alone stayed appropriate. TEXT & SOFT (exemestane) is the combined analysis of the shared question, exemestane versus tamoxifen on a background of ovarian suppression in 4,690 women. At 68 months exemestane improved disease-free survival (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.85, P<0.001) and freedom from breast cancer (HR 0.66, P<0.001) with no overall survival difference; at 13 years the recurrence advantage held (12-year disease-free survival HR 0.79, 0.70 to 0.90) while overall survival still did not differ (HR 0.93, 0.78 to 1.11), the survival hazard time-varying with early harm reversing to later benefit (N Engl J Med 2014;371:107-118; J Clin Oncol 2023;41:1376-1382). The EBCTCG premenopausal AI vs tamoxifen (ovarian suppression) meta-analysis of 7,030 women across four trials fixes the magnitude and the limits. An aromatase inhibitor reduced any breast cancer recurrence versus tamoxifen (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.90; p=0.0005), concentrated in years 0 to 4 when treatments differed (RR 0.68) with no further gain in years 5 to 9, an absolute 5-year reduction of 3.2% (6.9% vs 10.1%). There was no difference in breast cancer mortality (RR 1.01, 0.82 to 1.24) or all-cause mortality (RR 1.04, 0.86 to 1.27) at 8 years, and more fractures with the aromatase inhibitor (6.4% vs 5.1%, RR 1.27) (Lancet Oncol 2022;23:382-392). Practical selection: Higher-risk premenopausal disease (age under 35, tumour above 2 cm, grade 3): ovarian suppression with an aromatase inhibitor or tamoxifen, the aromatase inhibitor preferred; alternatives are 10 years of tamoxifen, or a sequential tamoxifen-then-aromatase-inhibitor schedule with extension. Lower-risk disease: tamoxifen alone for 5 to 10 years, or a sequential schedule. The observation behind the branch is that in NSABP B-30, premenopausal patients who developed chemotherapy-induced amenorrhoea had better disease-free and overall survival than those who did not. Duration and extended therapy Recurrence risk in ER-positive disease continues well past five years: the EBCTCG 2024 analysis put late recurrence in pN2 disease at about 2.7% per year, roughly 13% over years 5 to 10. That is the rationale for extending. MA.17 (NCIC CTG) randomised 5,187 postmenopausal women disease-free after about five years of tamoxifen to five further years of letrozole or placebo. It stopped at the first interim analysis (median follow-up 2.4 years) with 4-year disease-free survival of 93% versus 87% (HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.75, P=0.00008), a benefit at least as large in node-negative (HR 0.47) as node-positive disease (HR 0.60), and a non-significant overall survival trend (HR 0.76, P=0.25) (N Engl J Med 2003;349:1793-1802). NSABP B-33 tested exemestane in the same position and, read through 44% placebo-to-exemestane crossover after MA.17 reported, gave a borderline 4-year disease-free survival gain (91% vs 89%; HR 0.68, P=.07) and a significant relapse-free survival gain (HR 0.44, P=.004), the disease-free survival benefit confined to node-positive disease (HR 0.50) and absent node-negative (HR 1.13) (J Clin Oncol 2008;26:1965-1971). ATLAS answered the same question for tamoxifen. Continuing to 10 years reduced recurrence in years 5 to 14 (21.4% vs 25.1%) and breast cancer mortality (12.2% vs 15.0%, absolute reduction 2.8%), the benefit emerging mainly after year 10, at the cost of more endometrial cancer and pulmonary embolism (Lancet 2013;381:805-816). The EBCTCG extended AI meta-analysis of 22,031 women summarises extending an aromatase inhibitor beyond five years. Any further aromatase-inhibitor therapy reduced recurrence by 27% (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.80, p<0.0001). In the narrower subgroup who had already had some aromatase inhibitor (7,511 women), five further years cut recurrence (RR 0.71; years 5–15 risk 11.6% vs 15.2%) and distant recurrence (RR 0.73), but breast cancer mortality fell only non-significantly (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.15, p=0.40; 4.4% vs 5.0%). Five-year fracture risk rose (RR 1.35, 1.13 to 1.61), and non-adherence was widespread and similar in both arms (39.0% vs 37.6%) (Lancet 2025;406:603-614). The underlying rates are 3.4% rising to 4.6% (p=0.0009). Extending an aromatase inhibitor therefore buys recurrence reduction, not demonstrated survival, at a measurable skeletal cost. The absolute gain was larger in node-positive disease, reflecting higher baseline risk rather than a different proportional effect. Options among the extended-therapy trials: Two to five years of tamoxifen followed by five years of an aromatase inhibitor: a disease-free survival benefit, with a survival benefit in node-positive disease (MA.17, GIM4). Aromatase inhibition to a total of 10 years: a disease-free survival benefit without a survival benefit and with more bone toxicity (MA.17R, NSABP B-42, AERAS). Seven to eight years: a reasonable compromise where tolerance is the problem, with no apparent loss of survival (IDEAL, ABCSG-16/SALSA). Tamoxifen to 10 years: superior to five years, with the effect appearing only in the second decade after diagnosis (ATLAS). Oral SERDs lidERA (BC) is the first adjuvant trial of a next-generation oral selective oestrogen receptor degrader to report. It randomised 4,170 patients with ER-positive, HER2-negative stage I–III disease to giredestrant 30 mg daily or standard-of-care endocrine therapy for five years, with an LHRH agonist for premenopausal patients on giredestrant or an aromatase inhibitor. Giredestrant improved invasive disease-free survival (3-year 92.4% vs 89.6%; HR 0.70, p=0.0014), with greater benefit in stage II–III disease, a stage I hazard ratio crossing 1.00, and immature overall survival. Discontinuation for adverse events was lower than with an aromatase inhibitor (J Clin Oncol 2026;44(suppl):502). The primary readout was presented at SABCS 2025 and is not yet a full publication, so this is a signal to watch rather than a standard. Pregnancy after diagnosis POSITIVE followed 516 women aged 42 or under with prior stage I–III HR-positive disease who interrupted adjuvant endocrine therapy for up to two years to attempt pregnancy, after 18 to 30 months of treatment. The design was a fixed-threshold safety trial rather than a hazard-ratio comparison: 44 breast cancer events occurred against a prespecified boundary of 46 over 1,638 patient-years, and an external-control comparison against the SOFT/TEXT cohort found no excess 3-year event incidence (8.9% vs 9.2%; adjusted HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.15). Of the cohort, 74.0% achieved at least one pregnancy and 63.8% at least one live birth (N Engl J Med 2023;388:1645-1656). Median follow-up was 3.4 years against a protocol-specified 10-year endpoint, so interruption is supported on short-term safety and the long-term question is open. Deciding on chemotherapy: genomic assays Not every ER-positive tumour needs chemotherapy, and the assays exist to identify the ones that do not. The old St Gallen rule gave chemotherapy to everyone except node-negative invasive ductal carcinoma that was strongly ER-positive, T1, grade 1, lymphovascular-invasion-negative, HER2-negative and in a patient over 35. The 2021 St Gallen consensus omits chemotherapy in stage I disease under 1 cm and allows omission in postmenopausal patients with favourable biology: strong ER expression, low to intermediate grade, low Ki67 and a low-risk genomic signature (Burstein, Ann Oncol 2021). Risk calculators such as PREDICT estimate recurrence, mortality and expected chemotherapy benefit, but do not substitute for a molecular assay because they capture neither all biomarkers nor the interaction between biology and treatment effect. Oncotype DX, MammaPrint and PAM50 are all prognostic; only Oncotype DX is validated as predictive of chemotherapy benefit. Oncotype DX is an RT-PCR assay of 16 cancer-related and 5 reference genes returning a recurrence score of 0 to 100. Paik et al. (NSABP B-20 validation) established the predictive claim retrospectively on 651 node-negative, ER-positive patients randomised to tamoxifen with or without chemotherapy: high-score tumours (≥31) derived large chemotherapy benefit (relative risk 0.26, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.53; absolute 10-year distant-recurrence reduction 27.6%), low-score tumours (<18) derived minimal benefit (relative risk 1.31), and the interaction was significant (p=0.038) (J Clin Oncol 2006;24:3726-3734). The cut points were validated prognostically in NSABP B-14, where 10-year distant recurrence-free survival was 93%, 86% and 70% across the low, intermediate and high-risk groups. TAILORx tested the midrange prospectively in 10,273 patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative disease, randomising the 6,711 (69%) with a score of 11 to 25 to endocrine therapy alone or chemoendocrine therapy. Endocrine therapy alone was non-inferior for invasive disease-free survival (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.24, P=0.26; 9-year 83.3% vs 84.3%). A prespecified age interaction (P=0.004) showed residual chemotherapy benefit in women aged 50 or under with a score of 16 to 25, freedom from distant recurrence higher by up to 6.5 percentage points at 9 years in the 21–25 band, without a demonstrated survival difference (N Engl J Med 2018;379:111-121). RxPONDER (SWOG S1007) extended the assay to 5,018 patients with one to three positive nodes and a score of 25 or below. The score-by-treatment interaction was not significant (P=0.35), so the score stayed prognostic but stopped predicting relative chemotherapy benefit, while a prespecified menopausal-status interaction was significant (P=0.008) and became the governing variable. Postmenopausal women (66.8%) derived no chemotherapy benefit (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.26, P=0.89); premenopausal women derived a clear one (invasive disease-free survival HR 0.60, 0.43 to 0.83, P=0.002; distant relapse-free HR 0.58, P=0.009), even at low scores (N Engl J Med 2021;385:2336-2347). Whether that premenopausal signal is direct cytotoxic benefit or indirect ovarian suppression is unresolved, and it matters because the alternative to chemotherapy in a young woman is ovarian suppression, not nothing. The resulting decision rules: Node-negative One to three positive nodes Score ≥26 Chemotherapy Chemotherapy Score 16–25 Integrate clinicopathological risk; chemotherapy if aged 50 or under with a score of 21–25, or 16–20 with high clinical risk Postmenopausal: no chemotherapy benefit. Premenopausal: benefit on invasive disease-free and distant relapse-free survival Score ≤15 Chemotherapy unlikely to help As above MammaPrint is a 70-gene signature validated for FFPE tissue in tumours of 5 cm or less with 0 to 3 positive nodes, irrespective of receptor status or menopausal state, returning a binary low-or-high genomic risk. MINDACT randomised 6,693 patients on the discordance between clinical and genomic risk. Its primary analysis was a single-arm rate against a fixed threshold, not a between-arm comparison: among the 1,550 women (23.2%) at high clinical but low genomic risk who forwent chemotherapy, 5-year survival without distant metastasis was 94.7% (95% CI 92.5 to 96.2), clearing the prespecified 92% boundary. The secondary randomised comparison in that group was underpowered (adjusted HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.21, P=0.27) (N Engl J Med 2016;375:717-729). About 46% of clinically high-risk women could avoid chemotherapy, and in the reverse discordant group chemotherapy conferred no benefit. PAM50 identifies intrinsic subtype: luminal A tumours have a very good prognosis without chemotherapy, while luminal B tumours are more likely to recur on endocrine therapy alone and may warrant it. OPTIMA tested the Prosigna PAM50 risk-of-recurrence score as a chemotherapy-direction tool in 4,429 patients with high-clinical-risk ER-positive, HER2-negative disease, 73% node-positive. Test-directed management was non-inferior on 5-year invasive breast-cancer-free survival (90.4% vs 91.5%; HR 0.99, 90% CI 0.81 to 1.20; non-inferiority p=0.013), and the 68% with a low score could safely avoid chemotherapy, with no heterogeneity by menopausal or nodal status (J Clin Oncol 2026;44(suppl):500). This is an ASCO 2026 abstract rather than a full publication, and what it validates is a test-directed management strategy rather than a treatment-by-assay interaction, so it does not make PAM50 predictive in the sense Oncotype DX is. The assays are not interchangeable: platforms, risk definitions, nodal populations and primary estimands all differ, so a threshold from one does not transfer to another. ASTER 70s randomised 1,089 women aged 70 or over with ER-positive, HER2-negative disease and a high-risk genomic grade index to chemotherapy then endocrine therapy or endocrine therapy alone, and found no significant survival benefit (8-year overall survival 72.7% vs 68.3%; HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.11, p=0.21) at grade 3 or higher toxicity of 34% versus 9% (Lancet 2025;406:489-500). Genomic high risk in an older patient is not by itself an indication for chemotherapy. CDK4/6 inhibitors monarchE randomised 5,637 patients with node-positive, high-risk HR-positive, HER2-negative disease to two years of abemaciclib 150 mg twice daily added to standard endocrine therapy, or endocrine therapy alone. High risk meant four or more positive nodes, or one to three with a tumour above 5 cm, grade 3 disease, or Ki67 of 20% or above. Invasive disease-free survival improved at the primary analysis (2-year 92.2% vs 88.7%; HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.93, P=.01) and deepened with maturity (7-year HR 0.734). At the 2026 primary overall survival analysis, with 661 deaths at a median 6.3 years, abemaciclib met its prespecified boundary (HR 0.842, 95% CI 0.722 to 0.981, P=0.027; 7-year overall survival 86.8% vs 85.0%) (J Clin Oncol 2020;38:3987-3998; Ann Oncol 2026;37:155-165). That makes monarchE the first adjuvant CDK4/6 trial to convert a recurrence benefit into a demonstrated survival benefit. Ki67 was prognostic but not predictive, so a high Ki67 identifies risk but is not itself the reason to give abemaciclib. Toxicity is diarrhoea, neutropenia and fatigue. NATALEE extended the class to a broader population: 5,101 patients with stage II–III disease including selected node-negative tumours, given ribociclib 400 mg daily three weeks on and one week off for three years with a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor. Three-year invasive disease-free survival was 90.4% versus 87.1% (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.91, P=0.003), and at the prespecified 5-year follow-up the benefit deepened rather than faded (HR 0.716, 95% CI 0.618 to 0.829, the gap widening from 2.7 to 4.5 percentage points between years 3 and 5) and held in node-negative disease (HR 0.606, 0.372 to 0.986), while overall survival remained a non-significant trend (HR 0.800, 95% CI 0.637 to 1.003) (N Engl J Med 2024;390:1080-1091; ESMO Open 2025;10:105858). Toxicity is neutropenia, transaminitis and QTc prolongation. Eligibility is wider than monarchE: node-positive disease of any burden, or node-negative disease with a T3 tumour, grade 3 histology, or grade 2 histology plus high genomic risk (Ki67 ≥20%, recurrence score ≥26, or high-risk MammaPrint, PAM50 or EndoPredict). The class does not generalise. PALLAS gave two years of palbociclib to 5,760 patients with stage II–III disease and was negative, crossing its futility boundary (3-year invasive disease-free survival 88.2% vs 88.5%, HR 0.93), with 45% not completing treatment (Lancet Oncol 2021;22:212-222). PENELOPE-B gave one year of palbociclib to 1,250 patients with high-CPS-EG residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and was equally negative (HR 0.93, p=.53), with no benefit in any subgroup (J Clin Oncol 2021;39:1518-1530). Duration, continuity, adherence, eligibility and timing relative to chemotherapy all differ between the positive and negative trials, so what exists is a set of evidence-backed regimens rather than a class rule. Adjuvant palbociclib cannot be recommended; abemaciclib and ribociclib are given in the risk envelopes their own trials defined. Olaparib for germline BRCA-mutated disease OlympiA randomised 1,836 patients with a germline BRCA1/2 pathogenic variant and HER2-negative high-risk early breast cancer, 82.2% of them triple-negative and the remainder HR-positive, to one year of olaparib 300 mg twice daily or placebo after (neo)adjuvant chemotherapy. Invasive disease-free survival improved (3-year 85.9% vs 77.1%; HR 0.58, 99.5% CI 0.41 to 0.82, P<0.001), as did distant disease-free survival (HR 0.57), and the overall survival benefit reached significance at the second interim analysis (4-year 89.8% vs 86.4%; HR 0.68, 98.5% CI 0.47 to 0.97, P=0.009) (N Engl J Med 2021;384:2394-2405; Ann Oncol 2022;33:1250-1268). At the 2021 interim the overall survival hazard ratio was also 0.68 but did not cross its boundary (P=0.02 against P<0.01), so the survival claim belongs to the 2022 analysis and not to the primary publication. Eligibility is defined by prior treatment and residual risk rather than by phenotype: Triple-negative disease: residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy; or, without neoadjuvant chemotherapy, node-negative disease with a primary tumour of 2 cm or more, or node-positive disease, after adjuvant chemotherapy. HR-positive disease: a CPS-EG score of 3 or above after neoadjuvant chemotherapy; or, without neoadjuvant chemotherapy, pN2 or above. Anaemia is the signature toxicity, at 23.5% any grade and 8.7% grade 3 or higher against 3.9% and 0.3% with placebo, and grade 3 or higher adverse events were roughly twice as frequent overall (24.3% vs 11.3%). Myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia were not increased at this cut (0.2% vs 0.3%), but at a median 2.5 years the investigators state longer follow-up is needed before that is settled.

records.title: HER2-positive disease
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: The trastuzumab backbone The EBCTCG trastuzumab meta-analysis pooled 13,864 women across seven randomised trials at a median 10.7 years and found reductions of about one-third in recurrence (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.71) and breast cancer mortality (RR 0.67, 0.61 to 0.73), with absolute 10-year reductions of 9.0% in recurrence, 6.4% in breast cancer mortality and 6.5% in all-cause mortality, and no increase in death without recurrence (Lancet Oncol 2021;22:1139-1150). The proportional reduction was similar irrespective of ER and nodal status while the absolute benefit scaled with baseline risk (5-year recurrence reduction 10.7% with four or more positive nodes versus 5.7% node-negative). Uniform relative benefit with risk-proportional absolute benefit is the arithmetic that licenses both escalating high-risk and de-escalating low-risk disease. NSABP B-31 / NCCTG N9831 (joint analysis) tested AC followed by paclitaxel with or without concurrent trastuzumab in about 4,046 patients with node-positive or high-risk node-negative disease. Adding trastuzumab roughly halved recurrence at the interim analysis (disease-free survival HR 0.48, P<0.0001), and the mature joint analysis at 8.4 years gave disease-free survival HR 0.60 (0.53 to 0.68) and overall survival HR 0.63 (0.54 to 0.73), with 10-year overall survival of 84% versus 75.2%, consistent across subgroups (N Engl J Med 2005;353:1673-1684; J Clin Oncol 2014;32:3744-3752). Three-year class III/IV heart failure or cardiac death was 4.1% in B-31 and 2.9% in N9831, concentrated in the anthracycline arms. Because trastuzumab was given concurrently with the taxane, concurrent administration became standard. HERA (BIG 1-01) confirmed the backbone with a sequential design and fixed the duration, randomising 5,102 patients after completion of chemotherapy to observation, one year of trastuzumab, or two years. One year against observation gave an initial disease-free survival HR of 0.54 settling to 0.76 (0.68 to 0.86) at the 11-year final analysis, with overall survival HR 0.74 (0.64 to 0.86) and 10-year disease-free survival 69% versus 63%, diluted by 52% crossover from the observation arm. Two years added nothing over one (HR 1.02, 0.89 to 1.17) and caused more mild cardiac events; severe cardiotoxicity was low at 0.5% with sequential post-chemotherapy dosing (N Engl J Med 2005;353:1659-1672; Lancet 2017;389:1195-1205). FinHer gave only nine weeks of trastuzumab alongside docetaxel or vinorelbine before FEC, and improved 3-year recurrence-free survival (89% vs 78%, HR 0.42) in the 232-patient HER2-positive subgroup, with docetaxel also outperforming vinorelbine on distant disease-free survival (HR 0.66, P=0.01) (N Engl J Med 2006;354:809-820). It raised the short-duration question the trials below answered, without an associated LVEF decline. Duration One year is the standard. Six months is a defensible option in a patient who cannot complete a year, and the two trials that tested it returned near-identical hazard ratios and opposite verdicts. PERSEPHONE randomised 4,089 UK patients pragmatically across all chemotherapy regimens and schedules, and demonstrated non-inferiority of six months (4-year disease-free survival 89.4% vs 89.8%; HR 1.07, 90% CI 0.93 to 1.24, non-inferiority P=0.011 against a 3% margin), with fewer severe adverse events (19% vs 24%, P=0.0002) and less early stopping for cardiotoxicity (3% vs 8%, P<0.0001) (Lancet 2019;393:2599-2612). PHARE asked the same question in 3,384 French patients against a stricter margin of 1.15 and failed: the final 7.5-year analysis gave HR 1.08 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.25, P=0.39), the interval still crossing the margin, and concluded 12 months should remain standard (Lancet Oncol 2013;14:741-748; Lancet 2019;393:2591-2598). Seven-year overall survival was 80.6% versus 82.3% (HR 1.13, p=0.26). The verdict turns on the prespecified margin rather than on the biology: shortening carries a small, real excess hazard. PHARE's subgroup analyses favoured 12 months in patients given taxane-based chemotherapy and concurrent rather than sequential trastuzumab, which is contemporary practice. ShortHER tested nine weeks against one year in 1,253 Italian patients and did not meet non-inferiority (disease-free survival HR 1.13, 90% CI 0.89 to 1.42, against a margin of 1.29), on an accrual cut from 2,332 to 1,252 for funding reasons. Ten-year outcomes were close overall (disease-free survival 77% with one year versus 78% with nine weeks; overall survival 89% vs 88%), but nodal status was a stratification factor and the protocol-defined subgroups separate sharply: node-negative and one-to-three-node disease showed negligible differences numerically favouring the short course, whereas four or more positive nodes clearly favoured a year (10-year overall survival 84% vs 64%, HR 1.87) (Ann Oncol 2018;29:2328-2333; J Clin Oncol 2023;41:4976-4981). No interaction test is reported for any subgroup. Chemotherapy partner BCIRG 006 randomised 3,222 patients with node-positive or high-risk node-negative disease to AC followed by docetaxel, the same with trastuzumab, or non-anthracycline docetaxel with carboplatin and trastuzumab. Both trastuzumab arms beat chemotherapy alone (5-year disease-free survival 84% for AC-TH and 81% for TCH versus 75%; 5-year overall survival 92% and 91% versus 87%) with no significant efficacy difference between them (N Engl J Med 2011;365:1273-1283). The reported hazard ratios against AC-T are 0.64 for AC-TH and 0.75 for TCH on disease-free survival, and 0.63 and 0.77 on overall survival. The trial was not powered to compare the two trastuzumab-containing regimens, so the absence of a difference between them is exploratory rather than demonstrated equivalence. What separates them is toxicity: congestive heart failure and cardiac dysfunction were significantly higher with AC-TH than TCH (P<0.001), acute leukaemia occurred in seven anthracycline-arm patients against one on TCH, and TCH caused less arthralgia, myalgia, hand-foot syndrome, stomatitis, vomiting and neutropenia. Dual blockade APHINITY added a year of adjuvant pertuzumab to chemotherapy and trastuzumab in 4,805 patients with node-positive or high-risk node-negative disease, excluding those treated neoadjuvantly. Invasive disease-free survival improved (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.00, P=0.045), the benefit sitting in node-positive disease (8-year 86.1% vs 81.2%, HR 0.72) and absent node-negative (HR 1.13). Overall survival was not significant at the 8.4-year peer-reviewed analysis (HR 0.83, P=0.078) and reached significance only at the final 11.3-year analysis (HR 0.83, P=0.044; 10-year overall survival 91.6% vs 89.8%), which remains a congress report pending full publication (N Engl J Med 2017;377:122-131; J Clin Oncol 2024;42:3643-3651; ESMO Breast Cancer 2025, LBA1). There was no cardiac penalty; grade 3 or higher diarrhoea ran at about 10% versus 4%. Adjuvant dual blockade is therefore for node-positive disease. A patient treated neoadjuvantly who was clinically node-positive at diagnosis continues pertuzumab post-operatively; one node-negative at diagnosis continues trastuzumab alone. Extended adjuvant therapy ExteNET gave a year of neratinib 240 mg daily after completed trastuzumab-based therapy in 2,840 patients with stage 1–3 disease and improved 5-year invasive disease-free survival (90.2% vs 87.7%; HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.92, P=0.0083), with the benefit concentrated in hormone-receptor-positive disease and in patients starting within about a year of trastuzumab (Lancet Oncol 2016;17:367-377; Lancet Oncol 2017;18:1688-1700). The corresponding rates are 91.2% versus 86.8% in hormone-receptor-positive and 88.9% versus 88.8% in hormone-receptor-negative disease, with 8-year overall survival of 90.1% versus 90.2%. Diarrhoea dominates the toxicity, grade 3 in 40% without loperamide prophylaxis and the leading cause of early discontinuation. Neratinib is used selectively for two reasons: there is no overall survival benefit, and no patient in ExteNET received (neo)adjuvant pertuzumab, so the population does not match contemporary practice. It is the only therapy shown to improve outcomes beyond a completed trastuzumab year, in contrast to HERA's null second year: extending helps with a different drug, not more of the same. Small node-negative tumours Small node-negative HER2-positive tumours were largely excluded from the pivotal adjuvant trials, so their question is how little treatment suffices rather than how much. APT (Adjuvant Paclitaxel + Trastuzumab) is a single-arm phase II study of 406 patients with tumours of 3 cm or less that were node-negative or had a single nodal micrometastasis, treated with weekly paclitaxel 80 mg/m² for 12 weeks with trastuzumab, then trastuzumab to complete a year. In practice the population was smaller than that ceiling: 91% of tumours were 2 cm or less and 98.5% were node-negative. At the final 10-year analysis, invasive disease-free survival was 91.3% (95% CI 88.3 to 94.4), overall survival 94.3% and breast-cancer-specific survival 98.8%, with grade 3 neuropathy in 3.2% and symptomatic heart failure in 0.5% (N Engl J Med 2015;372:134-141; Lancet Oncol 2023;24:273-285). ATEMPT asked whether adjuvant T-DM1 could make stage I treatment less toxic. It randomised 512 patients 3:1 to 17 cycles of T-DM1 or to paclitaxel with trastuzumab, with co-primary endpoints of toxicity and invasive disease-free survival in the T-DM1 arm. T-DM1 efficacy was excellent (5-year invasive disease-free survival 97.0%, 95% CI 95.2 to 98.7), but clinically relevant toxicity was unchanged at 46% versus 47% (P=0.83); the profile shifted rather than shrank, with less neuropathy and alopecia and more thrombocytopenia and transaminitis (J Clin Oncol 2021;39:2375-2385; J Clin Oncol 2024;42:3652-3665). Early discontinuation was higher with T-DM1, at 17% versus 6%. Paclitaxel with trastuzumab therefore remains the standard for small node-negative tumours, with T-DM1 a validated alternative chosen on which toxicities a patient most wants to avoid. Residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy Where neoadjuvant therapy has been given, adjuvant anti-HER2 therapy is directed by pathological response: continue trastuzumab with or without pertuzumab to complete a year after a pathological complete response, and escalate to T-DM1, or to T-DXd for high-risk residual disease, when invasive disease remains (KATHERINE; DESTINY-Breast05). That pathway is developed in the neoadjuvant chapter. Cardiac monitoring Risk factors for trastuzumab-related cardiotoxicity are age over 50, pre-existing cardiac dysfunction, high BMI and treatment with antihypertensives. Echocardiography is performed 3-monthly during trastuzumab. Treatment may resume if LVEF returns to normal within 4 to 8 weeks and the fall from baseline remains no greater than 15%. Discontinue permanently for an LVEF decline persisting beyond 8 weeks, or after more than three treatment interruptions for cardiomyopathy.

records.title: Triple-negative disease
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: Where neoadjuvant chemotherapy was not given, adjuvant treatment is chemotherapy and the threshold is low. Stage II–III disease receives a third-generation anthracycline- and taxane-containing regimen; stage I disease receives four cycles of docetaxel and cyclophosphamide; below 0.5 cm the survival advantage is minimal, and above 0.5 cm chemotherapy is offered. RJBC-1501 tested adding carboplatin to adjuvant chemotherapy in 786 patients with resected early triple-negative disease, giving four cycles of epirubicin and cyclophosphamide then a taxane with or without carboplatin. Carboplatin improved disease-free survival (3-year 93.1% vs 89.8%; HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.97, P=0.034), distant disease-free survival (HR 0.61, P=0.040) and overall survival (HR 0.39, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.94, P=0.029) at 4.5 years, with more grade 3–4 haematological toxicity (any grade 3–4 event 49.9% vs 38.7%) (J Clin Oncol 2026;44:143-152). This is the adjuvant counterpart to the neoadjuvant platinum question, where the phase 3 test of adding carboplatin missed its primary event-free-survival endpoint and its overall survival and menopausal subgroup findings are nominal, pointing towards platinum in premenopausal disease and away from it postmenopausally. A germline BRCA1/2 variant changes the plan: a patient who has completed adjuvant chemotherapy and meets the OlympiA criteria set out above is a candidate for a year of adjuvant olaparib. Where neoadjuvant chemotherapy was given, adjuvant therapy is directed by response: pembrolizumab continues to a year on the KEYNOTE-522 protocol regardless of response, with capecitabine added for residual disease (CREATE-X) or olaparib where a germline BRCA variant is present. Those decisions are developed in the neoadjuvant chapter; no trial has tested how to combine or sequence the three in a patient who qualifies for all of them.

records.title: Bone-modifying agents
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: Adjuvant bisphosphonates reduce bone recurrence and breast cancer mortality in postmenopausal women. The EBCTCG adjuvant bisphosphonate meta-analysis pooled 18,766 women in 26 trials. Overall reductions were only borderline (recurrence RR 0.94, 2p=0.08; distant recurrence 0.92, 2p=0.03; breast cancer mortality 0.91, 2p=0.04), while the bone-recurrence reduction was definite (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.94, 2p=0.004). Among the 11,767 postmenopausal women, recurrence (RR 0.86), distant recurrence (0.82), bone recurrence (0.72; 10-year gain 2.2%) and breast cancer mortality (0.82; 10-year gain 3.3%) all fell significantly, while premenopausal women showed no apparent effect on any outcome (Lancet 2015;386:1353-1361). The postmenopausal boundary is less secure than those figures suggest: heterogeneity for bone recurrence was only borderline by menopausal status (2p=0.06 for trend) and correlated with age (2p=0.03), and no preferred agent, schedule or duration was established. Oral clodronate, oral ibandronate and intravenous zoledronate performed comparably; oral pamidronate showed no benefit. In practice, adjuvant bisphosphonates are considered for 3 to 5 years in postmenopausal women with node-positive or high-risk node-negative disease, usually as 6-monthly intravenous zoledronate. Denosumab is not used for this indication because the two trials disagree: ABCSG-18 reduced clinical fractures (HR 0.5, p<0.0001) with a disease-free survival improvement on interim analysis, whereas D-CARE found no difference in disease-free survival or bone-metastasis-free survival, its primary endpoint, with osteonecrosis of the jaw in 5.4% (Lancet 2020).

records.title: Older and less fit patients
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: Surgery followed by endocrine therapy remains preferred for older women with HR-positive disease. Primary endocrine therapy alone is an option for those unfit for surgery: a 2007 Cochrane meta-analysis found no significant overall survival difference between surgery plus endocrine therapy and endocrine therapy alone, only a trend, with progression-free survival favouring surgery plus tamoxifen. Anti-HER2 therapy should be incorporated in a fit older patient on the same basis as in a younger one. Triple-negative and HER2-positive tumours derive the greatest absolute benefit from chemotherapy, and PREDICT is a reasonable starting point for quantifying it. Regimen choice runs TC, or AC followed by a taxane in a very fit patient, with CMF where neither anthracycline nor taxane is tolerable. Where the patient is not a surgical candidate at all: ER-positive disease receives primary endocrine therapy, while HER2-positive and triple-negative disease are observed if asymptomatic, reserving HER2-directed therapy with single-agent chemotherapy, or single-agent chemotherapy such as capecitabine or weekly paclitaxel, for symptomatic or metastatic disease.

records.title: Follow-up
records.subtitle: Early breast cancer · Breast
records.body: History and examination 3- to 6-monthly for the first three years, 6- to 12-monthly in years four and five, and annually thereafter, with annual mammography. There is no indication for laboratory tests or imaging to screen for metastases in an asymptomatic patient.
