records.title: Make four decisions before treatment
records.subtitle: NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular profile · Lung
records.body: For every new lung carcinoma, establish the histological family, the anatomical stage, the molecular profile and whether one specimen can answer more than one question. Obtain enough viable tumour for morphology, focused immunohistochemistry and biomarker testing; a technically successful biopsy that exhausts the block before genotyping is not an adequate diagnostic episode. The practical sequence is: Confirm carcinoma and assign the most specific lineage that the specimen supports. Complete TNM staging before declaring treatment intent. Sample the site that gives the highest stage safely, while preserving tissue for molecular testing. Match each biomarker to an assay that can detect its alteration class. Screening eligibility and low-dose CT evidence are addressed in NSCLC: early and locally advanced disease ; this chapter begins once a lesion requires pathological and anatomical classification.

records.title: Classify by morphology first
records.subtitle: NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular profile · Lung
records.body: Use the current WHO thoracic classification rather than the historical small-cell-versus-NSCLC binary alone. Within NSCLC, the major families are adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma and other defined or undifferentiated epithelial tumours. Pulmonary carcinoids belong with lung neuroendocrine neoplasms, not under NSCLC 1 . Record each pattern in a resected invasive non-mucinous adenocarcinoma in 5% increments. Grade 1 is lepidic-predominant disease with less than 20% high-grade pattern; grade 2 is acinar- or papillary-predominant disease with less than 20% high-grade pattern; grade 3 contains at least 20% solid, micropapillary or complex-glandular pattern, whatever the predominant pattern 2 . Do not infer a complete resection diagnosis from a small sample. Adenosquamous carcinoma requires at least 10% each of glandular and squamous components in a resection; a biopsy showing both should be reported descriptively. Large cell carcinoma is likewise a resection diagnosis of exclusion after morphology and ancillary testing fail to establish a more specific lineage 1 . Pulmonary lymphoepithelial carcinoma is now classified under squamous cell carcinoma. Demonstrate tumour-cell EBV association where this morphology is suspected, correlate with imaging and clinical findings, and exclude a nasopharyngeal primary rather than assuming that a lung lesion is primary solely because it was biopsied in the chest 1 .

records.title: Use a minimal, question-led immunohistochemistry panel
records.subtitle: NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular profile · Lung
records.body: On a poorly differentiated non-small-cell carcinoma without clear glandular, squamous or neuroendocrine morphology, TTF-1 and p40 are usually the first lineage pair. Prefer p40 to p63 for squamous differentiation and add napsin A or mucin only when the initial result and morphology remain unresolved. This conserves tissue for predictive testing 3 . Diagnostic question Morphology and first-line markers Interpretation trap Adenocarcinoma Glands or intracytoplasmic mucin; TTF-1 and/or napsin A support pulmonary lineage TTF-1 is not lung-specific; thyroid and some neuroendocrine carcinomas can express it Squamous carcinoma Keratinisation or intercellular bridges; diffuse p40 supports squamous lineage Focal p63 alone is less specific; CK7 does not exclude squamous carcinoma Small-cell carcinoma Small blue cells, nuclear moulding, scant cytoplasm, necrosis and brisk mitoses; INSM1, synaptophysin, chromogranin or CD56 support neuroendocrine differentiation Neuroendocrine-marker expression alone does not override non-neuroendocrine morphology Large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma Non-small-cell cytology with neuroendocrine architecture, high mitotic activity and necrosis, plus neuroendocrine differentiation It is not synonymous with large cell carcinoma Adenosquamous carcinoma Distinct glandular and squamous areas, each at least 10% in a resection A small biopsy cannot establish the required whole-tumour proportions Large cell carcinoma Undifferentiated non-small-cell carcinoma after exclusion of glandular, squamous and other defined lineages Reserve the label for a thoroughly sampled resection CD45 is an exclusion marker for lymphoma, not a positive marker of small-cell carcinoma. Ki-67 can support separation of a carcinoid from a high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma in a crushed small specimen, but pulmonary carcinoid classification is not assigned from a gastrointestinal Ki-67 grading scheme 3 . When the differential includes a metastasis, select markers from the clinical and morphological question rather than applying a fixed organ panel. Useful anchors include thyroglobulin or PAX8 for thyroid; SATB2 and CDX2 for colorectal; GATA3 and ER for breast; PAX8 and CAIX for renal; NKX3.1 or PSA for prostate; PAX8 and WT1 for Müllerian; and arginase-1 or HepPar-1 for hepatocellular lineage. No single result proves origin 3 .

records.title: Choose a specimen that establishes the highest stage
records.subtitle: NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular profile · Lung
records.body: If a distant lesion is safely accessible and its nature will change intent, biopsy it in preference to the lung primary: one procedure can establish diagnosis and M stage. Confirm an isolated or unexpected metastatic focus before abandoning curative treatment, because infection, inflammation and a second primary can mimic metastatic disease 4 . When disease appears confined to the thorax, choose between image-guided core biopsy, bronchoscopy, EBUS-TBNA, EUS-guided sampling or surgical biopsy according to lesion position and the staging question. Communicate the need for histology, PD-L1 and molecular testing before the procedure, request a cell block where appropriate, and avoid serial single-gene tests that consume the specimen 5 .

records.title: Stage with TNM-9
records.subtitle: NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular profile · Lung
records.body: This chapter uses the IASLC/UICC lung TNM ninth edition descriptors and stage groups. T descriptors are unchanged from the eighth edition; N2 is split by single versus multiple ipsilateral mediastinal stations, and M1c is split by one versus multiple extrathoracic organ systems. Confirm the version used by the local cancer registry when dates or jurisdictions differ 6 . T category Category Definition Tis Carcinoma in situ T1mi Minimally invasive adenocarcinoma no larger than 3 cm, lepidic-predominant, with invasion no greater than 5 mm T1a / T1b / T1c No greater than 1 cm / greater than 1–2 cm / greater than 2–3 cm T2a Greater than 3–4 cm, or a tumour no greater than 4 cm with visceral-pleural invasion, main-bronchus involvement without carinal invasion, atelectasis or obstructive pneumonitis extending to the hilum, or direct invasion across a fissure into an adjacent lobe T2b Greater than 4–5 cm T3 Greater than 5–7 cm; separate nodule in the same lobe; or invasion of chest wall/parietal pleura, pericardium, phrenic nerve, azygos vein, T1–T2 nerve roots or stellate ganglion T4 Greater than 7 cm; separate nodule in a different ipsilateral lobe; or invasion of mediastinum, thymus, trachea, carina, recurrent laryngeal or vagus nerve, oesophagus, diaphragm, heart, great vessels, vertebral body, spinal canal or brachial plexus For a part-solid non-mucinous adenocarcinoma, use the invasive component, rather than the total lepidic span, for pathological T size. Record both total and invasive dimensions because radiological and pathological measurements answer different questions. N and M categories Category Definition N0 No regional nodal metastasis N1 Ipsilateral intrapulmonary, peribronchial or hilar nodes, including direct extension N2a One ipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal nodal station N2b Multiple ipsilateral mediastinal and/or subcarinal nodal stations N3 Contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular node M0 No distant metastasis M1a Contralateral-lung nodule, pleural or pericardial nodule, or malignant pleural or pericardial effusion M1b One extrathoracic metastasis in one organ system, including one non-regional node M1c1 Multiple extrathoracic metastases confined to one organ system M1c2 Multiple extrathoracic metastases in more than one organ system Station 1 comprises low cervical, supraclavicular and sternal-notch nodes and is N3. Stations 2–9 are mediastinal, including station 7 subcarinal; stations 10–14 are hilar, interlobar, lobar, segmental and subsegmental N1 stations. State the station and side, not merely “mediastinal node,” because single-station N2a and multi-station N2b now group differently. Stage groups Stage TNM-9 grouping 0 Tis N0 M0 IA1 T1mi/T1a N0 M0 IA2 T1b N0 M0 IA3 T1c N0 M0 IB T2a N0 M0 IIA T2b N0 M0; or T1 N1 M0 IIB T1 N2a M0; T2 N1 M0; or T3 N0 M0 IIIA T1 N2b M0; T2 N2a M0; T3 N1–N2a M0; or T4 N0–N1 M0 IIIB T1 N3 M0; T2 N2b–N3 M0; T3 N2b M0; or T4 N2a–N2b M0 IIIC T3–T4 N3 M0 IVA Any T, any N, M1a or M1b IVB Any T, any N, M1c1 or M1c2 The changes most likely to alter a treatment pathway are T1N1 from IIB to IIA, T1N2a from IIIA to IIB, T3N2a from IIIB to IIIA, and T2N2b from IIIA to IIIB. Do not translate an old trial’s eligibility label into TNM-9 without reconstructing its T, N and M descriptors.

records.title: Complete imaging before fixing treatment intent
records.subtitle: NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular profile · Lung
records.body: Start with contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and upper abdomen, including adrenals. Add FDG PET-CT for a patient being considered for curative local treatment to identify occult nodal or distant disease and to choose the best biopsy target; a solitary PET-positive distant lesion needs pathological confirmation if it would change intent. Brain MRI is preferred when brain staging is indicated, particularly for stage III or neurological symptoms 4 . In a randomised staging trial of 189 patients referred for preoperative staging, the alpha-protected primary thoracotomy-subgroup analysis found futile thoracotomy in 38/73 (52%) with conventional staging and 21/60 (35%) with PET-CT plus conventional staging (P=.05). Mediastinoscopy was mandatory in both groups 7 . The prespecified exploratory all-randomised analysis found futile thoracotomy in 38/91 (42%) versus 21/98 (21%), with no inferential test reported: an absolute reduction of 21 percentage points, or about one avoided futile thoracotomy for every five patients staged. The trial stopped early and showed no survival difference 7 . Whole-body MRI is not a default substitute for standard staging. In the prospective paired Streamline L study, 353 participants were enrolled but only 187 entered the primary accuracy analysis; among the 52 patients with metastases, there was no evidence of a difference in sensitivity (50% versus 54%; difference -4 percentage points, 95% CI -15 to 7; P=.73). MRI shortened median staging time from 19 to 13 days and lowered mean staging cost from £620 to £317 8 .

records.title: Confirm mediastinal disease when it can change intent
records.subtitle: NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular profile · Lung
records.body: Invasive mediastinal staging can usually be omitted for a peripheral tumour no larger than 3 cm with no enlarged or FDG-avid nodes and no clinical N1 disease. Use systematic EBUS-TBNA, with EUS where it adds access, when mediastinal or hilar nodes are enlarged or avid, or when the tumour is central, larger than 3 cm, FDG-nonavid or associated with clinical N1 disease. A malignant result establishes nodal stage. After a negative endosonographic result, review whether the relevant stations were systematically examined, whether sampling was adequate and whether imaging remains discordant. Surgical staging remains appropriate when suspicion is high or endosonography was incomplete; it is not an automatic consequence of every negative EBUS or EUS 4 . In the randomised MEDIASTrial, immediate resection after systematic negative endosonography produced an unforeseen N2 rate of 8.8%, non-inferior to 7.7% with confirmatory mediastinoscopy; mediastinoscopy itself found N2/3 disease in 8.0%. This supports omitting routine confirmatory mediastinoscopy after a high-quality negative systematic examination in appropriately selected resectable disease, not omitting surgical confirmation when the examination was inadequate or discordant 9 .

records.title: Build the molecular profile before systemic treatment
records.subtitle: NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular profile · Lung
records.body: For advanced non-squamous NSCLC, use a broad validated tumour NGS panel rather than serial single-gene testing. Test a confident pure squamous carcinoma when clinical or pathological features raise the possibility of an occult non-squamous component or actionable driver: for example young age, never/light smoking or limited tissue. Do not use ethnicity, sex or smoking history to withhold testing from an adenocarcinoma 5 . At minimum, the advanced-disease profile should resolve EGFR , ALK , ROS1 , BRAF , KRAS , MET exon 14 skipping, RET , NTRK1/2/3 and ERBB2/HER2 . A sufficiently broad panel should also identify relevant copy-number changes and rarer fusions such as NRG1 . Determine PD-L1 by a validated immunohistochemistry assay; PD-L1 is not a substitute for genotyping 10 . In potentially curable disease, order the biomarkers required by the contemplated perioperative, adjuvant or consolidation pathway early enough that results can change the plan. The early-stage and metastatic treatment chapters define regimen-specific eligibility; this chapter defines what the reported alteration means. Match the assay to the alteration Biomarker Reportable alteration Preferred approach and caveat EGFR Exon 19 deletion, L858R, G719X, L861Q, S768I, exon 20 insertion and other named variants Validated DNA NGS; a hotspot PCR assay is acceptable only if its report makes coverage and blind spots explicit ALK Fusion/rearrangement Validated IHC can establish positivity; FISH or DNA/RNA NGS can resolve discordance, and RNA NGS can identify the expressed fusion ROS1 Fusion/rearrangement RNA NGS or FISH; if IHC is used to screen, confirm a positive result molecularly RET , NTRK1/2/3 , NRG1 Fusion/rearrangement RNA-based sequencing is preferred when feasible; DNA panels may miss rearrangements because of intronic coverage BRAF , KRAS Named sequence variant DNA NGS or a validated allele-specific assay; report the exact variant rather than gene-positive status MET Exon 14 skipping DNA and/or RNA NGS with validated splice-site coverage; RNA directly demonstrates the skipped transcript MET Amplification Copy-number-capable NGS or FISH; report method, copy number and/or MET /CEP7 ratio rather than “MET-positive” ERBB2/HER2 Activating mutation, amplification or protein overexpression DNA NGS for mutation, copy-number assay for amplification, IHC for protein; these are distinct biomarkers and are not interchangeable PD-L1 Tumour-cell protein expression Validated IHC; report clone/platform, tumour proportion score and adequacy Multiplex NGS is preferred because it conserves tissue and detects mutually uncommon events in parallel. The CAP/IASLC/AMP guideline supports multiplex panels over serial single-gene assays and permits cell-free DNA to rule in a targetable alteration when tissue is limited; an uninformative plasma result does not rule one out 11 . Use plasma as a complement, not a negative biopsy A clearly pathogenic, therapeutically relevant alteration detected by a validated plasma assay can establish the molecular result when the clinical context fits. A negative or low-shedding plasma result requires tissue testing if feasible. Obtain tissue when histological transformation, a second primary or a mechanism requiring morphology is suspected, even if plasma is positive 12 . Interpret the alteration class, not merely the gene EGFR exon 19 deletion and L858R are common sensitising variants; G719X, L861Q and S768I are heterogeneous uncommon variants; exon 20 insertions form a distinct group; and a resistance alteration must be reported with specimen timing and treatment context. The approximately 10% figure in older summaries applies to the uncommon G719X/L861Q/S768I group collectively, not to S768I alone. Structure can be more informative than exon number for uncommon EGFR variants. A retrospective translational analysis of 16,715 patients proposed classical-like, T790M-like, exon-20-loop-insertion and P-loop/αC-helix-compressing classes; the framework predicted inhibitor sensitivity better than exon grouping with nominal P<0.0001, but it was not a randomised treatment comparison 13 . Treatment outcomes for uncommon EGFR variants, including the pooled LUX-Lung analysis, are addressed in NSCLC: metastatic disease . Keep these distinctions explicit: An ALK , ROS1 , RET , NTRK or NRG1 fusion is not equivalent to nonspecific protein expression. MET exon 14 skipping, focal high-level amplification and c-MET protein overexpression are separate biomarkers. ERBB2/HER2 mutation, amplification and protein overexpression are separate biomarkers. BRAF V600E must be distinguished from non-V600E classes, and KRAS must be reported by variant. Co-alterations, tumour content, assay limits and whether the result came from tissue or plasma belong in the report.

records.title: Use epidemiology to anticipate, never to exclude
records.subtitle: NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular profile · Lung
records.body: Driver prevalence varies by population and selection. In Asian NSCLC series, EGFR alterations occur in roughly 40%–60%, ALK in 2.3%–6.7%, BRAF in about 1.3%, RET in 1%–2%, MET exon 14 skipping in 2%–4%, MET amplification in 1%–5%, ERBB2/HER2 mutation in 1%–4%, and NTRK fusion in less than 1%. These are planning estimates, not patient-selection rules 5 . Alterations involving EGFR , ALK , ROS1 , RET , ERBB2/HER2 and NTRK are enriched in never-smokers, while KRAS and some other RAS–MAPK alterations are enriched with tobacco exposure; BRAF and MET occur across smoking categories. None of these associations is sufficiently deterministic to replace testing.

records.title: Lung-cancer screening
records.subtitle: NSCLC: early and locally advanced disease · Lung
records.body: Lung-cancer screening eligibility must follow the current local programme, not an old age-and-pack-year fragment. As one reference point, the USPSTF recommends annual LDCT for adults aged 50-80 years with at least 20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within 15 years 1 . TALENT was a prospective single-arm cohort of 12,011 never- or very-light smokers with additional risk factors; it reported baseline detection, not a randomised mortality comparison, and explicitly raised overdiagnosis as a possibility. It therefore cannot establish a survival benefit or no benefit for screening never-smokers 2 .

records.title: Define stage, intent and resectability before choosing treatment
records.subtitle: NSCLC: early and locally advanced disease · Lung
records.body: Use the current ninth-edition TNM system and record both clinical and pathological stage when available. The classification chapter owns the T, N and M definitions, histopathology and molecular interpretation; the treatment consequence here is that N2a and N2b disease are distinct and that an apparently small primary may still require multimodality therapy 3 . Curative-intent decisions require a thoracic multidisciplinary review that integrates technical resectability, mediastinal nodal burden, the operation required for an R0 resection, cardiopulmonary reserve and the systemic-treatment plan. Stage IIIA(N2) disease is not uniformly resectable; surgery is reasonable only when complete resection is feasible, N3 disease is excluded and expected 90-day mortality is low 4 . Confirm curative-intent stage before selecting local treatment Complete the imaging and invasive nodal-staging pathway in NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular profile before choosing surgery, SABR or definitive chemoradiation. The treatment meeting needs three outputs: whether any distant lesion that would change intent has been resolved, the mediastinal nodal status when it changes resectability, and brain MRI for stage III or otherwise clinically high-risk disease. Establish whether the proposed operation is physiologically tolerable Measure FEV1 and DLCO in every surgical candidate, calculate predicted postoperative values for the planned resection, and assess cardiovascular risk. Values above 60% predicted for both measures identify low pulmonary risk; values from 30% to 60% require a low-technology exercise test, while either value below 30% or poor exercise performance should prompt cardiopulmonary exercise testing 5 . A peak oxygen uptake below 10 mL/kg/min or 35% predicted indicates high risk for major anatomical resection, whereas a value above 20 mL/kg/min or 75% predicted indicates low risk. Do not substitute fixed absolute FEV1 cut-offs for this integrated assessment; the relevant question is whether the patient can tolerate the operation required for complete resection 5 .

records.title: Choose the least extensive oncologically adequate local treatment
records.subtitle: NSCLC: early and locally advanced disease · Lung
records.body: Anatomical resection with systematic hilar and mediastinal nodal evaluation is preferred for operable disease. Lobectomy remains appropriate for most tumours, while sleeve resection can avoid pneumonectomy when it achieves an R0 result. En-bloc resection of an involved adjacent structure is justified only when complete resection is technically achievable and the patient can tolerate the procedure. For peripheral, node-negative tumours measuring no more than 2 cm, anatomical segmentectomy is an evidence-based alternative to lobectomy after rigorous intraoperative nodal confirmation. CALGB 140503 established non-inferior disease-free survival for sublobar resection, while JCOG0802 showed superior overall survival with segmentectomy but more local recurrence; wedge resection is less favoured when an anatomical segmentectomy is feasible 6 7 . Systematic nodal evaluation is part of curative resection. In patients with T1-2, N0 or non-hilar N1 disease whose specified hilar and mediastinal stations were negative on thorough sampling, complete mediastinal dissection did not improve survival or recurrence outcomes; that result does not apply to radiographic staging alone or to higher-stage disease 8 . Offer stereotactic ablative radiotherapy to medically inoperable patients with node-negative stage I disease and consider it when operative risk is prohibitive after multidisciplinary review. Surgery remains standard for patients at usual operative risk; non-operative treatment does not remove the need for adequate staging or tissue diagnosis when safely obtainable 9 .

records.title: Stage I: surgery is usually definitive
records.subtitle: NSCLC: early and locally advanced disease · Lung
records.body: After complete resection of stage IA disease, surveillance is standard and adjuvant cytotoxic chemotherapy is not indicated. The individual-patient-data LACE analysis suggested no benefit in stage IA and established that the survival gain from postoperative cisplatin-based chemotherapy is concentrated in higher-stage disease 10 . Routine chemotherapy is also not supported for all stage IB tumours. CALGB 9633 did not improve overall or disease-free survival in resected T2N0 disease; its unplanned subgroup with tumours at least 4 cm suggested benefit but remains hypothesis-generating. A tumour at least 4 cm, adverse pathological features and nodal uncertainty should therefore trigger individualised discussion rather than an automatic rule 11 . Two years of oral uracil-tegafur improved survival after resection of pathological stage I adenocarcinoma in a Japanese phase III trial, but this regional regimen has not become a general substitute for contemporary stage- and biomarker-directed care. Its positive result should therefore be read as historical evidence of adjuvant sensitivity, not as a universal treatment recommendation 12 . Test resected nonsquamous tumours for actionable alterations before selecting adjuvant immunotherapy. Patients with an EGFR exon 19 deletion or L858R mutation may receive three years of osimertinib after complete resection, with adjuvant platinum chemotherapy given when otherwise indicated; patients with ALK-positive tumours at least 4 cm or node-positive disease may receive two years of alectinib 13 14 . Earlier-stage and longer-duration osimertinib remain research questions rather than extensions of the ADAURA standard. ADAURA2 is testing three years after complete resection of stage IA2-IA3 EGFR-mutant disease, while the single-arm TARGET study is testing five years after resection of stage II-IIIB disease; neither currently supports treatment beyond its studied setting 15 16 .

records.title: Resectable stage II and selected stage III: plan the entire perioperative course
records.subtitle: NSCLC: early and locally advanced disease · Lung
records.body: Before starting treatment, document that an R0 resection is technically plausible and choose between surgery-first and neoadjuvant or perioperative therapy. Tumours at least 4 cm or node-positive disease without EGFR or ALK alterations generally warrant platinum-doublet chemotherapy plus an immune-checkpoint inhibitor before surgery; a surgery-first pathway remains appropriate when treatment delay, diagnostic uncertainty or anatomical urgency makes neoadjuvant therapy unsuitable. Molecular results must be available before immune-checkpoint therapy whenever feasible. EGFR- or ALK-driven tumours should usually follow a resection-first pathway with stage-appropriate chemotherapy and genotype-directed adjuvant therapy, because the pivotal perioperative immunotherapy trials excluded known EGFR and ALK alterations and because targeted perioperative evidence remains less mature. Neoadjuvant and perioperative chemoimmunotherapy Earlier phase II studies established feasibility but do not supersede the randomised phase III regimens below. NADIM and NADIM II supported perioperative nivolumab-chemotherapy in selected stage III disease 17 18 . NEOSTAR tested chemotherapy-free and chemotherapy-containing nivolumab-ipilimumab strategies 19 20 , while LCMC3 tested neoadjuvant atezolizumab alone 21 ; their pathological responses remain hypothesis-generating across differing populations and designs. Three cycles of neoadjuvant nivolumab plus platinum-doublet chemotherapy improved five-year overall survival, event-free survival and pathological complete response without reducing definitive surgery in CheckMate 816 (five-year overall survival 65.4% versus 55.0%; HR 0.72). Grade 3-4 treatment-related toxicity was similar to chemotherapy alone, making this a concise neoadjuvant option without mandated postoperative nivolumab 22 . Perioperative regimens add approximately one year of checkpoint inhibition after surgery. Their comparative efficacy and the independent contribution of the postoperative component are not established, so selection should account for trial population, regulator access, toxicity, pathological findings and the practical likelihood of completing postoperative therapy. Pembrolizumab plus four cycles of neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy followed by up to 13 postoperative cycles improved both overall and event-free survival in KEYNOTE-671 (36-month overall survival 71% versus 64%; HR 0.72). Grade 3-5 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 44.9% versus 37.3%, and postoperative mortality was numerically higher 23 . Durvalumab plus four cycles of neoadjuvant platinum chemotherapy followed by up to 12 postoperative cycles improved interim event-free survival and pathological complete response in the EGFR/ALK-negative efficacy population in AEGEAN (EFS HR 0.68; pCR 17.2% versus 4.3%). Overall survival was not mature in the accepted primary report 24 . Nivolumab plus four cycles of neoadjuvant platinum chemotherapy followed by one year of nivolumab improved interim event-free survival in CheckMate 77T (18-month 70.2% versus 50.0%; HR 0.58). Pathological response comparisons were descriptive, and two treatment-related pneumonitis deaths occurred with nivolumab 25 . Toripalimab improved event-free survival and major pathological response in the reported stage III cohort of Neotorch, but overall survival was still uncertain and grade 3 or worse adverse events were more frequent. The stage II cohort remained blinded at that publication, so the result should not be generalized beyond the analysed population 26 . Perioperative tislelizumab improved final overall survival and event-free survival in stage II-IIIA disease in RATIONALE-315 (36-month overall survival 79.3% versus 69.3%; HR 0.65). Grade 3 or worse treatment-related events occurred in 73.0% versus 67.3%; use the locally approved regimen-specific protocol for chemotherapy selection and dosing 27 . EGFR- and ALK-directed neoadjuvant therapy remains selective NeoADAURA increased major pathological response with neoadjuvant osimertinib with or without chemotherapy, but event-free survival was immature and more than 90% of operated patients in every arm received adjuvant osimertinib. The trial therefore does not establish that preoperative osimertinib should replace prompt resection followed by indicated chemotherapy and adjuvant osimertinib 28 . Single-arm neoadjuvant targeted studies can inform trials and exceptional multidisciplinary decisions but do not define a general standard. LORIN reported high pathological response among operated patients with stage III ALK-fusion disease, including some initially considered unresectable, but survival follow-up was short and the operated analysis was post-randomisation 29 .

records.title: After surgery: match adjuvant therapy to pathological risk and genotype
records.subtitle: NSCLC: early and locally advanced disease · Lung
records.body: Platinum chemotherapy remains the backbone for stage II-III disease Offer four cycles of a cisplatin-based doublet after complete resection of stage II or III disease when chemotherapy was not given preoperatively and the patient is fit. LACE showed a 5.4-point absolute overall-survival gain at five years (HR 0.89), with a 0.9% chemotherapy-death rate and increased early non-lung-cancer mortality 10 . Cisplatin-vinorelbine has direct survival evidence from JBR.10 and ANITA but causes substantial neutropenia and febrile neutropenia. Histology-appropriate cisplatin-pemetrexed is often better tolerated in nonsquamous disease; cisplatin-gemcitabine or cisplatin-docetaxel are alternatives for squamous disease. Carboplatin should usually be reserved for patients unable to receive cisplatin 30 31 . The IALT experience supports both the benefit and the need for long-term caution: the early overall-survival advantage attenuated with extended follow-up, while disease-free survival remained improved and late non-lung-cancer mortality was higher. This does not reverse the pooled standard for fit stage II-III patients, but it reinforces careful selection and survivorship management 32 . Genotype-directed adjuvant treatment For completely resected EGFR exon 19 deletion or L858R disease, osimertinib for three years improved both disease-free and overall survival (five-year overall survival 88% versus 78% in stage IB-IIIA; HR 0.49). Give platinum chemotherapy first when indicated; osimertinib is not a substitute for the established chemotherapy benefit in fit stage II-III patients 13 . For completely resected ALK-positive disease at least 4 cm or node positive, alectinib for two years improved disease-free survival over four cycles of platinum chemotherapy (stage II-IIIA two-year DFS 93.8% versus 63.0%; HR 0.24). Overall survival was immature, and the comparator means this strategy replaces rather than follows chemotherapy in the pivotal trial 14 . Adjuvant ensartinib and selpercatinib have positive 2026 disease-control results in ALK-positive and RET fusion-positive disease, respectively, but overall survival is immature and availability is jurisdiction-specific. Discuss them only within current regulatory access or a clinical trial rather than extrapolating a class effect from metastatic disease 33 34 . Adjuvant immunotherapy is for selected oncogene-negative disease After complete resection and cisplatin-based chemotherapy, atezolizumab improved disease-free survival in the alpha-protected stage II-IIIA PD-L1 tumour-cell ≥1% population. The largest point estimates occurred in unadjusted PD-L1 tumour-cell ≥50% subgroups, but no treatment-by-PD-L1 interaction test was reported. Final ITT DFS was not significant and interim ITT overall survival was nonformal 35 . Pembrolizumab for up to one year improved interim disease-free survival in the overall resected stage IB at least 4 cm to IIIA population, but not in the PD-L1 TPS at least 50% co-primary population; overall survival was immature. The evidence does not support using PD-L1 alone to predict benefit 36 . Negative trials constrain cross-trial extrapolation. One year of adjuvant nivolumab did not improve disease-free or overall survival in ANVIL 37 , and durvalumab did not improve disease-free survival in BR.31 38 . Do not assume that any checkpoint inhibitor, assay threshold or treatment duration is interchangeable with a positive regimen. Postoperative radiotherapy is not routine after R0 resection Do not give routine PORT after complete resection solely because pN2 disease is present. Lung ART did not improve disease-free or overall survival, reduced mediastinal relapse and increased grade 3 or worse toxicity; PORT-C likewise did not improve its primary disease-free-survival analysis after complete resection and chemotherapy 39 40 . Use postoperative radiotherapy selectively for microscopically or macroscopically positive margins when re-resection is not feasible, after multidisciplinary review of recurrence risk, field size and cardiopulmonary toxicity. High-risk nodal features alone do not establish an overall-survival benefit from PORT in an R0-resected patient.

records.title: Stage III: separate potentially resectable from unresectable disease
records.subtitle: NSCLC: early and locally advanced disease · Lung
records.body: Potentially resectable stage III disease is a multidisciplinary category, not a TNM label. Surgery after induction therapy may be considered when R0 resection of the primary and involved nodes is plausible, N3 disease is absent, perioperative mortality is expected to be no more than 5%, and lobectomy or sleeve resection is feasible; planned pneumonectomy, bulky multistation N2 or progressive disease weighs against surgery 4 . For an incidental pathological N2 finding after upfront R0 resection, give adjuvant platinum chemotherapy if not previously delivered and select genotype-directed or immune therapy according to the postoperative algorithm. PORT is not routine for R0 disease. For known N2 disease, either a planned multimodality surgical pathway in a high-volume team or definitive chemoradiation is preferable to unplanned surgery followed by rescue therapy.

records.title: Unresectable stage III: definitive chemoradiation followed by biomarker-directed consolidation
records.subtitle: NSCLC: early and locally advanced disease · Lung
records.body: Deliver concurrent chemoradiation when the patient is fit Concurrent platinum-based chemoradiation improves overall survival over sequential treatment, principally through better locoregional control (HR 0.84; absolute gain 4.5% at five years), but increases grade 3-4 acute oesophagitis from 4% to 18%. Use sequential chemotherapy and radiotherapy when comorbidity, frailty or treatment volume makes concurrent therapy unsafe 41 . Use definitive thoracic radiotherapy to about 60 Gy with a concurrent radiosensitising platinum doublet. Do not escalate routinely to 74 Gy: the randomised RTOG 0617 comparison showed worse survival with 74 Gy, and adding cetuximab did not improve outcome 42 . Common concurrent regimens are cisplatin-etoposide, weekly carboplatin-paclitaxel, or cisplatin-pemetrexed for nonsquamous histology. PROCLAIM did not show superior overall or progression-free survival with cisplatin-pemetrexed over cisplatin-etoposide. Grade 3–4 toxicity was lower across the whole treatment course, which used different consolidation regimens, while any-grade pneumonitis was more frequent; the comparison does not isolate concurrent-doublet tolerability. Choose according to histology, renal function, marrow reserve and pulmonary risk 43 . Consolidate according to EGFR status For unresectable stage III disease without progression after platinum-based concurrent chemoradiation and without a sensitising EGFR alteration, offer durvalumab for up to 12 months. PACIFIC improved progression-free and overall survival, with five-year overall survival of 42.9% versus 33.4%; pneumonitis or radiation pneumonitis occurred in 33.9% versus 24.8% 44 . Durvalumab can be considered after sequential chemoradiation when concurrent treatment was unsuitable, but the specific evidence is less secure. PACIFIC-5 improved progression-free survival across a mixed concurrent and sequential population, while the sequential subgroup was exploratory, both confidence intervals crossed 1 and no interaction test was reported 45 . For unresectable stage III disease with EGFR exon 19 deletion or L858R and no progression during or after concurrent or sequential platinum chemoradiation, give osimertinib 80 mg daily until progression or unacceptable toxicity. LAURA improved median progression-free survival from 5.6 to 39.1 months (HR 0.16); overall survival was immature, and interstitial lung disease requires active monitoring 46 47 . Starting immunotherapy concurrently with chemoradiation has not improved on the consolidation strategy. PACIFIC-2 did not improve progression-free or overall survival with durvalumab from the start of chemoradiation, and CheckMate 73L did not improve progression-free survival with concurrent nivolumab followed by nivolumab-ipilimumab compared with chemoradiation followed by durvalumab 48 49 .

records.title: Surveillance after curative-intent treatment
records.subtitle: NSCLC: early and locally advanced disease · Lung
records.body: Use history, examination and chest CT including the adrenals every six months for two years, then annually to detect recurrence and new primary lung cancers. Contrast is preferred during the first two years when appropriate. Do not use routine PET-CT, brain MRI or circulating biomarkers for asymptomatic surveillance; investigate symptoms and indeterminate radiographic abnormalities outside this schedule 50 . Offer surveillance only when detection of recurrence or a new primary could lead to treatment the patient would accept. At suspected relapse, restage according to the clinical problem, obtain tissue when it can change management, and use the metastatic NSCLC chapter for systemic selection and sequencing.

records.title: Choose the molecular compartment before treatment
records.subtitle: NSCLC: metastatic disease · Lung
records.body: Do not start a checkpoint inhibitor until an actionable-driver result is available unless clinical urgency makes delay unsafe. Histopathology, staging, assay selection and biomarker interpretation belong in NSCLC: classification, staging and molecular features ; this chapter starts after those results have assigned the patient to a treatment compartment. The first systemic choice depends on four questions: Is there a targetable genomic alteration? If no target is found, what is the PD-L1 tumour proportion score? Is the tumour squamous or non-squamous? Does disease burden, tempo, CNS involvement or performance status require the fastest attainable response? IPASS showed why genotype precedes phenotype. In clinically enriched East Asian never- or light-smokers, gefitinib improved progression-free survival overall, but the treatment interaction reversed by EGFR status: HR 0.48 in mutant tumours and 2.85 in wild-type tumours (interaction P<0.001).

records.title: No actionable driver
records.subtitle: NSCLC: metastatic disease · Lung
records.body: Select first line by fitness, histology and PD-L1 For a fit patient, chemo-immunotherapy is the default across PD-L1 strata when rapid cytoreduction is important. Checkpoint monotherapy is reasonable with high PD-L1 expression when lower early toxicity matters more than maximal response probability; no randomised trial directly compares those strategies, and indirect evidence favours chemo-immunotherapy for overall and progression-free survival at the cost of greater toxicity 2 . For platinum-ineligible disease, atezolizumab monotherapy is an evidence-based alternative to single-agent gemcitabine or vinorelbine. IPSOS enrolled 453 patients unsuitable for platinum doublets and improved overall survival (10.3 vs 9.2 months; HR 0.78), with fewer grade 3–4 treatment-related events (16% vs 33%) 3 . High PD-L1 expression KEYNOTE-024 established pembrolizumab for PD-L1 TPS ≥50% disease without EGFR or ALK : five-year overall survival was 31.9% versus 16.3% with chemotherapy (HR 0.62). Treatment-related grade 3–5 events were 31.2% versus 53.3%. KEYNOTE-042 extended pembrolizumab to TPS ≥1%, but the exploratory TPS 1–49% estimate was inconclusive (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.75–1.04). Monotherapy is therefore most persuasive when PD-L1 is high, disease is not immediately threatening and chemotherapy avoidance has value. IMpower110 supports atezolizumab monotherapy in SP142-high disease (overall survival 20.2 vs 13.1 months; HR 0.59). Assay definition matters: its TC3/IC3 population is not interchangeable with a TPS threshold. HARMONi-2 improved progression-free survival with ivonescimab over pembrolizumab in PD-L1 TPS ≥1% disease (11.1 vs 5.8 months; HR 0.51), but overall survival was immature and possible severe VEGF-related events were more frequent. The study was conducted in China. OptiTROP-Lung05 added sacituzumab tirumotecan to pembrolizumab and improved interim progression-free survival (HR 0.35; 12-month rate 62% vs 29%). Overall survival is immature, so this does not yet replace established first-line regimens. CAMPASS improved blinded-review progression-free survival with benmelstobart–anlotinib over pembrolizumab (11.0 vs 7.1 months; HR 0.70), but overall survival was immature and severe hypertension was common. This is not a low-toxicity substitute for checkpoint monotherapy. Non-squamous disease KEYNOTE-189 supports pembrolizumab with platinum–pemetrexed followed by pembrolizumab–pemetrexed maintenance. At five years, overall survival was 19.4% versus 11.3% with chemotherapy (HR 0.60); treatment-related grade 3–5 events were 52.3% versus 42.1%. IMpower130 supports atezolizumab with carboplatin–nab-paclitaxel in EGFR / ALK -wild-type disease (overall survival 18.6 vs 13.9 months; HR 0.79; progression-free survival 7.0 vs 5.5 months; HR 0.64). IMpower132 improved progression-free survival with atezolizumab–platinum–pemetrexed (7.6 vs 5.2 months; HR 0.60), but final overall survival was inconclusive (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.71–1.06). It is supportive rather than defining evidence. RATIONALE-304 improved progression-free survival with tislelizumab–platinum–pemetrexed (9.8 vs 7.6 months; HR 0.63), but the final, unprotected overall-survival estimate was inconclusive (21.4 vs 21.3 months; HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.63-1.28). IMpower150 adds bevacizumab to atezolizumab–carboplatin–paclitaxel. In wild-type disease, overall survival was 19.5 versus 14.7 months (HR 0.80); bleeding risk, vascular comorbidity and the paclitaxel burden govern selection. Squamous disease KEYNOTE-407 supports pembrolizumab with carboplatin–paclitaxel or nab-paclitaxel. Five-year overall survival was 18.4% versus 9.7% (HR 0.71); exploratory PD-L1 subgroup estimates had no reported interaction test. RATIONALE-307 improved progression-free survival with tislelizumab plus carboplatin and either paclitaxel formulation, but final overall-survival estimates were inconclusive. Grade ≥3 treatment-related events exceeded 80% in all three arms. HARMONi-6 compared two active chemo-immunotherapy regimens in China. Ivonescimab–carboplatin–paclitaxel improved progression-free survival over tislelizumab–chemotherapy (11.1 vs 6.9 months; HR 0.60) and updated overall survival (27.9 vs 23.7 months; HR 0.66), with more grade ≥3 treatment-related toxicity (69% vs 59%). Dual-checkpoint strategies CheckMate 227 supports nivolumab–ipilimumab in PD-L1 TPS ≥1% disease (five-year overall survival 24% vs 14%; HR 0.77). In the descriptive TPS <1% cohort, five-year survival was 19% versus 7%. CheckMate 9LA adds two cycles of chemotherapy to nivolumab–ipilimumab, giving early disease control without committing to prolonged cytotoxic therapy. Six-year overall survival was 16% versus 10% with four-cycle chemotherapy (HR 0.74); grade 3–4 treatment-related events were 48% versus 38% at three years. POSEIDON adds a limited course of tremelimumab to durvalumab–chemotherapy. Five-year overall survival was 15.7% versus 6.8% with chemotherapy (HR 0.76); the durvalumab–chemotherapy arm without tremelimumab had an inconclusive survival estimate. POD1UM-304 supports retifanlimab with histology-based platinum chemotherapy (overall survival 18.1 vs 13.4 months; HR 0.75). It confirms the class effect but does not establish superiority over other chemo-immunotherapy options. The POSEIDON translational analysis suggests that STK11 and KEAP1 alterations may enrich benefit from CTLA-4-containing therapy, but this is not a validated cross-regimen predictive test. Do not convert subgroup biology into a universal mandate; use it only as hypothesis-generating context when discussing a trial. Choose the chemotherapy backbone deliberately Use pemetrexed only for non-squamous disease. Platinum–pemetrexed and carboplatin–taxane are the common backbones; cisplatin causes more nephrotoxicity and emesis, whereas carboplatin causes more thrombocytopenia. The patient's renal function, hearing, neuropathy, marrow reserve and treatment goal matter more than a default preference. After four induction cycles of cisplatin–pemetrexed with response or stable disease, PARAMOUNT showed that maintenance pemetrexed improved overall survival (13.9 vs 11.0 months; HR 0.78) and progression-free survival (4.1 vs 2.8 months; HR 0.62). Treat progression according to prior exposure Re-biopsy or broad plasma genotyping is useful when a new actionable mechanism would change treatment; tissue is required when histologic transformation is suspected. Otherwise choose by prior drugs, histology, residual performance status, toxicity and access. A negative plasma result is not equivalent to a negative tissue assay. CURB tested stereotactic body radiotherapy to every extracranial oligoprogressive site alongside physician-selected standard systemic therapy. The alpha-protected mixed NSCLC/breast-cancer primary analysis improved progression-free survival (7.2 vs 3.2 months; HR 0.53); the prespecified NSCLC subgroup was nominally positive (10.0 vs 2.2 months; HR 0.41), without a reported treatment-by-disease interaction. Pooled overall survival was inconclusive, and 16% had SBRT-attributed grade ≥2 toxicity. REVEL supports ramucirumab 10 mg/kg with docetaxel 75 mg/m² every three weeks after platinum therapy (overall survival 10.5 vs 9.1 months; HR 0.86). Neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, hypertension and bleeding are the practical costs. EAST-LC established oral S-1 as non-inferior to docetaxel for overall survival in an East Asian population (12.75 vs 12.52 months; HR 0.945, upper 95% CI below the 1.2 margin), with much less severe neutropenia and febrile neutropenia. RATIONALE-303 improved overall survival with tislelizumab over docetaxel after platinum chemotherapy (16.9 vs 11.9 months; HR 0.66), with fewer grade ≥3 treatment-related events. This evidence predates routine first-line checkpoint exposure and should not be extrapolated to immune-refractory disease without qualification. TROPION-Lung01 improved progression-free survival with datopotamab deruxtecan over docetaxel (4.4 vs 3.7 months; HR 0.75) but not overall survival (12.9 vs 11.8 months; HR 0.94). Drug-related interstitial lung disease included seven fatal events; the exploratory histology interaction prevents generalisation across squamous and non-squamous disease. BR.21 is historical evidence that erlotinib can prolong survival over placebo in molecularly unselected pretreated NSCLC (6.7 vs 4.7 months; HR 0.70). Modern use of an EGFR TKI requires a susceptible molecular target; this row no longer defines routine salvage treatment.

records.title: EGFR-mutant disease
records.subtitle: NSCLC: metastatic disease · Lung
records.body: Classical exon 19 deletion or L858R Osimertinib monotherapy remains the lowest-burden first-line reference. Intensification with chemotherapy or amivantamab–lazertinib improves efficacy but changes toxicity substantially; the choice should be explicit rather than presented as one ranked ladder. Baseline CNS disease, tempo and patient preference should guide whether to intensify. FLAURA improved progression-free survival (18.9 vs 10.2 months; HR 0.46) and overall survival (38.6 vs 31.8 months; HR 0.80) over gefitinib or erlotinib. Final grade ≥3 adverse events were 42% versus 47%. LUX-Lung 3 is the earlier comparator for afatinib: progression-free survival improved to 11.1 versus 6.9 months over cisplatin–pemetrexed (HR 0.58). The pooled post-hoc survival advantage was confined to exon 19 deletion; L858R showed no benefit, so the two classical variants should not be treated as biologically identical. FLAURA2 added four cycles of platinum–pemetrexed and maintenance pemetrexed. Progression-free survival improved to 25.5 versus 16.7 months (HR 0.62) and final overall survival to 47.5 versus 37.6 months (HR 0.77), with grade ≥3 events in 70% versus 34%. AENEAS2 reproduced the progression-free-survival effect with aumolertinib–chemotherapy (28.9 vs 18.9 months; HR 0.47). Overall survival is immature; grade ≥3 events were 80% versus 35%, driven by chemotherapy-associated myelosuppression. MARIPOSA improved progression-free survival with amivantamab–lazertinib over osimertinib (23.7 vs 16.6 months; HR 0.70) and later overall survival (HR 0.75; three-year survival 60% vs 51%). Grade ≥3 events were 80% versus 52%, and venous thromboembolism occurred in 40% versus 11%. Give prophylactic anticoagulation during the first four months of amivantamab–lazertinib unless contraindicated; vitamin K antagonists are not recommended for prophylaxis. Monitor for thrombosis, rash and interstitial lung disease, plan infusion-reaction prevention before the first dose, and reassess bleeding risk at each visit 34 . For a fit patient with high-volume or rapidly threatening disease, chemotherapy intensification gives the clearest cytoreductive option. Amivantamab–lazertinib avoids platinum cytopenias but adds infusion burden, rash, oedema and thrombosis. Monotherapy remains reasonable when the marginal benefit does not justify either toxicity profile. Sampath (osimertinib + consolidative RT) tested response-adapted radiotherapy to residual disease after 8–10 weeks of osimertinib. Median progression-free survival was 32.3 months in 42 patients, but the uncontrolled design precludes comparison with osimertinib alone; one of two pneumonitis events was grade 4. Progression on osimertinib Distinguish oligoprogression, isolated CNS progression and systemic progression. Local ablative therapy with continued TKI may prolong control in selected oligoprogression, but comparative evidence remains limited and clinical-trial enrolment is preferred. Multisite progression usually requires a new systemic strategy rather than indefinite TKI continuation 36 . MARIPOSA-2 improved progression-free survival over platinum–pemetrexed with amivantamab–chemotherapy (6.3 vs 4.2 months; HR 0.48) and with the amivantamab–lazertinib triplet (8.3 vs 4.2 months; HR 0.44). The experimental arms were not compared with each other; grade ≥3 events were 72%, 92% and 48%. COMPEL continued osimertinib with platinum–pemetrexed after extracranial progression (progression-free survival 8.4 vs 4.4 months; HR 0.43). Enrolment stopped at 98 patients and analyses were descriptive; overall survival was inconclusive. INSIGHT 2 matched MET amplification with tepotinib–osimertinib after first-line osimertinib. The single-arm combination produced a 50% response rate and median progression-free survival of 5.6 months; comparisons with the small tepotinib-alone cohort were descriptive. SACHI randomised savolitinib–osimertinib against chemotherapy in EGFR -mutant, MET -amplified disease. Progression-free survival improved in the third-generation-TKI-naive and intention-to-treat populations (HR 0.34 in each); overall survival was immature and inconclusive. HARMONi-A added the PD-1×VEGF bispecific ivonescimab to platinum–pemetrexed after TKI progression in China. Final overall survival improved to 16.8 versus 14.1 months (HR 0.74), after progression-free survival improved to 7.1 versus 4.8 months (HR 0.46). ATTLAS (KCSG-LU19-04) added atezolizumab–bevacizumab–carboplatin–paclitaxel after relevant TKI progression. Progression-free survival improved to 8.48 versus 5.62 months (HR 0.62), but the unprotected overall-survival estimate was inconclusive (20.63 vs 20.27 months; HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.69-1.46). OptiTROP-Lung04 compared sacituzumab tirumotecan with platinum–pemetrexed after EGFR-TKI progression. Progression-free survival improved to 8.3 versus 4.3 months (HR 0.49) and interim overall survival favoured the antibody–drug conjugate (HR 0.60); the study population was predominantly Chinese. HERTHENA-Lung02 improved blinded-review progression-free survival with patritumab deruxtecan over platinum chemotherapy (5.8 vs 5.4 months; HR 0.77). Evidence remains conference-abstract level; overall survival was immature and adjudicated interstitial lung disease included two fatal cases. TROPION-Lung05 provides single-arm data for datopotamab deruxtecan after targeted therapy and platinum. In the EGFR -mutant subgroup, response was 43.6% and median progression-free survival 5.8 months; drug-related interstitial lung disease occurred in 3.6%, including one fatal event. OptiTROP-Lung03 compared sacituzumab tirumotecan with docetaxel after an EGFR TKI and platinum in China. Progression-free survival improved to 6.9 versus 2.8 months (HR 0.30) and interim overall survival favoured the antibody–drug conjugate (HR 0.49); grade ≥3 treatment-related events were 56.0% versus 71.7% 46 . AURA3 remains the historical model for mechanism-matched treatment after first- or second-generation TKI: in acquired T790M disease, osimertinib improved progression-free survival to 10.1 versus 4.4 months (HR 0.30), including CNS disease. It does not define sequencing after first-line osimertinib. For cytology-confirmed leptomeningeal progression after an EGFR TKI, BLOOM used osimertinib 160 mg daily and reported a 62% leptomeningeal response, 15.2-month response duration, 8.6-month progression-free survival and 11.0-month overall survival. This was a single-arm phase 1 study, so local therapy and dose escalation remain individualised 48 . There is no established standard for acquired C797S. Allelic configuration is mechanistically relevant, but combined first- and third-generation EGFR inhibition is supported only by case-level evidence and should not be presented as a routine regimen. Prefer a clinical trial when available. Small-cell transformation The cohort supports repeat tissue biopsy at progression when transformation is suspected. It included 58 patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC followed by small-cell or high-grade neuroendocrine transformation after EGFR-TKI exposure and 9 patients with de novo or mixed histology; all 59 patients genotyped at first small-cell evidence retained the founder EGFR mutation 49 . Among the 58 transformed cases, median time from advanced NSCLC diagnosis to transformation was 17.8 months (95% CI 14.3–26.2). The small, selected baseline-tissue subsets cannot estimate absolute transformation risk from TP53 or RB1 status. Platinum–etoposide produced an investigator-estimated response in 54% of 46 evaluable patients during pooled post-SCLC treatment; the transformed-only progression-free-survival curve began with 48 patients at risk and median progression-free survival was 3.4 months. Taxane-containing regimens produced an investigator-estimated response in 50% of 20 evaluable patients in a selected, heavily pretreated cohort; transformed-only median taxane progression-free survival was 2.7 months with 17 at risk. No response was seen among 17 checkpoint-inhibitor recipients. Treatment groups were uncontrolled and non-comparative, and assessment intervals were not standardized. CNS progression occurred in 38 of 59 patients with follow-up radiographic information after SCLC diagnosis. Pooled median overall survival was 31.5 months (95% CI 24.8–41.3) from initial metastatic lung-cancer diagnosis and 10.9 months (95% CI 8.0–13.7) from transformation or SCLC diagnosis. The study was retrospective, lacked central pathology and radiology review, used no formal RECIST measurement or confirmation, and reported no regimen-level safety table. Exon 20 insertions and uncommon sensitising variants PAPILLON established first-line amivantamab with carboplatin–pemetrexed for exon 20-insertion disease (progression-free survival 11.4 vs 6.7 months; HR 0.40; response 73% vs 47%). Overall survival was immature; grade ≥3 events were 75% versus 54%. WU-KONG28 established oral sunvozertinib as another first-line option (progression-free survival 10.3 vs 7.5 months; HR 0.65; response 58.9% vs 31.1%). Overall survival was immature and inconclusive at the 38.9%-mature interim analysis (29.8 vs 28.8 months; HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.70-1.40), and CNS efficacy was not established. Use the exact variant and structural class defined in the classification chapter before selecting treatment; activity remains variant-specific and the available evidence is uneven. ACHILLES/TORG1834 supports afatinib over platinum–pemetrexed for sensitising uncommon variants excluding exon 20 insertions and T790M (progression-free survival 10.6 vs 5.7 months; HR 0.421). Mutation-specific response estimates were exploratory without an interaction test. LUX-Lung 2/3/6 pooled (Yang) showed that afatinib activity concentrated in point mutations and duplications (response 71.1%; progression-free survival 10.7 months), while de novo T790M and exon 20 insertions were relatively resistant. This was a post-hoc pooled analysis without formal between-group comparisons. KCSG-LU15-09 (Cho) produced a 50% response rate and median progression-free survival of 8.2 months with osimertinib. Variant-specific response estimates were exploratory and based on small denominators. UNICORN (Okuma) produced a 55% response rate and median progression-free survival of 9.4 months with first-line osimertinib. It was single-arm, and interstitial lung disease occurred in 5 of 40 patients. CHRYSALIS-2 Cohort C (Tomasini) produced a 52% response rate and median progression-free survival of 11.1 months with amivantamab–lazertinib in atypical variants. Grade ≥3 events occurred in 70% and venous thromboembolism in 30%; this remains single-arm evidence.

records.title: ALK-rearranged disease
records.subtitle: NSCLC: metastatic disease · Lung
records.body: Choose a CNS-active ALK inhibitor first line. Crizotinib established targeted therapy but now serves mainly as the control that defines the gains from later agents. Choice among alectinib, brigatinib and lorlatinib should balance intracranial control against toxicity, comorbidity and access. PROFILE 1014 improved progression-free survival with crizotinib over platinum–pemetrexed (10.9 vs 7.0 months; HR 0.45). Final survival was inconclusive with 70% crossover. ALEX improved progression-free survival and reduced CNS progression with alectinib. Final overall survival was not statistically different from crizotinib (81.1 vs 54.2 months; HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.56–1.08). ALTA-1L improved blinded-review progression-free survival and intracranial response with brigatinib. Use the 90-mg seven-day lead-in before 180 mg daily; early-onset interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis occurred in 3%. CROWN provides the longest randomised control: seven-year progression-free survival was 55% with lorlatinib versus 3% with crizotinib (HR 0.19). Hyperlipidaemia, weight gain, oedema, cognitive and mood effects require active monitoring; overall survival remains immature. At progression, determine whether failure is isolated and locally treatable, CNS-predominant, or systemic. Repeat tissue or plasma genotyping can identify an ALK resistance mutation and help select the next inhibitor; suspected transformation requires tissue. Do not switch solely for an asymptomatic lesion that can be locally controlled.

records.title: ROS1-rearranged disease
records.subtitle: NSCLC: metastatic disease · Lung
records.body: The comparative evidence is weaker than for ALK: the usable efficacy studies are single-arm. CNS penetration and the resistance profile therefore carry considerable weight. Use a ROS1 inhibitor rather than extrapolating an ALK sequence, and treat the available response estimates as non-comparative. PROFILE 1001 (ROS1 cohort) produced a 72% response rate and median progression-free survival of 19.2 months with crizotinib in 50 patients. Entrectinib (integrated ALKA/STARTRK) produced a blinded-review response rate of 77% (41/53), 24.6-month response duration and 19.0-month progression-free survival in ROS1-inhibitor-naive disease. Among 20 patients with baseline CNS disease, intracranial response was 55%. The pooled analysis was single-arm; in the 134-patient safety set, grade 3–4 treatment-related events occurred in 34% and treatment-related discontinuation in 5%. TRIDENT-1 produced a 79% response rate, 34.1-month response duration and 35.7-month progression-free survival with repotrectinib in TKI-naive disease. After one prior ROS1 TKI, response was 38%; activity included G2032R and intracranial disease. Taletrectinib is another approved ROS1 inhibitor. The FDA analysis pooled two single-arm studies: response was 90% and 85% in TKI-naive cohorts, and 52% and 62% after one ROS1 inhibitor; monitor liver tests, pulmonary symptoms, QTc, uric acid, myalgia and creatine kinase 64 .

records.title: HER2-mutant disease
records.subtitle: NSCLC: metastatic disease · Lung
records.body: Keep HER2 mutation separate from HER2 overexpression. Current systemic evidence in NSCLC is strongest for activating tyrosine-kinase-domain mutations; IHC-defined overexpression is a different biomarker and does not inherit these results. Confirm which assay and alteration generated the result before choosing therapy. In previously treated HER2-overexpressing, mutation-negative non-squamous disease, the single-arm DESTINY-Lung01 cohorts produced response rates of 26.5% with 6.4 mg/kg and 34.1% with 5.4 mg/kg. Fatal adjudicated interstitial lung disease occurred at both doses; this signal supports further study, not extrapolation of the HER2-mutant indication 65 . DESTINY-Lung01 established activity for trastuzumab deruxtecan 6.4 mg/kg after prior therapy (response 55%; progression-free survival 8.2 months), but interstitial lung disease occurred in 26%, including fatal events. DESTINY-Lung02 supports the 5.4-mg/kg dose: response was 49.0% versus 56.0% with 6.4 mg/kg, while grade ≥3 drug-related events were 38.6% versus 58.0% and interstitial lung disease 12.9% versus 28.0%. The study was not powered for between-dose efficacy comparison. Monitor new respiratory symptoms promptly during trastuzumab deruxtecan. Withhold treatment for suspected interstitial lung disease and permanently discontinue for symptomatic grade ≥2 disease; also monitor full blood count and left-ventricular function. Do not rechallenge after symptomatic disease, and involve respiratory assessment early 68 . Beamion LUNG-1 (zongertinib) produced a 71% response rate, 14.1-month response duration and 12.4-month progression-free survival after prior therapy. Drug-related grade ≥3 events were 17%, and no interstitial lung disease was reported. SOHO-01 (sevabertinib) produced a 64% response rate and median progression-free survival of 8.3 months after prior therapy. Grade 3 diarrhoea occurred in 23%; no interstitial lung disease or drug-related fatal event was reported.

records.title: Other actionable drivers
records.subtitle: NSCLC: metastatic disease · Lung
records.body: KRAS G12C Use a KRAS G12C inhibitor after standard systemic therapy. Neither available randomised trial demonstrated a survival advantage over docetaxel; selection is therefore driven by response, progression-free survival, toxicity, interactions and access. Check concomitant medicines before prescribing because clinically important interactions differ between agents. CodeBreaK 200 improved progression-free survival with sotorasib over docetaxel (5.6 vs 4.5 months; HR 0.66) but not overall survival (10.6 vs 11.3 months; HR 1.01). KRYSTAL-12 (adagrasib) improved progression-free survival with adagrasib over docetaxel (5.5 vs 3.8 months; HR 0.58) and response (32% vs 9%). Overall-survival data were not part of the accepted row. BRAF V600E Dabrafenib + trametinib (BRF113928) supports dabrafenib–trametinib in untreated BRAF V600E disease: response was 64%, median progression-free survival 10.9 months and overall survival 24.6 months. The evidence is single-arm; fever, gastrointestinal toxicity, oedema and transaminitis require active management. Counsel before the first dose. Encorafenib 450 mg daily with binimetinib 45 mg twice daily is an approved alternative for metastatic BRAF V600E NSCLC. Its evidence is also single-arm; monitor ventricular function, ocular toxicity, blood pressure, creatine kinase and hepatic toxicity. Review interacting medicines before treatment 74 . MET exon 14 skipping Both pivotal datasets are single-arm, so line-specific differences are descriptive rather than comparative. Choose between capmatinib and tepotinib by access, prior therapy, comorbidity and toxicity rather than cross-trial response estimates. Neither dataset provides a randomised comparison between agents in this setting. GEOMETRY mono-1 produced a 68% response rate and 12.4-month progression-free survival with capmatinib when treatment-naive, versus 41% and 5.4 months after prior treatment. The confidence intervals overlapped; oedema is the characteristic toxicity. VISION produced a 46% response rate and median progression-free survival of 8.5 months with tepotinib. Monitor oedema, renal function and interstitial lung disease. High-level MET amplification is a different biomarker. In VISION cohort B, 24 patients selected by liquid biopsy had a 41.7% response rate and 14.3-month response duration with tepotinib; the small, prematurely closed single-arm cohort is hypothesis-generating and does not establish routine MET-inhibitor treatment for amplification 77 . High c-MET protein overexpression is distinct from MET exon 14 skipping and genomic amplification. After prior systemic therapy, telisotuzumab vedotin has accelerated approval for non-squamous, EGFR -wild-type disease with strong 3+ staining in at least 50% of tumour cells; this should not be extrapolated to lower expression 78 . RET fusion LIBRETTO-431 established selpercatinib over platinum–pemetrexed–pembrolizumab in the prespecified pembrolizumab-intent population (progression-free survival 24.8 vs 11.2 months; HR 0.46). Overall survival was immature; monitor liver enzymes, blood pressure, QT interval and pulmonary symptoms. AcceleRET Lung was terminated early for sponsor organisational and commercial reasons. Its nominal, truncated analysis reported progression-free survival of 18.7 versus 9.0 months (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.42-0.84); the unprotected overall-survival estimate was inconclusive (not reached vs 39.8 months; HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.65-1.85), with optional crossover to pralsetinib after progression. Infection-related deaths occurred in eight patients versus none. NTRK and NRG1 fusions Larotrectinib is a tissue-agnostic option for an NTRK fusion without a known acquired resistance mutation when disease is metastatic and no satisfactory alternative exists; the adult dose is 100 mg twice daily. Confirm that the fusion is functional and clinically relevant before treatment 81 . Zenocutuzumab is an accelerated-approval option for advanced NRG1 -fusion NSCLC after progression on prior systemic therapy. The indication rests on a multicohort, single-arm study and should not be moved into first line. Confirm the fusion with an appropriate assay and discuss uncertainty about durability 82 .

records.title: Monitoring during metastatic treatment
records.subtitle: NSCLC: metastatic disease · Lung
records.body: Assess symptoms, performance status, weight, organ function and regimen-specific toxicity at each cycle or dispensing visit. Repeat CT of the chest and relevant metastatic sites at intervals that can alter management; an 8–12-week schedule is a practical default when another line remains available, shortened for rapidly progressive disease or a new symptom 36 . Use the same imaging modality and response framework across serial assessments. Brain MRI follows baseline CNS disease, a CNS-active regimen or new neurological symptoms; PET is not a routine serial response tool. Do not continue a regimen through unequivocal systemic progression unless a defined mixed-response or oligoprogression strategy justifies it. Monitoring should be mechanism-specific: EGFR and ALK TKIs: pulmonary symptoms, liver tests, ECG and electrolytes where QT prolongation is relevant; lipids, cognition, mood and weight with lorlatinib. Amivantamab-containing therapy: infusion reactions, rash, paronychia, oedema, albumin, thrombosis and pulmonary symptoms. VEGF-directed therapy: blood pressure, proteinuria, bleeding, thrombosis and wound-healing risk. Antibody–drug conjugates: pulmonary symptoms and prompt CT evaluation for suspected interstitial lung disease; blood count, ocular or mucosal toxicity according to payload and construct. Checkpoint inhibitors: thyroid, liver and renal tests with symptom-directed evaluation for pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathy and other immune toxicity. At progression, record the pattern rather than only the date: oligoprogression, isolated CNS or leptomeningeal progression, and multisite systemic progression lead to different decisions. Reassess goals, performance status, symptom burden and clinical-trial eligibility before choosing another systemic line. Do this before issuing the next prescription.
