records.title: At a glance
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is managed as limited-stage or extensive-stage disease because the first treatment decision is whether definitive thoracic radiotherapy can be delivered safely within one tolerable field. Obtain contrast-enhanced chest and upper-abdominal imaging, brain MRI, and usually FDG-PET/CT before assigning stage; confirm any solitary finding that would change curative intent when feasible 1 . For fit limited-stage disease beyond a small node-negative tumour, use early concurrent platinum–etoposide and thoracic radiotherapy, then offer durvalumab when there has been no progression after concurrent chemoradiotherapy. For extensive-stage disease, use platinum–etoposide with atezolizumab or durvalumab when immunotherapy is suitable, followed by the corresponding maintenance strategy; reassess thoracic and intracranial disease before choosing consolidation. At relapse, treatment depends on the treatment-free interval, performance status, organ function, previous toxicity, and access. Tarlatamab improves survival over standard chemotherapy after platinum and now requires a step-up and monitored-start pathway; lurbinectedin, topotecan, platinum rechallenge, and selected single agents remain useful alternatives. Early palliative care and symptom-directed radiotherapy should accompany, not await failure of, systemic therapy.

records.title: Diagnosis, biology, and staging
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: SCLC accounts for roughly 15% of lung cancers and is strongly associated with tobacco exposure. It is a high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma with rapid proliferation, early dissemination, and frequent initial chemosensitivity followed by resistance. Central bulky disease, mediastinal adenopathy, cough, dyspnoea, weight loss, superior vena cava obstruction, and brain metastases are common clinical patterns. Paraneoplastic presentations include syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, ectopic-ACTH Cushing syndrome, and Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome; hypercalcaemia is less characteristic than in non-small cell lung cancer. Common genomic abnormalities include TP53 mutation, RB1 loss, and MYC amplification, but none currently selects standard first-line treatment in de novo SCLC. Obtain adequate tissue for morphology and neuroendocrine immunophenotyping, while avoiding a nonessential invasive procedure that delays treatment in a clinically unstable patient. Routine broad molecular profiling does not select standard first-line therapy in de novo SCLC. Preserve tissue or plasma for a targeted question when mixed histology, an atypical clinical course, or transformation from a molecularly defined non-small cell cancer is suspected. Record both TNM stage and the practical two-stage category. Limited-stage disease is confined to one hemithorax with regional nodes that can be encompassed safely in a definitive radiation plan; extensive-stage disease exceeds that field or includes distant metastasis. Contralateral mediastinal or ipsilateral supraclavicular nodes may remain limited-stage, whereas malignant pleural or pericardial effusion generally defines extensive-stage disease 2 . Baseline assessment should include performance status, weight, full blood count, renal and hepatic function, electrolytes, and smoking status. Use brain MRI rather than CT when available. Consider pulmonary function testing before definitive thoracic radiotherapy, and assess hearing, neuropathy, and kidney function before cisplatin; carboplatin is reasonable when cisplatin toxicity would compromise treatment delivery.

records.title: Limited-stage disease
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: Small node-negative tumours For clinical T1–2N0 disease, confirm mediastinal node negativity invasively when surgery is contemplated. In a fit patient with a resectable peripheral tumour, lobectomy with systematic nodal dissection followed by platinum–etoposide is an option; sublobar resection is generally inadequate. Unexpected nodal disease or a positive margin usually shifts postoperative management toward multidisciplinary chemoradiotherapy rather than surgery alone. Evidence supporting the surgical pathway Surgery is supported by retrospective selection rather than a modern randomized comparison. In 349 resected cases from the IASLC staging project, five-year survival was 48%, 39%, and 15% for pathological stages I, II, and III, respectively; these stage-conditioned outcomes cannot be compared directly with chemoradiotherapy series 3 . In a National Cancer Database analysis, surgery was associated with median survival of 38.6 versus 22.9 months for stage I disease, but residual confounding remains despite propensity matching. Among completely resected pT1–2N0 tumours, adjuvant therapy improved five-year survival from 40.4% to 52.7% in a separate observational cohort; these estimates support the pathway, not an individualized causal effect 4 5 . Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy followed by systemic therapy is a reasonable curative-intent alternative when a small node-negative tumour is medically inoperable, although randomized SCLC-specific evidence is limited. Do not extrapolate a surgery pathway to bulky or node-positive disease: most stage II–III limited-stage cancers are treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy because occult systemic disease is common even when imaging is apparently confined to the thorax. Stage II–III chemoradiotherapy Use four cycles of cisplatin–etoposide with thoracic radiotherapy starting during cycle 1 or 2 when tumour volume and organ-at-risk constraints permit. Carboplatin–etoposide is acceptable when cisplatin is unsuitable. Early multidisciplinary planning matters because postponing radiotherapy to complete chemotherapy can forfeit local control, while excessively large fields may require an individualized sequential approach to preserve safety. A common cisplatin–etoposide schedule is cisplatin 60–80 mg/m² on day 1 with etoposide 100–120 mg/m² on days 1–3 every three weeks; split cisplatin 25 mg/m² on days 1–3 can reduce hydration burden. Avoid unplanned early dose erosion where possible, but prioritize safe delivery and use current institutional protocols for renal, hepatic, marrow, and radiation-related adjustments. Choose the thoracic radiotherapy schedule Thoracic radiotherapy adds a modest but clinically meaningful survival benefit to chemotherapy. In an individual-patient meta-analysis of 2,103 analysable participants from 13 randomized trials, thoracic radiotherapy reduced the relative risk of death to 0.86 (95% CI 0.78–0.94; p=0.001) and increased three-year survival from 8.9% to 14.3%, an absolute gain of 5.4 percentage points 6 . Twice-daily radiotherapy remains the reference schedule for fit patients. In INT-0096, 45 Gy in 30 twice-daily fractions improved median overall survival from 19 to 23 months and five-year survival from 16% to 26% compared with 45 Gy once daily, at the cost of more grade 3 oesophagitis (27% versus 11%) 7 . CONVERT tested dose-escalated once-daily radiotherapy as a superiority strategy. Once-daily 66 Gy did not improve median overall survival over 45 Gy twice daily (25 versus 30 months; HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.95–1.45; p=0.14). This negative superiority result did not establish equivalence, but supports 66 Gy once daily as an alternative when twice-daily treatment is impractical 8 . Both twice-daily and once-daily guideline-concordant definitive schedules are used; select the schedule according to patient fitness, logistics, field size, organ-at-risk constraints and departmental expertise rather than treating one schedule as universally feasible 2 . Consolidation durvalumab Offer durvalumab to patients with stage I–III limited-stage SCLC, good performance status, and no progression after definitive concurrent platinum-based chemoradiotherapy, once acute toxicity has recovered. The current US regimen is 1,500 mg every four weeks until progression, unacceptable toxicity, or a maximum of 24 months; check the local label and contraindications before treatment 9 . Evidence for durvalumab In ADRIATIC, durvalumab improved median overall survival to 55.9 months versus 33.4 months with placebo (HR 0.73; 98.321% CI 0.54–0.98; p=0.01) and blinded independent-review progression-free survival to 16.6 versus 9.2 months (HR 0.76; 97.195% CI 0.59–0.98; p=0.02), crossing the prespecified interim boundaries 10 . Pneumonitis or radiation pneumonitis occurred in 38.2% with durvalumab and 30.2% with placebo; grade 3–4 events occurred in 3.1% and 2.6%, respectively, with one grade 5 event. Before starting treatment, distinguish resolving radiation injury from infection or immune pneumonitis. The tremelimumab comparison had not crossed its overall-survival boundary and does not establish a consolidation doublet. Atezolizumab does not establish a consolidation class effect Conference-abstract evidence does not establish a consolidation class effect. In ACHILES, one year of atezolizumab after concurrent chemoradiotherapy did not improve overall survival over observation (43.3 versus 38.8 months; HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.76–1.72; p=0.5) or secondary progression-free survival (21.1 versus 15.9 months; HR 0.88; nominal p=0.5). Grade 3–4 toxicity was 34% versus 20% and treatment-related deaths three versus none, but the one-page abstract did not report denominators, formal analysis-set definitions or complete safety detail 11 . Prophylactic cranial irradiation Discuss prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) after a good response to definitive treatment, especially in fit patients with stage II–III disease. In the individual-patient meta-analysis of 987 complete responders, PCI reduced mortality (RR 0.84; 95% CI 0.73–0.97; p=0.01), raised three-year survival from 15.3% to 20.7%, and reduced three-year brain-metastasis incidence from 58.6% to 33.3% 12 . The meta-analysis included only 140 patients with extensive-stage disease, and the stage interaction was not significant. Extensive-stage disease was imbalanced at baseline, 12% with PCI versus 17% without, driven by one component trial and no longer significant after trial adjustment. Neuropsychological testing was sparse, so the pooled evidence neither quantifies long-term cognitive harm nor excludes it. For an older, frail, or cognitively vulnerable patient, brain MRI surveillance is a reasonable alternative after shared decision-making. Explain fatigue, alopecia, memory effects, and the uncertainty around individual neurocognitive risk. The survival evidence arose from complete responders, whereas current recommendations often extend to broader responders; name that extrapolation during counselling rather than presenting the populations as identical.

records.title: Extensive-stage disease
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: First-line systemic therapy For most fit patients, use carboplatin or cisplatin plus etoposide for four cycles with atezolizumab or durvalumab, followed by maintenance with the same checkpoint inhibitor. Do not delay urgent therapy for routine biomarker testing. Select the platinum according to renal function, hearing, neuropathy, emesis risk, marrow reserve, and the practical likelihood of completing treatment. Select the platinum Carboplatin and cisplatin have similar efficacy at a population level. In the COCIS individual-patient meta-analysis of 663 participants, median overall survival was 9.6 versus 9.4 months (HR 1.08; 95% CI 0.92–1.27; p=0.37), progression-free survival was 5.5 versus 5.3 months (HR 1.10; p=0.25), and response rates were 67.1% versus 66.0% 13 . Carboplatin caused more haematological toxicity and cisplatin more non-haematological toxicity in COCIS; 32% of participants had limited-stage disease. This supports toxicity-based platinum selection, not a claim that either drug is globally better tolerated. Etoposide is highly protein-bound and requires regimen-specific hepatic and renal review; avoid an automatic dose rule based on albumin alone. Place the cytotoxic backbone in context Historical randomized comparisons established platinum–etoposide as the cytotoxic backbone. In 437 eligible patients, etoposide–cisplatin, CAV and alternating CAV/EP produced similar median overall survival (8.6, 8.3 and 8.1 months; p=0.425); the trial was not designed to establish equivalence 14 . A Japanese mixed-stage trial likewise found no robust survival advantage for alternating CAV/PE over either regimen alone. The nominal alternating-versus-CAV comparison lost significance after prognostic adjustment, and stage-specific analyses were unpowered without an interaction test 15 . In the Norwegian trial, etoposide–cisplatin improved overall survival over CEV in 436 eligible patients (10.2 versus 7.8 months; one-sided p=0.0004). Limited- and extensive-stage results were descriptive because no treatment-by-stage interaction was reported 16 . Add a survival-positive checkpoint inhibitor In IMpower133, atezolizumab plus carboplatin–etoposide improved median overall survival from 10.3 to 12.3 months (HR 0.70; 95% CI 0.54–0.91; p=0.007) and progression-free survival from 4.3 to 5.2 months (HR 0.77; p=0.02). Confirmed response rates were similar in a post-hoc analysis (60.2% versus 64.4%); this analysis does not identify the mechanism of the survival benefit 17 . In CASPIAN, durvalumab plus platinum–etoposide improved median overall survival from 10.3 to 13.0 months at the primary interim analysis (HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.59–0.91; p=0.0047); the updated comparison was 12.9 versus 10.5 months (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.62–0.91; nominal p=0.0032). The trial permitted cisplatin and did not use maintenance etoposide 18 . At the primary interim analysis, CASPIAN progression-free survival was 5.1 versus 5.4 months (HR 0.78), and confirmed response was 68% versus 58%; these were not alpha-protected efficacy claims in the reported hierarchy and should remain secondary context. In IMpower133, treatment-related grade 3–4 events occurred in 56.6% versus 56.1%, and immune-mediated adverse events in 39.9% versus 24.5%. Do not add tremelimumab routinely: the CASPIAN durvalumab–tremelimumab arm did not cross its prespecified overall-survival boundary. Pembrolizumab improved progression-free survival in KEYNOTE-604 (4.5 versus 4.3 months; HR 0.75; p=0.0023) but its overall-survival result (10.8 versus 9.7 months; HR 0.80; p=0.0164) missed the multiplicity-adjusted boundary of p=0.0128 19 . At 12 months, progression-free survival in KEYNOTE-604 was 13.6% versus 3.1%; response was 70.6% versus 61.8%, an exploratory comparison. Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 76.7% and 74.9%. These secondary signals do not reverse the failed overall-survival hypothesis and should not be used to promote pembrolizumab over an approved survival-positive first-line regimen. Consider regional and selected alternatives Serplulimab plus chemotherapy improved median overall survival to 15.4 months versus 10.9 months in ASTRUM-005 (HR 0.63; 95% CI 0.49–0.82; p<0.001). The enrolled population was predominantly Asian, 68.4% were Chinese, there were no US sites, and non-Asian follow-up was short; use must follow local approval and access rather than cross-trial efficacy ranking 20 . Blinded-review progression-free survival was 5.7 versus 4.3 months (HR 0.48), and response was 80.2% versus 70.4%, but these were exploratory and no formal PFS p-value was reported. Treatment-related grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 33.2% versus 27.6%; immune-related events occurred in 37.0% versus 18.4%, with study-drug deaths in 0.8% versus 0.5%. Other chemo-immunotherapy regimens may be approved regionally. In EXTENTORCH, toripalimab improved median overall survival to 14.6 versus 13.3 months (HR 0.80; p=0.03) and progression-free survival (HR 0.67; p<0.001) 21 . CAPSTONE-1 reported 15.3 versus 12.8 months with adebrelimab (HR 0.72; p=0.0017); neither comparison establishes superiority over atezolizumab or durvalumab 22 . Irinotecan–cisplatin produced longer survival than etoposide–cisplatin in the Japanese JCOG9511 trial: 12.8 versus 9.4 months (relative risk of death 0.60; 95% CI 0.43–0.83; p=0.002). Progression-free survival was 6.9 versus 4.8 months, and response was 84.4% versus 67.5%; these secondary comparisons were nominal 23 . The JCOG9511 result was not consistently reproduced outside Japan. Severe diarrhoea occurred in 16% versus 0%, while neutropenia was less frequent; three versus one treatment-related deaths occurred. These efficacy and toxicity patterns make irinotecan–cisplatin an alternative in selected settings rather than a universal first-line standard. Immediate complications and supportive care Treat symptomatic brain metastases according to neurological urgency, number and volume of lesions, extracranial control, and performance status; do not reflexively substitute PCI for therapeutic brain radiotherapy. Give corticosteroids for clinically significant oedema and involve radiation oncology early. Seizure prophylaxis is not routine without a seizure, while anticonvulsant treatment is indicated after one occurs. Bulky, highly chemosensitive SCLC can cause tumour lysis syndrome, particularly with renal impairment, elevated urate, high lactate dehydrogenase, or extensive liver involvement. Correct electrolytes and dehydration, stratify risk before chemotherapy, use urate-lowering prophylaxis when appropriate, and monitor closely during the first treatment cycle rather than assuming solid tumours carry no lysis risk 24 . Superior vena cava obstruction requires rapid assessment of airway, cerebral, and haemodynamic compromise. Obtain tissue first when safely possible, but do not delay stenting or other urgent stabilization in life-threatening obstruction. Systemic therapy often relieves SCLC-related obstruction promptly; radiotherapy and endovascular stenting are complementary options selected by severity, prior treatment, and expected speed of response 25 . Maintenance after induction Continue atezolizumab or durvalumab after first-line chemo-immunotherapy when disease is controlled and toxicity is acceptable. For patients treated with atezolizumab plus carboplatin–etoposide, maintenance lurbinectedin plus atezolizumab is an additional option after four induction cycles, provided there is no progression and the patient can tolerate increased marrow toxicity. Evidence for lurbinectedin plus atezolizumab In IMforte, 483 induction responders were rerandomized at maintenance. Lurbinectedin plus atezolizumab improved median progression-free survival from maintenance randomization from 2.1 to 5.4 months (HR 0.54; 95% CI 0.43–0.67; p<0.0001) and interim overall survival from 10.6 to 13.2 months (HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.57–0.95; p=0.017), crossing both prespecified boundaries 26 . Grade 3–4 all-cause adverse events occurred in 38% with the combination and 22% with atezolizumab alone; treatment-related grade 3–4 events occurred in 26% and 6%. Response from maintenance randomization was 19% versus 10%, and patients with brain metastases were excluded. The regimen received US approval in 2025 27 . Do not extrapolate across maintenance strategies Verify the current label, blood-count thresholds, dose modifications, and local access before prescribing rather than carrying induction lurbinectedin dosing into maintenance by assumption. Choosing durvalumab for first-line treatment also precludes direct extrapolation of IMforte, because the trial required atezolizumab-based induction and randomized only patients without progression after induction. Do not substitute nivolumab-based maintenance. CheckMate 451 did not improve its primary overall-survival endpoint with nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus placebo (9.2 versus 9.6 months; HR 0.92; p=0.37). The fixed hierarchy then stopped, so nivolumab overall survival and both progression-free-survival comparisons were not formally tested. Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 52.2%, 11.5% and 8.4% with the combination, nivolumab and placebo 28 . Thoracic radiotherapy after systemic therapy Evidence before checkpoint inhibition Post-chemotherapy thoracic radiotherapy is not routine for every patient. In 498 CREST participants, 30 Gy in 10 fractions after chemotherapy and PCI did not significantly improve the primary one-year overall-survival endpoint: 33% versus 28% (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.69–1.01; p=0.066). The nominal secondary two-year survival rates were 13% versus 3% 29 . CREST progression-free survival was 4 versus 3 months (HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.61–0.87; nominal p=0.001), with six-month rates of 24% versus 20%. These secondary results support a local-control discussion in selected responders but cannot repair the missed primary one-year overall-survival endpoint. Evidence with atezolizumab maintenance The randomized evidence predates first-line checkpoint inhibition. In the phase II TREASURE trial during atezolizumab maintenance, thoracic radiotherapy did not improve progression-free or overall survival and increased serious adverse events (61.3% versus 18.2%) and fatal events (19.4% versus 3.0%); early closure made efficacy estimates imprecise but argues against routine unselected use with atezolizumab maintenance 30 . Select patients narrowly Consider consolidative thoracic radiotherapy only after multidisciplinary review for a fit responder with limited residual thoracic burden, controlled extracranial disease, and acceptable lung and oesophageal constraints. The historical Jeremic trial enrolled 206 highly selected patients with an extrathoracic complete response and at least an intrathoracic partial response after three platinum–etoposide cycles; do not generalize its intensive regimen broadly 31 . PCI or MRI surveillance Evidence without mandated baseline MRI For extensive-stage responders, choose between PCI and scheduled brain MRI surveillance through shared decision-making. In 286 EORTC 08993-22993 participants, baseline brain imaging was not mandatory; PCI reduced symptomatic brain metastases (16.8% versus 41.3%; HR 0.27; 95% CI 0.16–0.44; p<0.001) and one-year incidence from 40.4% to 14.6% 32 . EORTC median overall survival was 6.7 versus 5.4 months (HR 0.68; 95% CI 0.52–0.88; nominal p=0.003), with one-year survival of 27.1% versus 13.3%. Because overall survival was secondary and occult baseline brain metastases could have been treated by PCI, the result does not directly answer the modern MRI-negative surveillance question. Evidence with MRI surveillance In the Japanese MRI-surveillance trial, 224 participants had no brain metastases on mandated baseline MRI and underwent MRI every three months in year 1 and at months 18 and 24. PCI did not improve median overall survival (11.6 versus 13.7 months; HR 1.27; 95% CI 0.96–1.68; p=0.094) 33 . The 12-month cumulative incidence of brain metastases was 32.9% with PCI versus 59.0% with observation, while progression-free survival was 2.3 versus 2.4 months (HR 0.98; p=0.75). Salvage brain radiotherapy was used in 46% versus 83%. Attrition in cognitive testing prevents a claim of neurocognitive equivalence. These trials answer different questions: PCI remains reasonable when reliable MRI surveillance or prompt salvage treatment is unavailable, or when a patient prioritizes reducing intracranial relapse. MRI surveillance is reasonable when high-quality follow-up is dependable or cognitive risk is a major concern. The MAVERICK trial is closed to accrual, and no practice-changing primary result has been reported 34 .

records.title: Relapsed or refractory disease
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: Reassess before choosing treatment Confirm progression and distinguish it from infection, radiation change, immune toxicity, or a second primary cancer. Refractory disease never responded to first-line therapy; resistant relapse occurs within three months, sensitive relapse after three months, and late relapse after six months. Use the exact interval from the last platinum dose rather than the label alone when selecting treatment. Prioritize a clinical trial whenever available. For rapidly symptomatic disease, choose a regimen that can start promptly and is deliverable with existing marrow, renal, hepatic, and neurological reserve. Re-biopsy is not routine for typical recurrent de novo SCLC, but it is important when pathology was uncertain, behaviour is atypical, or transformed disease would change a molecularly guided non-small cell pathway. Tarlatamab Randomized evidence Tarlatamab is a DLL3-directed bispecific T-cell engager for extensive-stage SCLC progressing on or after platinum. In DeLLphi-304, it improved median overall survival to 13.6 months versus 8.3 months with physician-selected chemotherapy (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.47–0.77; p<0.001). Twelve-month restricted mean progression-free survival was 5.3 versus 4.3 months; proportional-hazards assumptions were not satisfied 35 . DeLLphi-304 response was 35% versus 20% (relative risk 1.73), median response duration 6.9 versus 5.5 months, and 12-month response durability 41% versus 13%. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related events occurred in 27% versus 62%. Cytokine-release syndrome occurred in 56% with tarlatamab, including 1% grade 3, and ICANS in 6%, with one grade 5 event. Patient-reported chest-pain improvement did not meet the prespecified hierarchy, so physical functioning and global health were not formally tested. That failed hierarchy should temper symptom-benefit claims even though survival and comparative toxicity favoured tarlatamab in this otherwise survival-positive randomized comparison. Earlier single-arm evidence The earlier DeLLphi-301 selected-dose cohort showed a blinded independent-review response rate of 40% among 100 patients (97.5% CI 29%–52%) after platinum and at least one additional line. Median progression-free survival was 4.9 months and overall survival was immature at 14.3 months. Cytokine-release syndrome occurred in 51% at 10 mg, mostly low grade 36 . At 10 mg, grade 3 cytokine-release syndrome occurred in 1% and ICANS in 8%, without a grade 3 or higher ICANS event. Overall grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 59% of the 133-patient safety population, and one treatment-related respiratory-failure death occurred. These uncontrolled dose-expansion results establish activity and safety context, not comparative efficacy. Deliver tarlatamab safely Use the current label rather than the trial-era monitoring schedule: 1 mg on cycle 1 day 1, then 10 mg on days 8 and 15 and every two weeks thereafter. After cycle 1 days 1 and 8, monitor in an appropriate healthcare setting for 22–24 hours and require the patient to remain within one hour of care for 48 hours with a caregiver 37 . Cytokine-release syndrome and neurological toxicity, including ICANS, can be severe or fatal. Give label-specified premedication and hydration, ensure tocilizumab and emergency support are available, and establish a caregiver and proximity plan before the first dose. Later monitoring can be reduced only according to the current label and prior reaction history, not by assuming cycle 1 tolerance. Lurbinectedin, topotecan, and other chemotherapy Lurbinectedin Lurbinectedin is an option after platinum, especially when an outpatient every-three-week regimen is desirable. In the phase II PM1183-B-005 basket cohort, investigator-assessed response was 35.2% (37/105; 95% CI 26.2%–45.2%), median progression-free survival was 3.5 months, and median overall survival was 9.3 months. Grade 3–4 neutropenia occurred in 46% and febrile neutropenia in 5% 38 . Median response duration was 6.2 months when the chemotherapy-free interval was at least 90 days and 4.7 months when shorter; response rates were 45.0% and 22.2%. These were nonrandomized subgroup descriptions without a reported interaction, so the interval informs selection but does not prove differential treatment effect. Dose according to the current product information and adjust for hepatic function, cytopenias, and interacting medicines. Maintain vigilance for myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, extravasation injury, and rhabdomyolysis 39 . Topotecan and selected single agents Intravenous topotecan and cyclophosphamide–doxorubicin–vincristine had comparable activity in a randomized trial: response rates were 24.3% and 18.3% (p=0.285), time to progression 13.3 and 12.3 weeks (p=0.552), response duration 14.4 and 15.3 weeks (p=0.300), and survival 25.0 and 24.7 weeks (p=0.795) 40 . Both regimens require careful marrow monitoring. Seven treatment-related deaths from sepsis or myelosuppression occurred in the trial, and the reported symptom improvements were nominal analyses using nonvalidated measures. Topotecan commonly causes severe neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and anaemia; do not interpret similar median survival as equivalent tolerability. Oral topotecan prolonged median survival to 26 versus 14 weeks compared with best supportive care in patients unsuitable for intravenous treatment (p=0.0104), with a 7% response rate and 44% stable disease. In sensitive relapse, oral and intravenous topotecan produced median survival of 33 and 35 weeks and response rates of 18% and 22% 41 42 . Use the locally licensed formulation and renal dose adjustments. Other selected options include irinotecan, paclitaxel, temozolomide, gemcitabine, or vinorelbine, but evidence is generally noncomparative and choice should be individualized. The small irinotecan studies span heterogeneous populations and do not support a single pooled response estimate; vinorelbine access requirements depend on the formulation and local infusion practice. Platinum rechallenge For platinum-sensitive relapse, platinum–etoposide rechallenge is reasonable. In JCOG0605, 180 highly selected participants relapsing at least 90 days after platinum were randomized to cisplatin–etoposide–irinotecan or topotecan; median overall survival was 18.2 versus 12.5 months (HR 0.67; 90% CI 0.51–0.88; p=0.0079) 43 . The JCOG0605 experimental regimen used cisplatin on days 1 and 8, etoposide on days 1–3, irinotecan on day 8, and prophylactic G-CSF in a two-week schedule for five cycles. Its intensity and substantial toxicity limit generalizability; do not substitute this triplet automatically for a conventional platinum–etoposide rechallenge in a frail patient. GFPC 01-13 directly supports a simpler rechallenge strategy after a response and relapse at least 90 days from first-line platinum–etoposide. Carboplatin–etoposide improved centrally reviewed progression-free survival over oral topotecan (4.7 versus 2.7 months; HR 0.57, 90% CI 0.41–0.73; one-sided p=0.0041), but exploratory overall survival was unchanged (7.5 versus 7.4 months; HR 1.03; nominal p=0.94) 44 . Investigational antibody–drug conjugates Izalontamab brengitecan is an EGFR–HER3 bispecific antibody–drug conjugate with exploratory activity in relapsed extensive-stage disease. In a 52-patient single-arm phase Ib cohort, response was 48.1%, median response duration 4.9 months and median overall survival 12.2 months. The unplanned second-line subgroup response was 72.7%, but no comparator or formal hypothesis test supports a comparative claim 45 . Toxicity and uncertainty currently preclude routine use. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 75%, serious treatment-related events in 50%, dose reduction in 46.2%, treatment delay in 63.5%, and treatment-related death in two of 52 patients. Use should remain within a clinical trial or another governed investigational pathway.

records.title: Follow-up and survivorship
records.subtitle: Small cell lung cancer · Lung
records.body: After curative-intent treatment, use clinical review and contrast-enhanced chest imaging about every three months in year 1, every six months in years 2–3, and then less frequently according to risk and fitness for salvage. After extensive-stage treatment, tailor imaging to active therapy and symptoms. Investigate new focal or neurological symptoms immediately rather than waiting for the next surveillance scan 46 . For patients who do not receive PCI, obtain brain MRI every three months in the first year and every six months in the second year, with further imaging individualized. Surveillance imaging should be offered only when detection could lead to meaningful treatment. Continue smoking-cessation support, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation when appropriate, nutritional care, and assessment for hearing, neuropathy, cognition, mood, and treatment-related cardiopulmonary effects 47 . At every transition, document goals of care and the threshold for stopping disease-directed treatment. SCLC can change quickly, so provide clear contact instructions for new dyspnoea, haemoptysis, confusion, weakness, severe headache, fever, or uncontrolled pain. Integrate palliative care early, and revisit resuscitation preferences before an acute crisis rather than equating symptom care with treatment withdrawal.

records.title: Classification and cell of origin
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas arise from a non-malignant counterpart in normal B-lymphoid development, and recapitulate the characteristic morphological, phenotypic and gene-expression features of that counterpart with some aberrancy. This cell-of-origin concept is fundamental to the classification of B-cell lymphomas. Current classification follows the International Consensus Classification (ICC) and the WHO 5th edition. The major categories: Precursor lymphoid neoplasms: B- and T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia / lymphoblastic lymphoma, both aggressive. Mature B-cell neoplasms: chronic lymphocytic leukaemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, the monoclonal gammopathies and plasma cell neoplasms (including multiple myeloma), hairy cell leukaemia, marginal zone lymphoma (CD5- and CD10-negative), follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma (usually CD10-negative), DLBCL, and the high-grade B-cell lymphomas. Hodgkin lymphoma: classic Hodgkin lymphoma and nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, an uncommon, favourable-prognosis category. Mature T/NK-cell neoplasms: peripheral T-cell lymphoma and its relatives, including primary cutaneous forms. Within the mature B-cell group, classic follicular lymphoma carries the t(14;18)/IGH::BCL2 fusion, and follicular lymphoma grade 3B behaves like DLBCL. Burkitt lymphoma is highly aggressive and rapidly growing, with endemic, sporadic and immunodeficiency-associated forms. The non-Hodgkin lymphomas split by behaviour and cytology: Indolent, small B-cell: follicular, mantle cell and marginal zone lymphoma. Aggressive, large B-cell: DLBCL and Burkitt lymphoma. Many B-cell lymphomas express CD19 and CD20. The characteristic genetic and immunohistochemical markers: Follicular lymphoma: t(14;18); BCL2 and BCL6 positive. Mantle cell lymphoma: t(11;14)(q13;q32); BCL2, cyclin D1 and SOX11 positive. Marginal zone lymphoma: t(11;18) in MALT lymphoma; BCL2 positive. Burkitt lymphoma: BCL2 negative. Three further immunohistochemical markers matter in routine practice: Ki67 as the proliferative index, CD5 for its prognostic significance, and MYC with BCL2 protein expression. Assess MYC and BCL2 protein expression by immunohistochemistry, but identify double-hit disease by FISH: test for a MYC rearrangement and, if present, add BCL2 FISH ( ESMO Lymphomas Guideline (Eyre et al.) ). DLBCL divides by cell of origin into germinal-centre B-cell-like (GCB) and activated B-cell-like (ABC, non-GCB) disease, with the better prognosis in GCB. The split was established by gene-expression profiling: Alizadeh et al. (Lymphochip) separated GCB from ABC disease by unsupervised clustering and the division tracked survival after comparable anthracycline-based chemotherapy (76% vs 16% alive at 5 years across the 40 patients with survival data, nominal p=0.01), though the subgroups were derived post hoc from the expression data and no hazard ratio or multivariable model was reported (Nature 2000;403:503-511). The Hans immunohistochemical algorithm approximates the split, GCB when CD10-positive or BCL6-positive with MUM1-negative, non-GCB when CD10- and BCL6-negative or BCL6-positive with MUM1-positive, but published data on its prognostic effect are contradictory and it should not determine treatment. Cell of origin is prognostic in gene-expression studies, but cell-of-origin-directed frontline strategies have not improved outcomes.

records.title: Staging
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Most non-Hodgkin lymphomas are staged by the Lugano classification, which takes the number and location of tumour sites from the Ann Arbor system. The operational rules: Bone marrow, liver, lung or CSF involvement is generally classified as stage IV. Constitutional symptoms are not incorporated into NHL staging, unlike classic Hodgkin lymphoma, because they are not independently prognostic; the A/B suffix is documented for Hodgkin lymphoma. Limited extranodal extension is marked with the subscript E. Disease involving the spleen counts as nodal rather than extranodal. Bulky disease has no single definition; the cutoff varies by histology, 6 cm for follicular lymphoma and 6-10 cm for DLBCL.

records.title: Response assessment
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: On CT, involvement means a nodal longest diameter above 1.5 cm or an extranodal lesion above 1 cm; on PET-CT it means increased uptake. The routinely PET-avid histologies are Hodgkin lymphoma, DLBCL, follicular lymphoma grade 3 and nodal marginal zone lymphoma; PET avidity is variable in follicular lymphoma grade 1-2, extranodal marginal zone lymphoma and CLL/SLL. Under Lugano response criteria, CT response uses the sum of the products of perpendicular diameters (SPD) of up to 6 target lesions, with measurable disease defined as a node of 1.5 cm or more in longest diameter: Complete response: target nodes regress to 1.5 cm or less in longest diameter, with no extra-lymphatic disease. Partial response: at least a 50% decrease in SPD. Stable disease: less than a 50% decrease in SPD. PET-CT response uses the Deauville score: Complete response: score 1, 2 or 3. Partial response: score 4 or 5 with reduced uptake from baseline. Stable disease: score 4 or 5 with unchanged uptake. Progression: score 4 or 5 with increased uptake, or a new lesion. PET takes precedence: a PET-negative scan is a complete response even when a residual mass is visible on CT.

records.title: Prognostic indices
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: The International Prognostic Index (IPI) has value across all categories of NHL. IPI (five factors, APLES): age over 60, performance status 2 or more, LDH above normal, 2 or more extranodal sites, stage III-IV. Age-adjusted IPI (PLS): performance status 2 or more, LDH above normal, stage III-IV. Stage-modified IPI, for stage I-II disease (ALPS): age over 60, performance status 2 or more, LDH above normal, and non-bulky stage II. Disease-specific indices exist alongside it, including the Follicular Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (FLIPI) and an NK/T-cell lymphoma index, as do treatment-specific scores. The CNS-IPI estimates the risk of CNS relapse.

records.title: Clinical presentation
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Aggressive NHL presents with a rapidly growing mass, constitutional symptoms and tumour lysis syndrome; indolent NHL with a slowly growing nodal mass, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly or cytopenias. Site-specific presentations: GI lymphoma with early satiety, anorexia, weight loss, vomiting or a tumour complication (perforation, obstruction, bleeding); primary CNS lymphoma with headache, seizures, paralysis, cord compression or meningitis; cutaneous lymphoma with rash, plaques, tumours or ulcers. The oncological emergencies of lymphoma include cord compression, lymphomatous meningitis, airway obstruction, pericardial tamponade, superior vena cava obstruction, tumour lysis syndrome and hypercalcaemia.

records.title: Work-up
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: History and examination cover B symptoms (unexplained fever, weight loss, night sweats), lymphadenopathy including the tonsils and testes, personal or family history of lymphoma or other haematological malignancy, prior radiotherapy or chemotherapy, immunosuppression and organ transplantation, and associated disorders such as autoimmune disease and H. pylori chronic gastritis. Diagnosis and staging: Tissue diagnosis usually requires an excisional node biopsy, to provide adequate tissue for histological, immunological and molecular assessment. Histology, flow cytometry and cytogenetics, including MYC and BCL2 FISH to look for double-hit lymphoma. PET-CT for staging. Lumbar puncture and contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain (and spine if clinically indicated) when the CNS-IPI is high (4-6). PET-CT is more likely than bone marrow biopsy to detect marrow involvement with large B-cell lymphoma, and non-avid marrow disease does not confer a worse prognosis (BCSH 2024). A 2014 meta-analysis put PET at moderate sensitivity (88.7%) and high specificity (99.8%) for marrow involvement; about 3% of patients with involvement on biopsy had a negative PET, while 13% with involvement on PET had a negative biopsy. Bone marrow aspiration can still be considered to look for transformation from an indolent lymphoma (though this does not change management in DLBCL), where cytopenias raise concern for MDS that would affect chemotherapy dosing, or where the result would change management, for example apparently localised disease planned for abbreviated treatment in which marrow involvement would upstage and change treatment. Pre-treatment evaluation: full blood count, liver and renal function, LDH, tumour lysis labs including CMP and G6PD (which may affect management), hepatitis serologies, and cardiac assessment with echocardiography.

records.title: Tumour lysis syndrome
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Laboratory tumour lysis syndrome is defined by the Cairo-Bishop criteria; severity is graded on creatinine, cardiac arrhythmias and seizures. Prophylaxis: Rasburicase for high-risk cases, as a single dose of 0.2 mg/kg. Check G6PD first: rasburicase is contraindicated in deficiency, because urate degradation generates hydrogen peroxide that G6PD-deficient red cells cannot neutralise for lack of NADPH, causing oxidative stress, severe haemolytic anaemia and potentially fatal methaemoglobinaemia. Send the uric acid sample on ice, because ex vivo degradation of uric acid by rasburicase yields spuriously low serum levels and a failure to detect tumour lysis. Allopurinol for intermediate-risk cases, 100 mg/m² per dose every 8 hours (maximum 800 mg/day), checking HLA-B*5801 first. Give IV hydration according to renal and cardiac status and monitor urine output closely. Treatment: rasburicase as a single 3-6 mg IV dose; phosphate binders for hyperphosphataemia; treat electrolyte abnormalities urgently, with IV calcium reserved for a specific clinical indication rather than an isolated low calcium result; Resonium and insulin for hyperkalaemia; haemodialysis for uraemia or severe electrolyte abnormalities.

records.title: Limited-stage DLBCL (stage I–II)
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Treatment is stratified by age, bulk and risk: Fit patients younger than 60 with IPI 0 and non-bulky disease (<7.5 cm): four cycles of R-CHOP plus two further rituximab doses; this FLYER approach can also be considered at age 60–80 without additional risk factors ( ESMO Lymphomas Guideline (Eyre et al.) ). Fit patients younger than 80 with limited-stage bulky disease and aaIPI 0: after two cycles, give four total cycles of R-CHOP without further rituximab for CMR (Deauville 1–3), or six cycles plus ISRT for Deauville 4–5 ( ESMO Lymphomas Guideline (Eyre et al.) ). Limited-stage aaIPI ≥1: six cycles of R-CHOP; for IPI ≥2, six cycles of pola-R-CHP is an alternative; three to four cycles of R-CHOP plus ISRT is another option ( ESMO Lymphomas Guideline (Eyre et al.) ). Patients aged 80 or older: six cycles of R-miniCHOP ( LNH03-7B (R-miniCHOP) ). Abbreviated therapy does not apply to selected high-risk extranodal involvement (kidneys or adrenals), patients who cannot receive full-dose R-CHOP, double-hit lymphoma, transformed disease, primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma, or HIV-associated DLBCL. The trial base: SWOG S8736 randomised 401 patients with localised intermediate- or high-grade NHL to 3 cycles of CHOP with involved-field radiotherapy or 8 cycles of CHOP, and long-term follow-up showed no difference (median PFS 11.1 vs 12 years; median OS 13.7 vs 13 years, both non-significant). It generated the stage-modified IPI, in which a score of 0 predicts excellent outcomes. SWOG S0014, a single-arm phase 2 of 3 R-CHOP plus radiotherapy in 56 patients with localised disease and at least one stage-modified IPI risk factor, reported 5-year PFS of 77% falling to 58% at 10 years, so late relapses continue. MInT randomised young patients (18-60, age-adjusted IPI 0-1) to 6 cycles of CHOP-like chemotherapy with or without rituximab. Adding rituximab raised 3-year EFS from 59% to 79% and 3-year OS from 84% to 93%; the trial stopped early for efficacy at its first interim analysis, so the figures likely flatter the benefit, and the widely quoted HR 0.44 (95% CI 0.34-0.59) comes from a multivariable model rather than the primary analysis (Lancet Oncol 2006;7:379-391). Its most favourable subgroup, age-adjusted IPI 0 and non-bulky, did well enough to raise the question of whether such patients could receive less chemotherapy. FLYER tested this approach in 592 patients aged 18-60 with stage I-II non-bulky disease (largest mass below 7.5 cm), normal LDH and performance status 0-1. Four cycles of R-CHOP plus 2 rituximab doses were non-inferior to 6 cycles for 3-year PFS (96% vs 94%; lower limit of the one-sided 95% CI 0%, against a -5.5% margin), with fewer non-haematological adverse events (Lancet 2019;394:2271-2281). Both arms received 6 rituximab doses. Only non-inferiority was tested, and the primary endpoint was changed from event-free to progression-free survival by protocol amendment after the first interim analysis. PET-adapted strategies refine the same territory: LYSA/GOELAMS 02-03 (334 patients, stage I-II non-bulky below 7 cm) randomised radiotherapy after 4 cycles of R-CHOP-14 against R-CHOP alone in interim-PET complete responders: 5-year EFS 92% vs 89% and OS 96% vs 92%, both non-significant, so radiotherapy can be omitted when the PET after cycle 4 is negative; the design does not say whether interim PET allows less chemotherapy. LYSA LNH09-1B (650 patients, age-adjusted IPI 0, age 18-80) reduced treatment to 4 cycles of R-CHOP when the interim PET after cycle 2 was negative: 3-year PFS 92% vs 89% against 6 cycles, meeting the non-inferiority threshold, with 80% of the PET-adapted arm negative at interim PET. SWOG S1001 (132 patients, stage I-II non-bulky below 10 cm) gave one further cycle after a negative PET following cycle 3 (89% of patients): 5-year PFS 87% and OS 89%, but stage-modified IPI still stratified outcome (5-year PFS 97% for score 0, 86% for 1-2, 30% for 3), so it is inconclusive whether chemotherapy can be reduced or radiotherapy omitted in interim-PET-negative high-risk cases.

records.title: R-CHOP delivery
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Standard R-CHOP dosing: Rituximab 375 mg/m² IV day 1, starting at 50 mg/h and escalating in 50 mg/h increments. Adverse effects include hepatitis B and C reactivation, infections, infusion reactions and cytopenias. Cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m² IV day 1 over 30 minutes. Doxorubicin 50 mg/m² IV day 1 over 3-5 minutes. Vincristine dosing must follow the active local R-CHOP protocol, including its maximum-dose rule. Prednisolone 100 mg PO days 1-5. Give co-trimoxazole (one double-strength tablet three times a week) and aciclovir (800 mg twice daily) as prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia and HSV/VZV reactivation.

records.title: Advanced-stage DLBCL (stage II bulky to IV)
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Six cycles of R-CHOP every 21 days is the standard of care; the current ESMO guideline keeps 6 R-CHOP as standard for IPI 0-1 and admits 6 cycles of pola-R-CHP as a first-line option for IPI 2 or more ( ESMO Lymphomas Guideline (Eyre et al.) , Ann Oncol 2025). The backbone was settled in sequence: CHOP over intensified combinations. The SWOG comparison of CHOP against three second-generation regimens (m-BACOD, ProMACE-CytaBOM, MACOP-B) found no survival difference and more grade 5 adverse events with the intensified regimens (NEJM 1993). Rituximab over chemotherapy alone. LNH-98.5 (GELA) added rituximab to 8 cycles of CHOP in patients aged 60-80 and improved 2-year EFS (57% vs 38%, p<0.001) and OS (70% vs 57%, p=0.007), holding at 5 years (OS 58% vs 45%). The primary report found no clinically meaningful increase in toxicity; it was the first trial to show that adding an antibody to chemotherapy improves survival in lymphoma (N Engl J Med 2002;346:235-242). MInT extended the same result to younger good-prognosis patients on 6 cycles. Six cycles, not eight. RICOVER-60 , a 2x2 factorial of 6 vs 8 cycles of CHOP-14 with or without rituximab in 1,222 patients aged 61-80, found rituximab drove the benefit and the extra cycles bought nothing: only 6 cycles of R-CHOP-14 improved 3-year OS against CHOP-14 (78.1% vs 67.7%, a gain of 10.4 points), while the 8-cycle rituximab arm sat 5.6 points below the 6-cycle arm, attributed to more treatment-associated deaths (Lancet Oncol 2008;9:105-116). Every 21 days, not dose-dense. R-CHOP-14 v 21 (NCRI) set out to show 6 cycles of R-CHOP-14 superior to 8 of R-CHOP-21 in 1,080 patients and did not: 2-year OS 82.7% vs 80.8% (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.70-1.15), PFS HR 0.94, with treatment-related deaths 9 vs 3, a threefold numerical excess that did not reach significance (Lancet 2013;381:1817-1826). LNH03-6B asked the same question in patients aged 60-80 with age-adjusted IPI 1 or more (8 R-CHOP-14 vs 8 R-CHOP-21) and also found similar PFS and OS with more toxicity on the 14-day schedule. Rituximab has repeatedly erased chemotherapy advantages that existed before it, whether the variable was the schedule, an added cytotoxic or the dose intensity. Attempts to improve on R-CHOP Five phase 3 trials failed on their primary endpoint. REMoDL-B incorporated real-time cell-of-origin profiling, PHOENIX selected non-GCB disease and ROBUST selected ABC disease; GOYA and CALGB/Alliance 50303 were not cell-of-origin-selected. CALGB/Alliance 50303 : infusional DA-EPOCH-R did not improve PFS over R-CHOP (HR 0.93, p=0.65) and was substantially more toxic (J Clin Oncol 2019;37:1790-1799). GOYA : substituting obinutuzumab for rituximab missed its primary endpoint (3-year PFS 69.6% vs 66.9%; HR 0.92, p=0.39) with more toxicity; a more potent anti-CD20 does not beat rituximab in DLBCL, unlike in CLL and follicular lymphoma (J Clin Oncol 2017;35:3529-3537). REMoDL-B : bortezomib added to R-CHOP after real-time gene-expression profiling missed its primary endpoint (30-month PFS HR 0.86, p=0.28). A 5-year reanalysis reported a nominal treatment-by-subtype interaction favouring ABC and molecular high-grade disease; grade 3 or higher neuropathy was 3.8% versus 2.2% and serious adverse events 50.7% versus 42.5%, so the signal remains hypothesis-generating (Lancet Oncol 2019;20:649-662). PHOENIX : ibrutinib added to R-CHOP in non-GCB disease missed both co-primary endpoints; a prespecified exploratory age interaction showed benefit under 60 and numerical harm at 60 or over, tracking how much R-CHOP each group tolerated (J Clin Oncol 2019;37:1285-1295). ROBUST : lenalidomide added to R-CHOP in prospectively selected ABC-type disease missed its primary endpoint (PFS HR 0.85, p=0.29) (J Clin Oncol 2021;39:1317-1328). Pola-R-CHP Polatuzumab vedotin is an anti-CD79b antibody-drug conjugate with an MMAE payload. POLARIX replaced vincristine with polatuzumab in 879 previously untreated patients aged 18-80 with IPI 2-5, 90% stage III-IV. Pola-R-CHP improved the primary endpoint of PFS (2-year 76.7% vs 70.2%; HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.57-0.95, p=0.02), and the advantage held at 5 years (64.9% vs 59.1%; HR 0.77, 0.62-0.97), but no statistically significant overall-survival advantage had been demonstrated at the 5-year analysis (82.3% vs 79.5%; HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.63-1.15) (N Engl J Med 2022;386:351-363; J Clin Oncol 2025;43:3698-3705). Fewer patients required a subsequent line over 5 years (25.5% vs 35.3%). Grade 3 or higher adverse events were similar (60.7% vs 59.8%), with more grade 3-4 febrile neutropenia (13.8% vs 8.0%). Subgroup analyses suggested more benefit with age over 60, IPI 3-5, ABC subtype and the absence of bulky disease; these are exploratory analyses carrying no interaction test, and the 5-year cell-of-origin split (ABC PFS HR 0.38 vs GCB 1.07) licenses no comparison between subtypes POLARIX . Two further additions have beaten R-CHOP on a surrogate endpoint without a demonstrated survival advantage to date. frontMIND added tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP in high-risk disease (IPI 3-5 or age-adjusted IPI 2-3) and met its primary endpoint (PFS HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.59-0.96, p=0.0194; 2-year PFS 71.1% vs 62.9%); overall survival was formally tested at the interim analysis and not met (HR 0.85, p=0.2703), with the authors calling the data immature, and grade 3 or higher events rose from 76% to 87% (Lancet 2026;407:2528-2541). It is an option in high-risk disease, not an established standard. Upfront transplant consolidation SWOG 9704 randomised high-intermediate and high-risk responders after 5 cycles of (R-)CHOP to upfront autologous transplant or 3 further cycles: 2-year PFS improved (69% vs 55%, p=0.005) but overall survival did not (74% vs 71%, p=0.30), and both were primary endpoints; effective salvage transplantation at relapse explains the gap, and only 150 of 225 randomised B-cell patients received rituximab (N Engl J Med 2013;369:1681-1690). Upfront transplant is therefore not standard consolidation.

records.title: CNS prophylaxis
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Consider baseline CNS screening, imaging plus CSF analysis, in high-risk patients (BCSH guidelines): CNS-IPI 4-6, three or more extranodal sites, or disease at specific sites, testicular, renal or adrenal, intravascular, breast or uterine. The CNS-IPI (Schmitz, JCO 2016) was developed in 2,164 patients treated with R-CHOP in the German High-Grade NHL Study Group and validated in 1,597 DLBCL patients from the British Columbia registry; it adds kidney and/or adrenal involvement to the five IPI factors. Two-year CNS disease rates: 0.6% for score 0-1 (low), 3.4% for 2-3 (intermediate), 10% for 4 or more (high). Whether prophylaxis works is a separate question from who is at risk: Routine CNS prophylaxis is not supported. End-of-treatment high-dose methotrexate (two cycles of 3–3.5 g/m²) may be considered only for highly selected younger patients at ultra-high risk, such as CNS-IPI 5–6 or multiple/high-risk extranodal sites; this is a weak [IV,C] recommendation ( ESMO Lymphomas Guideline (Eyre et al.) ). The largest analysis is Lewis (International CNS Prophylaxis Study Group) : 2,418 high-risk patients, 425 given high-dose methotrexate. Analysed from diagnosis it appeared to lower CNS progression (adjusted HR 0.59, p=0.014), but the estimate is inflated by immortal-time bias; confined to the 1,616 patients in complete response at the end of induction, the association no longer stands (adjusted HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.4-1.3, p=0.30; adjusted 5-year CNS progression 5.0% vs 6.5%), with neither dose nor timing separating (J Clin Oncol 2023;41:5376-5387). IT methotrexate stays in CSF, penetrates brain tissue poorly and does not prevent parenchymal relapse; a systematic review suggested no benefit, on poor-quality evidence (Eyre et al., Haematologica 2020). It may still be considered for older patients with high-risk disease who are unfit for IV methotrexate.

records.title: Radiotherapy for bulky disease
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: RICOVER-noRTh, an amendment cohort of RICOVER-60's 6x R-CHOP-14 arm (n=164), compared involved-field radiotherapy against no radiotherapy to sites of bulky disease (7.5 cm or more) on CT-based imaging: radiotherapy improved PFS and OS, so consolidation can be considered for bulky disease, but there is no randomised evidence that involved-field radiotherapy improves outcomes in the PET-CT era (Held et al., JCO 2014). A population-based analysis of advanced DLBCL treated with R-CHOP and assessed by PET-CT (Freeman et al., Blood 2021) found 72% achieved complete metabolic response, with 3-year time to progression of 83% and OS of 87%, and baseline bulk of 10 cm or more did not appear to affect outcome within the complete responders. Of those not in complete metabolic response, 53% received radiotherapy and their outcomes matched the PET-negative cohort (3-year time to progression 76%, OS 80%); the poorest outcomes were in non-responders who did not receive radiotherapy, yet 30% of that group never relapsed, so radiotherapy consolidation may overtreat. BCSH 2024 advises considering radiotherapy consolidation for bulky disease patient by patient: for example, radiotherapy for an older patient with bulky disease who would not tolerate relapse treatment, against omission in a young patient facing decades of late radiotherapy effects.

records.title: DLBCL in older patients
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Treatment decisions rest on comprehensive geriatric assessment, covering comorbid conditions and functional status. R-miniCHOP attenuates the chemotherapy while keeping full-dose rituximab LNH03-7B (R-miniCHOP) : Rituximab 375 mg/m² LNH03-7B (R-miniCHOP) . Cyclophosphamide 400 mg/m² (instead of 750) LNH03-7B (R-miniCHOP) . Doxorubicin 25 mg/m² (instead of 50) LNH03-7B (R-miniCHOP) . Vincristine 1 mg flat (instead of 1.4 mg/m²) LNH03-7B (R-miniCHOP) . Prednisone 40 mg/m² (instead of 100 mg flat) LNH03-7B (R-miniCHOP) . LNH03-7B (R-miniCHOP) , a single-arm phase 2 in 150 patients over 80 (median age 83), reported median OS 29 months, 2-year OS 59% and 2-year PFS 47%; toxicity was not trivial, with 18% dying during treatment and 12 deaths attributed to treatment, and there is no comparator establishing that attenuation preserves efficacy (Lancet Oncol 2011;12:460-468). A successor LYSA phase 2 (120 patients over 80) added a pre-phase of oral vincristine 1 mg on day -7 and prednisone 60 mg for 4 days before cycle 1, then gave ofatumumab-miniCHOP: 2-year PFS 47% and OS 65% (Peyrade et al., Lancet Haematol 2017). SENIOR, a phase 3 RCT in 249 patients over 80, added lenalidomide to R-miniCHOP and found no benefit (2-year OS 66% vs 65.7%; 2-year PFS 56.2% vs 54.8%).

records.title: The anthracycline-unfit patient
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Refer to cardio-oncology for optimisation of cardiac function where possible. Non-anthracycline options: R-GCVP, substituting gemcitabine for doxorubicin: a single-arm phase 2 in 62 anthracycline-unfit patients gave 2-year PFS 50% and OS 56% (Fields et al., JCO 2014). R-CEOP, substituting etoposide for doxorubicin: a retrospective case-matched analysis of 70 patients reported similar 10-year time to progression and disease-specific survival (53% vs 62%) but lower 10-year OS (30% vs 49%), reflecting the impact of the comorbidity and frailty that made these patients anthracycline-unfit (Alden et al., Blood Advances 2021).

records.title: Double-hit and double-expressor disease
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Double-hit lymphoma is identified by FISH: test for MYC rearrangement, and if rearranged add BCL2 FISH ( ESMO Lymphomas Guideline (Eyre et al.) ). The standard options of R-CHOP and pola-R-CHP remain available. More intensive options: (DA-)R-EPOCH, with etoposide, doxorubicin and vincristine infused over 96 hours. A meta-analysis found R-EPOCH improved PFS over R-CHOP (22.2 vs 12.1 months) but not OS (31 vs 21 months) (Howlett et al., Br J Haematol 2015). In unselected untreated DLBCL, CALGB/Alliance 50303 showed no PFS or OS difference between DA-EPOCH-R and R-CHOP, and its double-expressor subset (MYC 40% or more and BCL2 50% or more by IHC) did not benefit. R-CODOX-M/R-IVAC. Double-expressor disease, MYC and BCL2 over-expressed by immunohistochemistry without the rearrangements, is a different entity, and DEB is its first dedicated phase 3: adding the HDAC inhibitor tucidinostat to R-CHOP (double-hit excluded by protocol) met its primary endpoint of event-free survival (2-year 60.3% vs 50.5%; HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54-0.96, p=0.02) on a higher complete-response rate (73.0% vs 61.8%). The trial was not designed to test survival endpoints, each of which ran the same way on an interval crossing 1, the toxicity concentrates in the maintenance phase (grade 3 or higher 77.4% vs 39.1%), and it was conducted entirely in China (JAMA 2026;335:1684-1693).

records.title: Relapsed or refractory DLBCL
records.subtitle: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Lymphoma
records.body: Assess transplant and CAR T-cell suitability individually using performance status, comorbidity, organ function, disease tempo and treatment goals. The benchmark for refractory disease is SCHOLAR-1 : before CAR T-cell therapy, refractory DLBCL responded to the next line in 26% (complete response 7%) with median OS 6.3 months and 20% alive at 2 years, pooled from 2 phase 3 trials and 2 institutional cohorts (Blood 2017;130:1800-1808). This is the population in which the CAR T-cell trials changed practice. Refractory disease and early relapse in fit patients Anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy is the second-line standard for disease refractory to first-line therapy or relapsing within 12 months; the current ESMO guideline names axicabtagene ciloleucel or lisocabtagene maraleucel here ( ESMO Lymphomas Guideline (Eyre et al.) ). Lymphodepletion is product-specific: axi-cel in ZUMA-7 used cyclophosphamide 500 mg/m²/day plus fludarabine 30 mg/m²/day on days −5 to −3 ( ZUMA-7 ), whereas liso-cel in TRANSFORM used cyclophosphamide 300 mg/m²/day plus fludarabine 30 mg/m²/day for three days ( TRANSFORM ). ZUMA-7 randomised 359 such patients, all intended for transplant, to axicabtagene ciloleucel or platinum-based salvage with transplant in responders. Axi-cel improved event-free survival (median 8.3 vs 2.0 months; HR 0.40; 24-month EFS 41% vs 16%) and response (ORR 83% vs 50%, CR 65% vs 32%); at the interim analysis overall survival had not reached significance (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53-1.01), with 56% of the standard-care arm receiving cellular immunotherapy off protocol and only 36% reaching transplant (N Engl J Med 2022;386:640-654). TRANSFORM tested lisocabtagene maraleucel in the same setting (184 patients): EFS median 10.1 vs 2.3 months (HR 0.35), CR 66% vs 39%; overall survival favoured liso-cel but the data are immature (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.26-1.00, an interval reaching 1), with heavy crossover (Lancet 2022;399:2294-2308). BELINDA is the negative member of the class: tisagenlecleucel missed its primary endpoint (EFS median 3.0 months in both arms; HR 1.07). The failure looks like delivery rather than the drug: median leukapheresis-to-infusion was 52 days, 83% needed bridging chemotherapy, and 26% had already progressed before the week-6 assessment (N Engl J Med 2022;386:629-639). Late relapse in fit patients Chemosensitive late relapse in transplant-fit patients proceeds to salvage chemoimmunotherapy and autologous transplant after a complete metabolic response or Deauville-4 partial metabolic response ( ESMO Lymphomas Guideline (Eyre et al.) ). PARMA established the strategy in the pre-rituximab era: transplantation improved 5-year EFS (46% vs 12%) and OS (53% vs 32%), and chemosensitivity is the gate the whole approach rests on, with 5-year OS 42% in randomised (DHAP-responding) patients against 11% in never-responders (N Engl J Med 1995;333:1540-1545). Salvage regimen choice depends on comorbidities, CNS involvement and setting; the options include R-ICE, R-GDP and R-DHAP. CORAL found R-ICE and R-DHAP interchangeable before transplant (3-year EFS 26% vs 35%, no significant difference on any measure). Three-year EFS was lower after prior rituximab (21% vs 47% without) and in refractory disease or relapse within 12 months (20% vs 45%) (J Clin Oncol 2010;28:4184-4190). NCIC-CTG LY.12 found GDP delivered the same response (45% vs 44%) and transplantation rate as DHAP with lower toxicity and hospitalisation (47% vs 99%) (J Clin Oncol 2014;32:3490-3496). HOVON 44 showed that adding rituximab to reinduction improved disease control (24-month failure-free survival 50% vs 24%) but not overall survival, in a largely rituximab-naive relapse population that no longer exists (Blood 2008;111:537-543). A partial response to salvage can still go to transplant, CAR T-cell therapy (tisagenlecleucel or axicabtagene ciloleucel) or a clinical trial. Transplant-ineligible patients: CAR T-cell therapy For transplant-ineligible patients without prior CAR T-cell exposure: ALYCANTE (axicabtagene ciloleucel, second line, 69 patients, median age 70): complete metabolic response at 3 months 71% (investigator-assessed; central review 66%), median PFS 11.8 months; non-relapse mortality was 10%, every fatal event an infection beyond 2 months after infusion (Nat Med 2023;29:2593-2601). PILOT (lisocabtagene maraleucel, second line, median age 74): ORR 80% with CR 54% among those infused; severe CRS and neurological events were uncommon but grade 3 or higher cytopenias persisted at day 28 in 30% (Lancet Oncol 2022;23:1066-1077). In third line and beyond, the registrational CAR T-cell studies: ZUMA-1 (axicabtagene ciloleucel): investigator-assessed ORR 82% (independent review gave a lower 71%) with CR 54%, median OS not reached with 52% alive at 18 months, in a population whose historical median survival is about 6 months. CRS occurred in 93% (grade 3 or higher 13%) and neurological events in 64% (28% grade 3 or higher); an early partial response should be observed rather than consolidated, since 23 patients converted to complete response without further therapy (N Engl J Med 2017;377:2531-2544). JULIET (tisagenlecleucel): ORR 52% with CR 40% among those evaluated; 111 of 165 enrolled were infused at a median 54 days. Among responders, 65% were relapse-free at 12 months (N Engl J Med 2019;380:45-56). TRANSCEND NHL 001 (lisocabtagene maraleucel): ORR 73% with CR 53% among those infused and evaluable, with low rates of severe CRS (grade 3 or higher 2%) and neurotoxicity (10%) (Lancet 2020;396:839-852). CRS grading scales differ across these trials, so toxicity rates are not directly comparable. Bispecific antibodies The bispecifics in DLBCL are CD20xCD3 T-cell engagers given with step-up dosing in cycle 1 to mitigate cytokine release syndrome. STARGLO : glofitamab plus GemOx against R-GemOx in transplant-ineligible relapsed/refractory DLBCL (transformed disease and double/triple-hit excluded) prolonged survival, the primary endpoint (median OS 25.5 vs 12.9 months, HR 0.62; median PFS 13.8 vs 3.6 months, HR 0.40; CR 59% vs 25%). Glofitamab is fixed-duration, stopping at 12 cycles, after obinutuzumab pre-treatment and 2.5/10/30 mg step-up with dexamethasone premedication; CRS occurred in 44% (grade 3 in 2%), and grade 3 or higher adverse events in 78% vs 41% (Lancet 2024;404:1940-1954). Epcoritamab plus GemOx (EPCORE NHL-2, phase 1b/2, single-arm) gave ORR 85%, median PFS 11.2 months and median OS 21.6 months, with transformed DLBCL (23%) and double/triple-hit disease (10%) allowed; CRS 52%. SUNMO : subcutaneous mosunetuzumab plus polatuzumab against R-GemOx, fixed at 8 cycles without hospitalisation (prior polatuzumab allowed only for late relapse), improved both primary endpoints (ORR 70% vs 40%; median PFS 11.5 vs 3.8 months, HR 0.41); overall survival has not separated at the interim analysis (median 18.7 vs 13.6 months; HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.5-1.2), and CRS was infrequent (26%, grade 3 in 0.7%) (J Clin Oncol 2025;43:3799-3811). As later-line monotherapy: Glofitamab pivotal (NP30179) : fixed-duration glofitamab gave CR 39% and ORR 52% by independent review among all 155 enrolled; among the third with prior CAR T-cell therapy the CR rate was 35%; median duration of complete response was not reached, and CRS occurred in 63% (grade 3 or higher 4%) (N Engl J Med 2022;387:2220-2231). EPCORE NHL-1 : subcutaneous epcoritamab, given until progression, gave ORR 63% and CR 39%, with ORR 54% after prior CAR T-cell therapy; CRS 50% (grade 3 in 2.5%), almost all after the first full dose (J Clin Oncol 2023;41:2238-2247). ELM-2 : odronextamab gave ORR 52% and CR 32% (median duration of response 17.9 months among complete responders), but prior CAR T-cell therapy was a protocol exclusion, so it says nothing about that setting. Grade 3 or higher infection occurred in 39%, with 15 deaths from infection (Nat Cancer 2025;6:528-539). Other antibody-based options Tafasitamab (anti-CD19) plus lenalidomide: L-MIND , single-arm in transplant-ineligible patients after 1-3 prior lines with primary refractory disease excluded, gave ORR 60% and CR 43%, with median duration of response 21.7 months and median PFS 12.1 months (Lancet Oncol 2020;21:978-988). RE-MIND2 , the sponsor's matched real-world comparison, benchmarked conventional therapy at median OS 9.9-11.6 months in this population; its comparisons favour tafasitamab-lenalidomide but score response differently on each side and are not randomised evidence (Clin Cancer Res 2022;28:4003-4017). Polatuzumab plus bendamustine-rituximab: GO29365 roughly doubled complete response (40% vs 18%) and more than doubled survival (median OS 12.4 vs 4.7 months, HR 0.42) against bendamustine-rituximab, on 40 patients per arm in a trial never powered to prove superiority, so the effect size is an estimate (J Clin Oncol 2020;38:155-165). Pola-R-GemOx: POLARGO improved overall survival over R-GemOx in patients ineligible for transplant and CAR T-cell therapy (median OS 19.5 vs 12.5 months, HR 0.60; median PFS 7.4 vs 2.7 months), as a bendamustine-free alternative to pola-BR that may preserve CAR T-cell eligibility (J Clin Oncol 2026, online ahead of print). Loncastuximab tesirine (anti-CD19 antibody-drug conjugate): LOTIS-2 , single-arm after 2 or more lines, gave ORR 48% and CR 24% (median duration of response 10.3 months), as outpatient monotherapy (Lancet Oncol 2021;22:790-800). Brentuximab vedotin plus lenalidomide-rituximab: ECHELON-3 prolonged overall survival at its interim analysis in patients after 2 or more lines ineligible for or pretreated with transplant and CAR T-cell therapy (median OS 13.8 vs 8.5 months, HR 0.63) (J Clin Oncol 2025;43:1061-1072).
